items.explanation: Cumulonimbus (CB) is the answer used in this question. Summer heating can make warm, moist air rise and form cumulus clouds. If the atmosphere allows continued vertical growth, these clouds can develop into cumulonimbus, which can produce showers and thunderstorms. This describes development under suitable conditions; small cumulus does not always become CB.

references.locator: “How does convection affect the weather?” and “Can convection be seen?”; surface heating, rising air, cloud growth, and stronger convection sometimes producing cumulonimbus.

references.title: Met Office — Tornadoes
references.locator: Explanation of thermals: shallow cumulus develops first; an unstable atmosphere allows much deeper ascent and deep cumulus/cumulonimbus.

items.explanation: Apparent drift results from the Earth rotating beneath a gyroscope whose axis tends to maintain its direction in space. To an observer on Earth, the gyro axis appears to change direction. The clue here is Earth’s rotation; transport effects instead involve moving the gyro over the Earth’s surface.

items.explanation: The question bank uses 75° latitude for this item. The principle being tested is reduced compass reliability at high latitudes. A conventional gyrocompass has weaker north-seeking action toward the poles, while a magnetic compass becomes less dependable where the horizontal magnetic field is weak. Actual operating limits depend on the instrument.

items.explanation: A cold front forms where advancing colder, denser air moves beneath and replaces warmer air. The warm air is forced upward, which can produce clouds and precipitation when sufficient moisture is present. The key idea is the advancing cold air undercutting the warm air.

items.explanation: Courses and bearings plotted in ordinary nautical chart work are normally expressed as true directions, referenced to geographic north. Compass-observed bearings must therefore be converted to true before plotting. For a magnetic compass, this means allowing for both deviation and variation.

items.explanation: The jet stream is a band of strong winds high in the atmosphere that helps steer weather systems. Changes in its position and path influence where weather systems move. That steering action explains the bank’s answer that the strong wind current pushes weather systems around the world.

items.explanation: The elapsed time is 25 minutes, or 25/60 hour. Taking the distance as 0.9 nautical mile, drift = distance ÷ time = 0.9 ÷ (25/60) = 2.16 knots. The bank’s answer, 2.1 knots, is the closest listed option. The southwest displacement indicates the current’s set; drift is its speed.

items.explanation: The bank uses one degree as the answer for Polaris as an approximate north reference. Polaris currently lies less than one degree from the north celestial pole, making it useful for finding north. Its precise bearing still varies with the observer’s latitude and time; an accurate bearing requires a Polaris azimuth correction.

items.explanation: When the Sun, Moon and Earth align, the solar and lunar tidal effects reinforce each other. This produces spring tides, with a larger difference between high and low water. That increased tidal range is the meaning of “stronger” in the bank’s answer.

Near tropical coasts, terrain, daytime heating and nighttime cooling can create local winds and changes in cloud or visibility. items.explanation: Declination measures how far a body lies north or south of the celestial equator. It is measured along the body’s hour circle, just as terrestrial latitude is measured from Earth’s equator along a meridian. Azimuth instead describes the body’s direction around the observer’s horizon.

items.explanation: A slack pressure gradient usually means light winds, which allow the ground and nearby air to cool at night without strong mixing. With enough moisture and clear skies, this favours radiation fog. Closely spaced isobars usually imply stronger winds and are less favourable for this process.

Although its range and bearing geometrically define a point, the buoy can move within its mooring or be off station. Treat the plotted position with that uncertainty and check it against fixed features when possible.

items.explanation: Correct a magnetic-compass bearing for both deviation and variation before plotting it as a true bearing. Deviation accounts for the vessel’s magnetism; variation accounts for the difference between magnetic and true north. Their algebraic sum is compass error, so the alternative wording about compass error expresses the same correction.

items.explanation: High pressure commonly brings descending air, which suppresses widespread cloud growth and favours dry, settled weather. Sunny and dry is therefore the expected answer. Local moisture, inversions or season can still produce fog, low cloud or cold conditions, so high pressure is not a guarantee of clear skies.

This tends to increase separation from the storm track. It assumes the semicircle and storm motion have been correctly identified and that sea room permits the manoeuvre.

The keyed answer identifies this component, although an actual vessel also has induced and subpermanent magnetism; it does not possess only one type.

items.explanation: A wet-bulb thermometer measures the temperature reached by a ventilated wetted bulb as evaporation cools it. At 100% relative humidity, evaporation causes no cooling and wet- and dry-bulb readings coincide. The keyed wording refers to that saturation condition; relative humidity normally requires both readings.

items.explanation: Magnetic declination is the angle between true north and magnetic north at a location; mariners also call it variation. items.explanation: Mixed icing forms when clear and rime ice accumulate together from supercooled droplets of differing sizes. Nimbostratus at −10°C can contain suitable liquid water, which explains the keyed choice. Cloud name and temperature alone do not establish a unique icing type; droplet size and liquid-water content also matter.

items.explanation: Hygroscopic particles provide condensation nuclei on which water vapour can form cloud droplets at ordinary atmospheric supersaturations. Sea salt is an important example. items.explanation: Very cold air passing over warmer water can produce an atmospheric structure that bends radar energy downward less than normal. This is sub-refraction: the beam lies higher relative to Earth’s surface, reducing detection of some distant low targets. Warm air over cold water more commonly favours super-refraction or ducting.

items.explanation: Magnetic remanence is the magnetism left in a material after the magnetizing field is removed. It explains why steel in a vessel can keep a permanent magnetic influence on the compass. items.explanation: Use the radar’s performance monitor during the watch to check whether transmitter and receiver performance has deteriorated. Compare its indications with the equipment’s normal reference and follow the maker’s procedure. A display that still paints echoes can have reduced detection capability, so visual appearance alone is insufficient.

items.explanation: A target moving on exactly the same course and at the same speed has zero velocity relative to own ship. Its echo therefore remains in the same place on a relative-motion display. Matching only speed or only course is insufficient, because a relative velocity can still remain.

items.explanation: Zenith distance is measured from the point directly overhead to the body. The rational horizon is 90° from the zenith, so a body on it has a zenith distance of 090°. Equivalently, zenith distance equals 90° minus altitude, and its altitude is zero.

items.explanation: Repeated reflections between the ship’s underside and seabed can return after the first bottom echo. The sounder may record these longer travel paths as extra depth marks, often at multiples of the real depth. Distinguish such multipath echoes from errors caused by sound-speed assumptions or separate transmit/receive transducers.

items.explanation: Magnetic flux describes the total magnetic field passing through a chosen surface. In the line-of-force model, it corresponds to how many field lines cross that area. Flux density instead describes flux per unit area; the two should not be confused when interpreting the stem.

items.explanation: One astronomical unit represents the familiar Earth–Sun distance scale, approximately 149.6 million kilometres. It is the appropriate unit for the mean-distance concept in this question. A parsec and a light-year are much larger units normally used for distances to stars and beyond.

items.explanation: Speed over the ground is the vessel’s speed relative to Earth’s surface. It includes the effect of current, so it may differ from speed through the water. A GNSS receiver can report it directly; it is the rate of movement along the actual ground track, not simply the steered heading.

The symptom alone does not prove pump failure: if local steering still works, the remote control or transfer system requires investigation instead.

Those climatological summaries support choosing an ocean route and anticipating likely conditions. They do not replace current forecasts, ice reports or the detailed nautical charts needed for safe navigation.

items.explanation: An echo sounder times a sound pulse travelling from its transducer to the seabed and back. Depth below the transducer is sound speed multiplied by round-trip time, divided by two. The division is essential because the measured interval includes both the downward and returning paths.

items.explanation: A barograph records atmospheric pressure continuously against time, traditionally with a pen on a clock-driven chart. The resulting trace shows pressure tendency and changes that may be missed between individual readings. A barometer indicates pressure, while a thermograph records temperature rather than pressure.

items.explanation: Using the approximate geographic-range formula gives 2.08 × (√26.0 + √18.25) ≈ 19.5 nautical miles. The closest listed answer is 20 nautical miles. Add both horizon distances because the object’s elevation and the observer’s height each extend the distance at which they can see one another.

items.explanation: Mountain waves are favoured when a stable airflow crosses the ridge and the wind strengthens with height while keeping approximately the same direction. That lets the disturbance propagate above and downwind of the ridge. A strong directional reversal can disrupt or trap the wave rather than supporting this pattern.

references.title: FAA — Aviation Weather Handbook, FAA-H-8083-28B
references.locator: Mountain Weather: stable cross-ridge flow and mountain waves; aviation weather charts: cumulonimbus-related icing and turbulence.

items.explanation: The intended trend is decreasing deviation toward the magnetic equator, where the horizontal directing field is generally stronger. A given permanent ship field then deflects the compass by a smaller angle. This concerns the uncorrected angular effect; the ship’s permanent magnetism does not itself reduce simply because latitude changes.

references.locator: Chapter 8, sections 804–806: Ship’s Magnetism, Magnetic Adjustment, and Effects of Induced Magnetism; section 810, Sources of Transient Error.

items.explanation: At a warm front, advancing warm air rises gradually over colder, denser air along a relatively gentle slope. The broad uplift can create extensive layered cloud and prolonged precipitation. The rainfall depends on available moisture; the cold-air-undercutting description instead characterizes a cold front.

references.locator: Chapter 38, sections 3811–3812, Cyclone and Anticyclone Air Flow and Cyclones and Fronts; Buys Ballot’s Law and frontal pressure troughs.

items.explanation: The intended term is hysteresis, misspelled “Hyteresis” in the keyed option. It describes magnetization lagging behind changes in the applied magnetic field. A material’s magnetic state therefore depends partly on its previous magnetization, which helps explain retained magnetism in iron and steel.

references.locator: Module 1, Magnetic Circuits, printed pages 40–41, Hysteresis and Figure 28: lag of flux behind magnetizing force and residual flux density after the field is removed.

items.explanation: Relative humidity compares the actual water-vapour content with the saturation value at the same temperature, usually expressed as a percentage. Thus 100% means saturation. Because saturation vapour pressure changes with temperature, cooling air can raise relative humidity even when no additional vapour is added.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, section 4007, Humidity: wet- and dry-bulb observations, relative humidity, and use of Volume II Tables 35–36.

items.explanation: Add the clockwise relative bearing to the ship’s true heading: 344° + 090° = 434°. Subtract 360° to bring it within the compass circle, giving 074° true. This assumes the stated course is also the heading used as the reference for the relative bearing.

items.explanation: GPS transmits coded navigation signals on several carrier frequencies, matching the broad wording of the keyed choice. Within a given band, satellites share the carrier and are distinguished by their ranging codes. The answer does not mean that every satellite has its own exclusive radio frequency.

items.explanation: High-permeability material gives magnetic flux a comparatively easy path, concentrating the field within that material. Used around an enclosed space, this diverts flux away from the interior and provides magnetic shielding. The answer concerns redirection of a field, rather than removal of magnetism or retained magnetization.

items.explanation: With 18 miles nominal range and visibility slightly better than the 10-mile nominal standard, the luminous-range diagram gives about 19 miles. The geographic limit is about 2.08 × (√36.5 + √12.75) ≈ 20 miles. Use the smaller limit, so the light becomes visible at approximately 19 miles.

items.explanation: Sailing Directions receive corrections when changes to their coastal and port descriptions are reported, rather than on a predictable schedule for each entry. That is the “sporadic” correction concept intended here. Keep the current edition and apply its issued updates; sporadic does not mean corrections may be ignored.

items.explanation: When the index and horizon mirrors are parallel, the reflected line of sight coincides with the direct line of sight. A correctly adjusted sextant therefore reads 0°. If it shows another reading with the images aligned, that difference is index error and must be allowed for.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)

items.explanation: The bank specifies 3 knots for this item. Speed adjustment compensates gyrocompass error associated with the vessel’s motion over Earth and depends on speed, course and latitude. There is no universal 3-knot threshold for all gyrocompasses; use that figure only for the particular procedure or instrument assumed by the question.

items.explanation: An ocean route should balance safety with passage time using the vessel’s capabilities, forecast weather and expected seas. Favourable winds or currents can save time, but a short or fast route may expose the ship to unacceptable conditions. Compare the complete passage consequences rather than one favourable factor.

items.explanation: Compass points are equal angular divisions of the compass rose, traditionally 32 points of 11.25° each. A point can be divided into half and quarter points; one quarter-point is 2.8125°. The keyed answer refers to that traditional subdivision rather than the separate 0–360° degree notation.

references.title: NOAA — Nautical Chart Manual, Volume 2: Definitions, Abbreviations, and Symbols

items.explanation: An echo sounder transmits a directional sound beam aimed toward the seabed. The beam has a finite width, so it insonifies a footprint that grows with depth. It is not an infinitely thin line; beam width and seabed slope can affect which return the instrument identifies as bottom.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 26, section 2604, Echo Sounders; Chapter 10, section 1015, Using the Fathometer. Acoustic transmission, bottom returns, and depth interpretation.

items.explanation: Choose the route by balancing safety and time for the complete passage. Prevailing winds, currents and seasonal storm risk all contribute, but none alone determines the best route. A diversion that avoids damaging weather can be preferable even when it increases distance, because it may reduce delay and ship stress.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)

items.explanation: Apply the stated approximation as 1.10 × height in feet ÷ 30, then add that many hectopascals to the observed pressure. The addition reduces an elevated instrument reading to approximate sea-level pressure. It is a rough rule; the more accurate correction also allows for air temperature.

items.explanation: The offset is 0.5 nautical mile over two hours, so drift is 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 knot, with set toward the east. This supports the numerical value in the keyed option. Its phrase “knot per hour” is incorrect for current speed; a knot already means nautical mile per hour.

items.explanation: A thunderstorm or cumulonimbus area on a significant-weather chart implies associated hazards including moderate or severe turbulence and icing. The keyed “and/or” wording allows their intensity and occurrence to vary within the cloud. It does not imply that every part of every thunderstorm simultaneously has severe turbulence and severe icing.

items.explanation: The visible horizon is the apparent boundary between sea and sky that limits an observer’s view. It depends on height of eye and atmospheric refraction. The sensible and rational horizons are geometric reference planes; they are not the sea-sky boundary actually seen from the bridge.

items.explanation: A separation line divides traffic lanes used by ships moving in opposite or nearly opposite directions, which is the purpose intended by the keyed answer. It is the boundary within a traffic separation scheme. The stem’s wording is incomplete: the line separates those streams rather than being a route followed by them.

items.explanation: Knowing that a revised edition is due soon helps manage updates and replacement of Sailing Directions. That is the practical point selected by the bank. Until the replacement is issued and carried, continue applying relevant corrections to the current edition; a forthcoming revision does not suspend the need to keep it current.

items.explanation: An isogonal line joins places with the same magnetic declination, or variation. Following one such contour therefore keeps the stated variation value the same for its chart epoch. An agonic line is the special zero-variation case; an isoclinal line instead joins equal magnetic dip.

items.explanation: An orange square or rectangle on a white information marker contains directions or general information, such as a destination or facility. Read the wording inside the shape for the specific message. The shape itself does not designate mid-channel or an anchorage; other regulatory shapes convey restrictions or danger.

items.explanation: Add the 2°E gyro error to 330° gyro to obtain 332° true. With 6°W variation, magnetic heading is 338°. The compass reads 345°, so the compass-to-magnetic correction is 338−345 = −7°. A negative correction is west, giving 7°W deviation.

items.explanation: Intracoastal Waterway aids carry additional yellow symbols: triangles, squares or horizontal bands. These distinguish the ICW route from intersecting waterways, even when ordinary lateral colours could be confusing. Follow the yellow symbol for the ICW passage direction, using the chart to establish that direction.

items.explanation: Add the ship and current velocity vectors. Their directions differ by 50°, so ground speed is √(10² + 0.9² + 2×10×0.9×cos50°) ≈ 10.60 knots. The bank’s 10.7 knots is the closest listed choice; it should be treated as an approximate plotted answer, not an exact arithmetic result.

items.explanation: The First Point of Capricorn lies at the Sun’s southernmost declination. For an observer on the equator, a body at this point crosses the upper meridian south of the zenith. Its bearing at that transit is therefore due south, 180°.

items.explanation: A cold wave is a sustained spell of unusually low temperature relative to the season and locality, lasting a day or longer. It describes a period of weather, rather than a cold front, the cold sector of a depression, or an ocean-current boundary.

items.explanation: On this Northern Hemisphere route, a steadily veering wind indicates the dangerous, right-hand semicircle of an approaching hurricane under the usual stopped-vessel assessment. The storm’s forward motion adds to its rotational wind there, increasing the hazard. Ship movement must be considered when interpreting observed wind changes.

items.explanation: A sling psychrometer carries dry-bulb and wetted-bulb thermometers. Whirling it ventilates both bulbs, while evaporation cools the wet bulb. The temperature difference, used with a psychrometric table or calculation, gives relative humidity; it does not measure liquid density or specific gravity.

items.explanation: A north cardinal buoy is normally a pillar or spar, rather than a can, cone or sphere. Its two black topmark cones both point upward, and black is above yellow on its body. These cardinal-mark conventions are the same in Regions A and B.

items.explanation: Pilotage requires the complete set of equipment needed for the passage to be ready, with clocks synchronized so observations and position plots share the same time reference. Radar, echo sounder, charts and communications each contribute; preparing only a selected pair leaves the wider requirement incomplete.

items.explanation: With separate transmitting and receiving transducers, the sound travels along a sloping path between the transducers and seabed reflection point. Treating half this path as vertical depth introduces a geometric, or Pythagoras, error. It is especially relevant in shallow water when transducer separation is significant.

items.explanation: In Region B, a port-hand lateral mark is green when proceeding in the conventional direction of buoyage. If a topmark is fitted, it is a single green cylinder or can. The cylindrical form identifies the port side, while red cones identify starboard marks.

items.explanation: A charted range gives a known true direction. If it is dead ahead at 185° true while the compass reads 180°, adding 5° brings compass to true: the error is 5° east. This interpretation treats the stated 180° as a compass reading despite its “T” suffix.

items.explanation: An east cardinal buoy is normally pillar or spar in either IALA region. Its identifying features are black-yellow-black bands and two black cones pointing apart. These features indicate that the safe side is east of the mark; a conical buoy shape alone does not identify it.

items.explanation: Relative bearing is measured clockwise from the ship’s head. Add it to the true heading: 355° + 275° = 630°. Subtract one full circle, 360°, to obtain 270° true, placing the mountain due west of the ship.

items.explanation: A running fix advances the first bearing by the distance assumed run before intersecting the second bearing. If actual speed is lower, that bearing is advanced too far. items.explanation: Gain increases the amplification of received echoes, helping weak seabed returns become visible. It also amplifies unwanted noise and other returns. Excessive gain can therefore clutter or confuse the trace; adjust it to obtain a distinct bottom record rather than assuming more gain always improves accuracy.

items.explanation: A south cardinal mark has yellow above black, with both black topmark cones pointing downward. The lower black portion matches the downward-pointing cones. These features are identical in Regions A and B and indicate that navigable water is on the south side of the mark.

references.title: IALA — R1001: The IALA Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: Section 3, Cardinal Marks: South cardinal mark specifications.

items.explanation: The bank selects 70% relative humidity. The wet-bulb depression is 80°F − 74°F = 6°F, used with the dry-bulb reading in a psychrometric table. A standard sea-level table gives about 75%, so the keyed 70% should not be treated as an exact result from the stated temperatures.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Table 35, Relative Humidity: dry bulb 80°F, wet-bulb depression 6°F gives 75%; contrasts with the bank’s keyed 70%.

authorNotes: The selected 70% is preserved, but NGA Table 35 gives 75% for dry bulb 80°F and wet bulb 74°F.

items.explanation: At meridian passage, the body’s corrected altitude gives its zenith distance. Combining that distance with the body’s declination determines the observer’s latitude. The resulting position line is therefore a latitude line; this observation alone does not provide an independent longitude fix.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 19, Sight Reduction: latitude by meridian altitude.

items.explanation: Compass heading is the direction in which the vessel’s bow points, measured clockwise from compass north. It is the heading actually indicated by the compass. Converting it to magnetic or true heading requires the appropriate deviation and variation; adjusting correctors is a separate operation.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “heading” and “compass heading.”

items.explanation: Magnetic susceptibility expresses how strongly a material becomes magnetized in an applied magnetic field: it is magnetization divided by magnetizing field strength. It describes the material’s response, whereas flux describes magnetic field flow and remanence describes magnetization retained after the external field is removed.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: induced magnetism and the response of magnetic materials.

references.title: USGS — Magnetic susceptibility measurements on rocks in Alaska to aid geophysical interpretation
references.locator: Description: susceptibility is the ratio of magnetization M to applied magnetic field intensity H.

items.explanation: At a cold front, advancing colder, denser air wedges beneath warmer air and replaces it at the surface. The displaced warm air rises, often producing cloud and showers. The defining feature is cold air advancing into warm air, rather than simply moving toward a pressure center.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements, section 3812: cyclones and fronts.

items.explanation: From roughly May to September, the Asian summer monsoon brings prevailing southwesterly flow over the China Sea. Strong seasonal heating over Asia helps draw moist maritime air toward the continent. The winter monsoon reverses the broad pattern and is generally associated with northeasterly winds there.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: monsoons and seasonal pressure patterns over Asia.

items.explanation: The selected answer refers to the stage when cloud droplets or ice particles grow large enough to fall. Gravity then overcomes the air motions supporting them, producing precipitation such as rain or snow. Clouds do not literally become unable to “hold” water; particle growth explains the wording.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: precipitation; Chapter 40, cloud formation.

items.explanation: Sailing Directions and Coast Pilot describe the coastal and regional environment relevant to navigation, including prevailing weather and climate. They support passage appraisal with general background information. Current warnings and weather broadcasts supply the changing forecast rather than replacing that climatic and geographical guidance.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Nautical Publications: Sailing Directions and United States Coast Pilot.

items.explanation: Gauss is the traditional centimetre-gram-second unit of magnetic induction, or magnetic flux density. One gauss equals 10⁻⁴ tesla. The bank uses this older unit; tesla is also a valid unit in the SI system, while oersted measures magnetic field strength in the older system.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “gauss.”

authorNotes: The question intends the traditional CGS unit; tesla is also a valid SI unit of magnetic induction.

items.explanation: The cold sector is the part of a depression containing cold air at the surface, outside its warm sector. As occlusion progresses, the warm air is lifted from the surface. After complete occlusion, cold surface air occupies the whole depression in the simplified model used here.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements, section 3812: frontal depressions and occlusion.

items.explanation: The keyed sequence starts with major aid failures, then dangerous wrecks or obstructions, depth changes and floating dangers. Each category can demand prompt action. This is the sequence to recognize in this bank item; the actual urgency of a warning depends on its proximity and effect on the passage.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Nautical Publications: navigational warnings and hazards covered.

authorNotes: The bank’s ordered list is not treated as an official universal priority ranking.

items.explanation: The intended DGPS accuracy is within about a 10-metre radius. A reference receiver at a surveyed position estimates common satellite-ranging errors and broadcasts corrections to nearby users. The figure is a conventional service-level expectation, not a guarantee for every receiver, location or operating condition.

references.title: USCG — Federal Radionavigation Plan 2001
references.locator: Section 3.1.3.1, Maritime Differential GPS: accuracy better than 10 metres (2 drms) for harbour entrance and approach areas.

items.explanation: GPS positions use the World Geodetic System 1984 reference framework. The navigator must check that the chart and receiver use compatible datums, or apply any stated datum correction. A precise satellite fix can otherwise be plotted in the wrong place relative to charted features.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 2, Geodesy and Datums in Navigation; Chapter 22, Satellite Navigation: WGS 84.

items.explanation: Resolve the 1.4-knot current relative to the intended 040° track. Its opposing component is about 1.21 knots, and its cross-track component is 0.70 knot. The corrected 10-knot water-speed vector then gives about 8.76 knots along track, rounding to the keyed 8.8 knots; leeway affects the heading to steer.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 9, Dead Reckoning: current triangles and course to steer.

items.explanation: A station observation reports measured or observed conditions, such as temperature, visibility, pressure and pressure tendency. A prediction for the next twelve hours is a forecast derived from observations and analysis. It is therefore the exception in a list of the observation’s own weather elements.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations: observed weather elements and reporting.

items.explanation: The aclinic line joins places where magnetic dip is zero, so the magnetic field is horizontal. It is the magnetic equator. An agonic line instead joins places of zero magnetic variation, while isoclinal and isogonal lines join equal dip and equal variation respectively.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “aclinic line” and “magnetic equator.”

items.explanation: Thunderstorm downdrafts can strike the surface and spread outward in several directions, creating strong and rapidly changing winds beneath and around the cell. Hazardous wind shear is therefore not confined to one particular side or compass quadrant. Maintain clearance from the whole thunderstorm area.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: thunderstorms, downdrafts and squalls.

items.explanation: A daymark’s distinctive colour and shape let the navigator identify the beacon by day and relate it to the charted buoyage system. Its construction method or size alone is less useful. A light or sound characteristic serves identification when that particular signal is observed.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 7, Short Range Aids to Navigation: daymarks and beacons.

items.explanation: An anticyclone generally brings subsiding, stable air. Over Europe this often gives clear skies or fair-weather cumulus in summer. In winter, weak winds and surface cooling can produce persistent fog or low cloud beneath an inversion, so high pressure does not always mean clear visibility.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: anticyclones, stability and radiation fog.

items.explanation: When the Sun, Moon and Earth align, their tide-producing effects reinforce each other and produce spring tides with a larger tidal range. This occurs around new and full Moon. “Stronger” here refers to this reinforcement; local tidal-current strength also depends on the waterway.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 35, Tides and Tidal Currents, section 3508: variations in range and spring tides.

items.explanation: The prefix fracto- describes ragged or broken cloud fragments. In the wet-weather setting intended here, these fragments often occur below a rain cloud and move rapidly in gusty conditions, supporting the rainy, windy choice. The fragmentary shape by itself does not guarantee strong winds.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations, low-cloud descriptions: stratus fractus and cumulus fractus.

items.explanation: Dew point is the temperature to which air must be cooled, at constant pressure and unchanged water-vapour content, to become saturated. Further cooling can cause condensation. It is a temperature, unlike relative humidity, which expresses the existing vapour content as a percentage of saturation.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations, section 4007, Humidity.

items.explanation: An event marker draws a reference mark on the echo-sounder recording when a timed observation or other event occurs. It helps match the depth trace to the navigation log or position plot. The range and unit selectors change the presentation rather than marking an event.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 26, Bathymetric Navigation: recording depth observations and sounder controls.

items.explanation: A land breeze blows from the land toward the sea, typically at night. Land cools faster than the water, creating relatively higher surface pressure over land and a pressure difference toward the warmer sea. A sea breeze has the opposite direction and is more typical during daytime heating.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements, section 3814: land and sea breezes.

items.explanation: VRM means Variable Range Marker. The operator adjusts this circular marker until its edge touches the target echo, then reads the target’s range. It measures distance from the radar’s reference point; an electronic bearing line supplies the corresponding angular direction.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 23, Radar Navigation: range measurement and variable range markers.

items.explanation: The numeral at the centre of a pilot-chart wind rose gives the percentage of calm observations for that area and month. The surrounding arrows describe winds by direction, frequency and average force. Read the chart legend to interpret arrow lengths and feathers correctly.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Nautical Publications: pilot charts and wind-rose interpretation.

items.explanation: The keyed interpretation is altocumulus indicating instability that may develop into thunderstorms, particularly when the clouds show turreted or castellanus growth. Viewing at a low elevation can make their vertical structure easier to see. Ordinary altocumulus alone is not a reliable thunderstorm prediction.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations, section 4015: middle-level clouds, altocumulus and instability.

items.explanation: Magnetic lines of force form complete loops: outside a magnet they run from its north pole toward its south pole, and inside they return south to north. The key selects the external field for the outward part of this description; the wording mixes the two directions.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses, section 801: magnetic poles and lines of force.

authorNotes: The wording combines external north-to-south and internal south-to-north magnetic field directions.

items.explanation: Sailing Directions, particularly the Planning Guides, provide regional passage-planning information and recommended ocean routes. For a San Francisco–Japan voyage, they support route selection across the ocean. Coast Pilot concentrates on coastal waters, World Port Index on ports, and the Nautical Almanac on celestial data.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Nautical Publications: Sailing Directions Planning Guides and ocean routes.

items.explanation: An aneroid barometer uses a thin, sealed metal capsule that is partly evacuated. Changes in atmospheric pressure compress or expand it, and a linkage magnifies this movement to drive a pointer. It therefore measures pressure without using the mercury column of a mercurial barometer.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations, section 4002, The Aneroid Barometer.

items.explanation: One complete turn of a conventional sextant’s micrometer drum moves the reading through 60 minutes of arc, equal to 1°. The drum allows those minutes and fractions of a minute to be read precisely, while the main arc supplies the whole-degree part of the observation.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 14, Instruments for Celestial Navigation: marine sextant and micrometer drum.

items.explanation: A lightning strike produces a very strong transient magnetic field and can alter the vessel’s existing magnetization, potentially changing its polarity and compass deviation. This is an exceptional, abrupt effect. Changes of cargo, heading history and magnetic latitude can also affect deviation through other mechanisms.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: changes in a vessel’s magnetism and compass adjustment.

items.explanation: The bank selects “.5 kilometres per second”; the intended conventional seawater value appears to be 1.5 km/s, with a leading digit omitted. Echo sounding relies on sound’s round-trip travel time. Actual sound speed varies with temperature, salinity and pressure, so 0.5 km/s should not be treated as the standard value.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 34, The Oceans, section 3410, Sound Speed.

authorNotes: The keyed .5 km/s appears to omit the leading 1 in the conventional 1.5 km/s seawater value.

items.explanation: The keyed 4.0905 seconds is the seconds component of a mean sidereal day, approximately 23 h 56 min 4.0905 s. A 24-hour mean solar day exceeds it by about 3 min 55.9095 s. The bank’s selected number therefore fits the sidereal-day expression rather than the stated difference.

references.title: USNO — Sidereal Time
references.locator: Explanation of the interval between successive meridian crossings: approximately 23h 56m 04s in solar time.

authorNotes: The keyed 4.0905 seconds is the trailing seconds in the sidereal-day length, not the difference from a mean solar day.

items.explanation: True altitude is the angle from the observer’s rational horizon to the centre of the celestial body. Sextant observations must be corrected for instrumental effects, dip and relevant astronomical effects before reaching this value. The rational horizon passes through the Earth’s centre, parallel to the observer’s sensible horizon.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “altitude,” “true altitude” and “rational horizon.”

items.explanation: Tropospheric ducting is the exception intended here: it is chiefly associated with abnormal propagation of near-horizontal radio and radar signals. GPS position errors include satellite or receiver clock error, ephemeris error and poor satellite geometry. Ordinary tropospheric signal delay can still affect GPS and should not be confused with ducting.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 22, Satellite Navigation: GPS error sources; Chapter 21, Radio Waves: refraction and ducting.

items.explanation: The deep scattering layer consists of concentrations of marine organisms that reflect sound. In deep water it can produce a broad, persistent echo trace above the real seabed. A navigator should distinguish this biological return from the bottom rather than accepting every continuous trace as depth.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 34, The Oceans, section 3410: sound scattering and the deep scattering layer.

items.explanation: Minimizing the chance of loss is the safety purpose intended by this choice. Routeing systems organize vessel movements, separate opposing traffic and guide ships around hazards, reducing collision and grounding risks. Environmental protection and efficient traffic flow are also benefits, but safety explains the selected wording.

references.title: IMO — Ships’ routeing
references.locator: Introduction and objective of routeing measures: reduction of collisions and groundings.

items.explanation: A GPS receiver measures the travel time between a satellite’s transmitted timestamp and reception, then multiplies that interval by the speed of light to form a pseudorange. Measurements from several satellites allow the receiver to solve position together with its clock offset; bearings are not the basic measurement.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 22, Satellite Navigation: GPS pseudoranges and receiver position solution.

items.explanation: The bank gives 0.4 m clearance at high water. A rock drying 0.9 m stands 0.9 m above chart datum, so clearance is tide height minus 0.9 m minus vessel draught. The stem omits tide height and draught, preventing independent verification of the keyed value.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 35, Tides and Tidal Currents: chart datum and tidal heights; Chapter 4, drying heights.

authorNotes: No high-water height or vessel draught is supplied, so 0.4 m cannot be independently calculated.

items.explanation: EBL stands for Electronic Bearing Line. It is a rotatable line on the radar display that the operator places through a target echo to read its bearing. Whether that reading is relative or true depends on the display reference and heading information being used.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 23, Radar Navigation: radar bearing measurement.

items.explanation: Trade winds are persistent tropical surface winds flowing toward the equatorial low-pressure belt from subtropical highs. They generally blow from the northeast in the Northern Hemisphere and southeast in the Southern Hemisphere, often maintaining a fairly steady direction for days or weeks over the open ocean.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements, section 3804, The Trade Winds.

items.explanation: Enter the luminous-range diagram with nominal range 14 miles and meteorological visibility 4 miles to obtain roughly 7.5 nautical miles. The geographic range for a 26-foot light and 20-foot eye height is about 11.2 miles. The shorter luminous range controls when the light can first be seen.

references.title: USCG — Light List, Volume VI (2022), Introduction
references.locator: Introduction: luminous range diagram, nominal range and geographic range.

items.explanation: All cardinal marks use a white light when fitted, including the west cardinal. The west mark is identified at night by groups of nine quick or very quick flashes. Its yellow-black-yellow colouring and two black cones pointing together identify it by day in either IALA region.

references.title: IALA — R1001: The IALA Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: Section 3, Cardinal Marks: West cardinal mark light specifications.

items.explanation: Dip, or magnetic inclination, is the angle between the direction of the Earth’s magnetic field and the horizontal plane. It is zero at the magnetic equator and becomes steep toward the magnetic poles. It differs from variation, which is the horizontal angle between true and magnetic north.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: the Earth’s magnetic field and magnetic dip.

items.explanation: The weather adjustment changes the gyro-pilot’s response to short-period yawing caused by waves. In rougher seas it helps avoid excessive rudder activity as the vessel oscillates around the ordered heading. The exact control names vary with the equipment; its purpose is to match steering response to sea conditions.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: autopilot or gyro-pilot controls and sea-state adjustment.

references.title: USCG — Proceedings, Winter 2014–2015: Nautical Deck Queries
references.locator: Page 89, Nautical Deck Queries, question 3: weather-adjustment control and the null band or dead zone before rudder actuation.

items.explanation: On the paper-chart convention intended here, the record of small corrections is entered in the lower-left margin. Notice numbers there show which published corrections have been applied. Compare that record with the latest correction information; the printed edition date alone does not show that a chart is fully updated.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 4, Nautical Charts: chart correction records and edition information.

items.explanation: Compass adjustment neutralizes unwanted magnetic effects from the vessel so that the compass more closely indicates magnetic north. Correcting magnets and soft-iron devices are arranged to oppose the ship’s magnetic influences. The process reduces deviation; it does not eliminate the Earth’s magnetic variation.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “compass adjustment”; Volume I, Chapter 8, magnetic compass compensation.

items.explanation: Speed made good is the direct distance between the departure and arrival positions divided by the elapsed passage time. It describes net progress over that interval. It can differ from speed through the water, or from the average speed along a longer route containing course changes.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 1, Introduction to Marine Navigation: speed made good between two positions.

items.explanation: A sling psychrometer determines relative humidity using paired dry-bulb and wet-bulb thermometer readings. Airflow from whirling the instrument promotes evaporation at the wetted bulb. A larger wet-bulb depression generally indicates drier air, and a psychrometric table converts the readings into relative humidity.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations, section 4007, Humidity.

items.explanation: The keyed sequence puts gale warnings first, followed by buoyage changes, vessels aground near approaches and exercise or underwater-activity areas. These are different threats to assess against the intended route. Their real priority depends on location, timing and exposure; the sequence is not a universal operational ranking.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Nautical Publications: navigational warnings; Chapter 38, weather warnings.

authorNotes: The selected order is retained as a bank sequence rather than an official universal ranking.

items.explanation: Ocean-route selection balances safety and passage time using expected weather, sea conditions and the vessel’s capabilities. The shortest geographical route may expose the ship to delays, damage or dangerous motions. Favourable winds and currents help, but they must be considered within that wider safety-and-time assessment.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 41, Weather Routing: routing objectives and ship/cargo considerations.

items.explanation: The bank uses a cloud thickness of 4,000 feet as the rule of thumb associated with light-or-greater precipitation. The intended idea is that appreciable precipitation usually requires enough vertical cloud depth for particles to grow. This figure is a study convention, not a universal meteorological minimum.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations: cloud formation and precipitation-producing clouds.

authorNotes: No universal 4000 ft cloud-thickness threshold is asserted; the number is the bank’s study rule.

items.explanation: A fix is obtained when two or more independent lines of position observed at nearly the same time intersect. Their common point establishes the vessel’s position, subject to observational error. A running fix instead combines observations at different times by transferring an earlier position line.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: fixes from intersecting lines of position.

items.explanation: With water-vapour content broadly unchanged, daytime warming raises the saturation vapour pressure and lowers relative humidity. Nighttime cooling reverses that effect, so relative humidity rises. Air-mass changes, rain and local moisture sources can alter the pattern, but warming by day and cooling at night explain the keyed trend.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations, section 4007: temperature and relative humidity.

items.explanation: Applying estimated current and wind effects to a course-and-speed DR plot gives an estimated position. It improves the predicted location by allowing for movement not represented by the vessel’s own progress through the water. It remains an estimate until checked by independent position observations.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 9, Dead Reckoning: estimated position and allowances for wind and current.

items.explanation: The master gyro transmits its heading to a repeater, where a servo system drives the display to match. Feedback compares the repeater’s indicated position with the received heading and corrects any difference. Repeaters should still be checked against the master because transmission or alignment errors can occur.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses, section 821: master gyrocompass and repeaters.

items.explanation: With the range aligned dead ahead, the true heading is the range’s 185° bearing. If the compass indicates 180°, the required correction is +5°, or 5° east. The calculation assumes “180 T” in the stem means a compass reading; two genuinely true headings would not establish compass error.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: checking compass error against a charted range.

authorNotes: Interpret the stated 180 T as a compass reading for the intended compass-error calculation.

items.explanation: The intended interval is weekly, matching the regular Notice to Mariners issues used to maintain paper charts and publications. Navigators apply the notices affecting their holdings and record them. Urgent warnings and electronic-chart updates also need attention and should not be postponed until a weekly correction session.

references.title: NGA — Notice to Mariners
references.locator: Weekly Notice to Mariners and chart-correction information.

items.explanation: Precipitation is the factor selected here: its long-term amount, seasonal distribution and type help describe a place’s climate. Climate is based on sustained weather patterns rather than one observation. Temperature, humidity and winds also contribute, so precipitation should not be understood as the only climatic factor.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: weather versus climate; Chapter 41, climatological routing information.

authorNotes: Precipitation is keyed but all four listed factors help describe climate.

items.explanation: North by west is 348.75°, almost the same as the 349° heading, so the current adds about 2 knots to 18.5 knots. In 45 minutes the ship makes about 15.375 miles. Bearings 45° and 90° relative to the course make distance off at the second bearing approximately equal to that run.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting, section 1021: running-fix geometry; Chapter 9, current allowance.

items.explanation: Lightning heats a narrow channel of air extremely rapidly. The sudden heating causes explosive expansion and a pressure wave, which is heard as thunder. The flash is seen before the sound arrives because light travels much faster than sound through the atmosphere.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements, section 3825, Atmospheric Electricity.

items.explanation: An isotherm joins points having the same temperature at a specified level and time. It shows the spatial temperature pattern on a weather chart. Isobars join equal pressure, isallobars join equal pressure change, and isoclinic lines relate to equal magnetic inclination rather than temperature.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “isotherm.”

items.explanation: The approximate middle-cloud band used here is 6,500–20,000 feet, including altocumulus and altostratus. These are broad classification heights rather than fixed limits for every latitude and season. Low clouds generally have lower bases, while the high-cloud family occurs above the middle band.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations, sections 4013 and 4015: cloud levels and middle-level clouds.

items.explanation: A normal GPS three-dimensional solution needs measurements from at least four satellites. The receiver solves four unknowns: latitude, longitude, altitude and its clock offset. Thus the bank’s four theoretical position lines refers to four independent satellite-ranging measurements, rather than only three spatial coordinates.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 22, Satellite Navigation: GPS position and receiver clock solution.

items.explanation: A small-scale chart covers a large geographical area with comparatively little detail, making it suitable for planning and following a long ocean passage. As the vessel approaches coastal dangers or harbour waters, larger-scale charts provide the detail needed for closer navigation.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 4, Nautical Charts: chart scale and sailing charts.

items.explanation: Arc of visibility is the horizontal sector over which a light can be seen, bounded by its limiting bearings. Here the bank specifies visibility from seaward. Read charted sector limits and obstructions as well as range; being within the arc does not guarantee the light is visible in poor weather.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “arc of visibility”; Volume I, Chapter 7, light sectors.

items.explanation: The selected workflow begins by identifying the new chart in the correction log, recording its folio details and applying outstanding corrections, then updating the catalogue. Finally reconcile the old edition with the replacement. If it has been superseded, mark or withdraw it from navigational use rather than continue maintaining it as current.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Nautical Publications: maintaining charts, corrections and new editions.

authorNotes: Reconcile or withdraw a superseded chart rather than interpreting “correct the old edition” as authority to keep navigating with it.

items.explanation: Satellite position fixing uses simultaneous ranges, or more precisely pseudoranges, to several satellites with known positions. Their geometric intersection provides the receiver’s location after allowance for clock error. The receiver does not need to measure the satellites’ bearings or angular elevations to obtain the normal GPS fix.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 22, Satellite Navigation: satellite ranging and position solution.

items.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, stand facing the wind and the lower-pressure centre lies generally to your right. With your back to the wind it would be to your left. Surface friction makes winds cross isobars toward the low, so this rule gives an approximate direction rather than an exact bearing.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: Buys Ballot’s law and pressure circulation.

items.explanation: An articulated beacon is buoyant but tethered directly to the seabed, typically through a jointed or tensioned arrangement. It stays over essentially one charted position instead of swinging around a mooring in a buoy’s watch circle. Its identifying signal can be a light or daymark.

references.title: IALA — International Dictionary of Marine Aids to Navigation: Articulated beacon
references.locator: Definition 8-4-0065: floating mark secured to a sinker through a joint or buoyancy-tensioned cable.

items.explanation: A relative bearing of 180° places the lighthouse directly astern. Add this to the true heading: 357° + 180° = 537°. Removing one full revolution gives 177° true, the reciprocal of the ship’s 357° heading.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 1, Introduction to Marine Navigation: relative and true bearings.

items.explanation: A steadily veering wind is the usual indication of the dangerous semicircle in the Northern Hemisphere when assessed without the vessel’s own motion distorting the observation. On this route that is the right-hand side of the hurricane’s track, where forward motion strengthens the rotational wind.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 39, Tropical Cyclones, section 3913: wind shifts and dangerous semicircle.

items.explanation: The bank places the compass card on the sensitive element, the north-seeking assembly that provides the compass’s directional reference. Its graduations let that reference be read against the ship’s heading index. Particular mechanical arrangements differ between gyrocompass designs, so this terminology belongs to the design assumed here.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: mechanical gyrocompass construction and the directional element.

authorNotes: Assume the mechanical gyrocompass construction and component naming intended by the bank.

items.explanation: An iceberg extends deep into the water and responds to currents below the surface, while relatively shallow sea ice is more influenced by surface currents and wind. They can therefore travel in markedly different directions. Neither a common direction nor a fixed relationship between their speeds should be assumed.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 32, Ice Navigation: movement of sea ice and icebergs.

items.explanation: The east cardinal’s body is black above and below a broad yellow middle band: black-yellow-black. Its two black cones point apart, matching black at the top and bottom. This combination distinguishes it from the yellow-black-yellow west mark and indicates safe passage to the east.

references.title: IALA — R1001: The IALA Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: Section 3, Cardinal Marks: East cardinal mark colours and topmarks.

items.explanation: First establish that the Sailing Directions volume is the latest edition for the required area. Applying supplements and later Notices to Mariners is only useful once the underlying edition is current. Then check all applicable updates so that new information is not added to an already superseded volume.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Nautical Publications: Sailing Directions editions and maintenance.

items.explanation: The elevated pole is whichever celestial pole lies above the observer’s horizon. It is the north celestial pole for a northern observer and the south celestial pole for a southern observer. Its altitude is equal to the observer’s latitude in magnitude, neglecting small observational effects.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “elevated pole.”

items.explanation: Sailing Directions is the bank’s choice because much of its geographical and descriptive information changes relatively slowly. Lists of Lights and radio-aid publications contain operational details that may change more frequently. Infrequent change does not remove the need to check the edition and apply published updates.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Nautical Publications: Sailing Directions and maintenance of navigational publications.

items.explanation: For the wet-and-dry-bulb hygrometer intended here, lower humidity permits faster evaporation from the wetted bulb. That evaporation removes heat, lowering its temperature below the dry-bulb reading. The greater cooling generally means drier air; high humidity reduces evaporation and narrows the temperature difference.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations, section 4007: psychrometers and evaporative cooling.

items.explanation: A wet bulb measures the temperature reached as evaporation cools its wetted surface toward saturation. At 100% relative humidity there is no net evaporative cooling, so wet- and dry-bulb readings coincide. This saturation relationship explains the bank’s wording; the wet bulb alone does not directly display relative humidity.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations, section 4007: wet-bulb temperature and saturation.

authorNotes: Interpret the keyed wording as the saturation relationship underlying wet-bulb temperature.

items.explanation: Correcting sextant altitude for index error and dip gives the apparent altitude above the sensible horizon in the convention used here. Further corrections, including refraction and relevant parallax or semidiameter, are needed for the body’s true central altitude. Computed altitude instead comes from calculation for an assumed position.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “apparent altitude”; Volume I, Chapter 19, altitude corrections.

items.explanation: A semicircle is the conventional symbol used here for a dead-reckoning position. Label it with the time so it identifies where the ship is predicted to be from course, speed and elapsed time. A fix or estimated position uses a different plotting symbol and evidential basis.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 9, Dead Reckoning: plotting symbols for DR positions.

items.explanation: The keyed remedy is to bleed trapped air through the designated vent valves at the pump and cylinders, following the maker’s procedure, particularly after refilling. Air compresses and disrupts smooth hydraulic operation, causing noise and poor response. The vents should not simply be left open during normal operation.

references.title: USCG — Steering Gear Piping Systems, Plan Review Guideline E1-26
references.locator: Steering-gear piping arrangements: means for removing air and restoring hydraulic operation.

items.explanation: Begin the DR plot at a known fix and record its time. From that departure point, advance the vessel using the steered course, speed and elapsed time. Regular plotted positions and updates at course or speed changes maintain the plot, but the initial timed fix is the essential starting reference.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 9, Dead Reckoning: starting and maintaining the DR plot.

items.explanation: The bank refers to the traditional 32-point compass rose, in which each point represents 11.25°. On a chart, the inner rose normally references magnetic north while the outer rose references true north. Degree graduations and named compass points are alternative ways of expressing direction around the same full circle.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 4, Nautical Charts: compass roses; Chapter 1, compass points and degrees.

authorNotes: The question intends traditional 32-point direction divisions; the inner chart rose normally supplies magnetic bearings.

items.explanation: Plan to cross a traffic lane on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the general traffic flow. This makes the crossing intention clearer and limits exposure to lane traffic. The rule specifies heading, so current may cause the actual ground track to cross at a different angle.

references.title: USCG — Navigation Rules, International and Inland
references.locator: International Rule 10(c), crossing traffic lanes.

items.explanation: The magnetic compass card remains aligned with compass north while the vessel and its lubber line turn around it. Thus a starboard alteration changes the heading shown at the lubber line. Relative to the vessel the card appears to turn to port, but its directional reference remains north.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses, section 801: magnetic compass principle and freely rotating card.

items.explanation: In the normal U.S. direction of buoyage, numbers increase when entering from seaward. Green port-hand buoys carry odd numbers and can buoys identify that side; red starboard-hand buoys carry even numbers. This is the Region B arrangement, often remembered as red to starboard when returning.

references.title: USCG — Light List, Volume VI (2022), Introduction
references.locator: Introduction: U.S. lateral buoyage, numbering and conventional direction of buoyage.

items.explanation: AIS exchanges digital messages in the maritime VHF band, normally using AIS 1 at 161.975 MHz and AIS 2 at 162.025 MHz. These radio channels carry identity, position and other vessel data. They are separate from the microwave bands used by marine radar.

references.title: USCG — International VHF Marine Radio Channels and Frequencies
references.locator: AIS 1 and AIS 2 entries: 161.975 MHz and 162.025 MHz.

items.explanation: A range charted as 243° defines the intended track in that true direction when proceeding toward the range. Keeping its marks vertically aligned shows that the vessel is on the range line. A heading adjustment may still be needed for current or leeway to remain on that track.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: ranges and steering along a charted range.

authorNotes: Assume travel toward the range along its 243°true alignment; heading may require current/leeway allowance.

items.explanation: The answer assumes a head-up radar display, with the ship’s heading represented by 000° at the top. Bearings read clockwise from that heading are relative bearings. Own ship at the centre alone does not establish the reference, since a centred display can also be north-up.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 23, Radar Navigation: relative bearings and head-up presentation.

authorNotes: Assume head-up presentation, since centring own ship alone does not establish the bearing reference.

items.explanation: A barograph records atmospheric pressure continuously, traditionally with a pen driven by aneroid capsules on a time-marked chart. The trace reveals pressure tendency and sudden changes as well as the pressure itself. A thermograph records temperature, while an ordinary barometer gives a pressure reading without a continuous record.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations, section 4003, The Barograph.

items.explanation: Trapped air bubbles in the hydraulic oil compress and expand as pressure changes, disturbing flow through the pumps and piping. The resulting pulsations can produce vibration and excessive noise, described as air hammer in the selected choice. This is the mechanism the question asks for, rather than only the symptom or remedy.

references.title: USCG — Steering Gear Piping Systems, Plan Review Guideline E1-26
references.locator: Hydraulic steering-gear piping: air removal and satisfactory operation.

items.explanation: The normal requirement is to check and test the steering gear within 12 hours before departure. This verifies readiness while the vessel is still in a position to address defects. Tests cover the applicable steering arrangements and associated indications, alarms and communications, subject to permitted short-voyage exemptions.

references.title: IMO — Survey Guidelines under HSSC, 2021, Resolution A.1156(32)
references.locator: SOLAS survey checks for operational requirements: steering-gear tests under SOLAS V/26.

items.explanation: The transducer converts an electrical pulse into a sound pulse transmitted through the water. On reception it converts the returning acoustic energy into an electrical signal. The sounder then uses the echo’s travel time to calculate depth; a transmitter or amplifier alone does not perform this energy conversion.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 3, Hydrography: echo sounding and transducers; Chapter 26, Bathymetric Navigation.

items.explanation: The Sun’s motion relative to nearby stars is approximately toward Vega at about 12 miles per second, the bank’s selected value. This is a motion of the solar system through its stellar neighbourhood. It is separate from the much greater speed of the Sun’s orbit around the Galaxy.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, Navigational Astronomy, section 1307, The Sun: motion toward Vega.

items.explanation: The outer ring of a typical nautical-chart compass rose gives true directions measured clockwise from true north. The inner ring normally gives magnetic directions using the charted variation. Use the correct ring when plotting a true course or bearing so that variation is not inadvertently applied twice.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 4, Nautical Charts: compass roses and true/magnetic direction.

items.explanation: The conventional main-steering-gear requirement is capability to move the rudder through 35° to port and 35° to starboard under the specified service conditions. The associated timed test is from 35° on either side to 30° on the other within 28 seconds, not 35° to 35° in that time.

references.title: IMO — Survey Guidelines under HSSC, 2021, Resolution A.1156(32)
references.locator: Main steering gear: SOLAS II-1/29, rudder movement from 35° each side and timed 35° to 30° movement.

items.explanation: The mercury ballistic is the connected system of mercury reservoirs used in certain mechanical gyrocompasses. As the assembly tilts, mercury movement applies a gravity-controlled torque, causing precession that helps the gyro seek the meridian. The rotor is the spinning wheel, rather than this liquid-control system.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses, section 819, Gyrocompass Operation.

items.explanation: The bank’s 100-metre radius reflects the older civilian GPS accuracy convention associated with Selective Availability. A 95% figure is a statistical performance measure rather than a boundary guaranteed for every fix. Modern GPS commonly performs substantially better, so this historical value should not be read as a universal present-day limit.

references.title: USCG — GPS Frequently Asked Questions
references.locator: Historical Standard Positioning Service accuracy and Selective Availability.

authorNotes: Treat 100 m as the historical civilian GPS/Selective Availability convention.

items.explanation: If the vessel travels more slowly than the speed used to transfer the first bearing, the plotted run is too long. In the stated same-landmark, coast-parallel case, the constructed running fix is too far offshore. The actual vessel is therefore closer to the coast than the fix indicates.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting, section 1019: head-current error in running fixes.

items.explanation: The cold wall is the sharp temperature boundary separating warm Gulf Stream water from much colder water to its north and west, associated with the Labrador-current system in this description. It is an oceanic temperature front, rather than an atmospheric cold front or a spell of cold weather.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 36, Ocean Currents: North Atlantic currents and the Gulf Stream cold wall.

items.explanation: A characteristic is the identifying feature or signal of an aid to navigation. It can be visual, audible or electronic, such as a light’s colour and rhythm, a sound pattern or a radar-beacon response. The complete definition therefore extends beyond electronic signals alone.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “characteristic”; Volume I, Chapter 7, identification of aids to navigation.

items.explanation: The bank selects Aero radio beacon as the exception. However, U.S. Chart No. 1, S16, depicts an aeronautical radiobeacon with a magenta circle, so that exclusion is not a reliable charting rule. Use the exact symbol specified by the chart’s producing authority when applying corrections.

references.title: NGA/NOAA — U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section S, Radar, Radio and Satellite Navigation Systems and Services: aeronautical radio beacons and marine radar/radio symbols.

authorNotes: Peer review: Explanation endorses excluding an aeronautical radiobeacon from magenta-circle symbols. U.S. Chart No. 1, S16 (page 106), actually depicts that beacon with a magenta circle; the keyed exception therefore needs an explicit qualification.

items.explanation: At long range, moderate or heavy rain is more likely than light precipitation to produce a detectable ship-radar echo. Such returns can help identify and follow showers when weather information is limited. Echo strength and detection also depend on range, radar settings and beam height, so absence of a return does not prove clear weather.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 23, Radar Navigation: rain clutter and propagation; Chapter 38, weather observation.

items.explanation: Speed of advance is the speed intended to be made good along the planned track over the Earth. Known or predicted current is allowed for when selecting the corresponding engine speed and heading. It is a planning quantity; speed made good describes progress achieved between actual positions.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “speed of advance”; Volume I, Chapter 1, speed definitions.
