items.explanation: Evaporation changes liquid water into water vapour and absorbs latent heat from the water and its surroundings. This energy is required to separate water molecules into the gaseous state. Condensation is the reverse process: vapour becomes liquid and releases latent heat.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: water-vapour phase changes and latent heat.

items.explanation: DGPS corrects ranging errors shared with a nearby reference station, including much atmospheric error and, historically, Selective Availability. It does not improve the geometric arrangement of the satellites. Geometric dilution of precision therefore remains a separate limitation, making that statement the false one.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 22, Satellite Navigation: differential corrections and dilution of precision.

items.explanation: The bank gives a northward set of 360° true and drift of 0.4 knot. Set and drift normally come from the vector difference between the final fix and the DR position over 1.25 hours. The stated coordinates and uncorrected compass course do not independently reproduce this keyed result.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 9, Dead Reckoning: current found by comparing a DR position with a fix.

authorNotes: The keyed north 0.4 kn current is retained, but missing compass correction and inconsistent motion data prevent its independent derivation.

items.explanation: An ex-meridian sight observes a body near, rather than exactly on, the meridian and applies a correction to obtain meridian altitude. The bank selects an observation within 28 minutes before local apparent noon. That is its stated working interval, not a universal limit independent of latitude, declination and required accuracy.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “ex-meridian altitude” and “ex-meridian observation.”

authorNotes: Treat 28 minutes before LAN as the bank’s working interval, not a universal ex-meridian limit.

items.explanation: The compass card carries the graduated directions and turns with the compass’s directional element. Its reading is taken at the lubber line aligned with the vessel’s fore-and-aft axis. The bowl houses the mechanism, while the binnacle supports and protects the compass installation.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary, “compass card”; Volume I, Chapter 8, magnetic compass construction.

items.explanation: A line squall can bring a sudden pressure rise as its dense, cool downdraft air spreads across the surface. This pressure jump is the indication selected here. Gusts, a wind shift and ragged dark cloud can accompany the passage, so the other descriptive signs are not necessarily absent.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: line squalls, thunderstorm outflow and pressure changes.

items.explanation: Absolute humidity describes the mass of water vapour in a unit volume of air, commonly expressed in grams per cubic metre. It concerns vapour actually present, not suspended water droplets or the maximum possible vapour content. Relative humidity compares the existing vapour pressure with saturation at that temperature.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, Weather Observations, section 4007, Humidity.

items.explanation: The bank identifies extensive snowfall as the least typical choice because very cold polar air generally contains little moisture, especially over polar interiors. Mirage effects, false horizons and sea smoke are familiar polar hazards. Snowfall and severe blowing snow can still occur, particularly in maritime polar regions.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 33, Polar Navigation: polar weather; Chapter 38, fog and mirage.

authorNotes: Interpret extensive snowfall as least typical of cold dry polar interiors, not impossible throughout the polar regions.

items.explanation: Latitude affects local gravity and therefore the height of a mercury column for a given pressure. Instrument height also matters when reducing pressure to sea level. These explain the keyed latitude-and-height corrections; a complete mercurial-barometer reduction may additionally require temperature and instrument corrections.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Tables 31–33: barometer corrections for height, gravity and temperature; Volume I, section 4004.

items.explanation: Doppler shift is the principle of the older Transit satellite navigation system: the received frequency changes as a satellite approaches and recedes, allowing position to be inferred. Modern GPS instead primarily measures signal travel times to obtain pseudoranges; the bank's broad wording needs that historical distinction.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Satellite navigation: Transit Doppler navigation versus GPS pseudoranging.

authorNotes: The bank intends the historical Transit system, not modern GPS.

items.explanation: Admiralty Tide Tables provide predicted times and heights of high and low water, together with instructions for secondary ports. Select the correct locality and date, apply the specified time convention, and ensure the tidal heights and charted depths use compatible vertical datums.

references.title: UKHO — Admiralty Tide Tables
references.locator: Daily high and low-water times and heights for standard ports; time/height differences for secondary ports.

items.explanation: The oersted is the centimetre–gram–second electromagnetic unit of magnetic field strength. In that system, a field of one oersted exerts a force of one dyne on a unit magnetic pole. This historical unit differs from magnetic flux density, commonly expressed in teslas or gauss.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigation glossary: oersted and magnetic field strength.

items.explanation: When the Sun is directly overhead at local apparent noon, the observer's latitude equals the Sun's declination. At the September equinox the declination is approximately zero, so the intended latitude is 00°00′, the equator. The exact equinox instant varies with the year.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Celestial navigation: meridian altitude, latitude and solar declination.

authorNotes: Treat the stated September date as the equinox and zero solar declination.

items.explanation: Leaving the buoy 100 yards to port requires passing slightly west of its present bearing of 178°. The offset angle is arcsin(100/3000), approximately 1.91°. Adding this gives 179.91°, or about 180° true, assuming no current or leeway changes the intended track.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Terrestrial navigation: passing distance and relative geometry; calculation from supplied data.

authorNotes: Bearing is true; yards govern the ratio; current and leeway are neglected.

items.explanation: The selected definition describes absolute humidity: the mass of water vapour per unit volume of air, often expressed in grams per cubic metre. Humidity more generally means atmospheric water vapour; relative humidity instead compares the existing vapour with saturation at the same temperature.

references.title: NOAA NESDIS — What Is Humidity?
references.locator: Absolute humidity versus relative humidity.

items.explanation: Light wind of 3 knots and almost clear skies favour strong overnight ground cooling, so the bank selects this combination. However, air initially at 8°C must cool to its 3°C dew point before fog forms. The listed conditions favour radiation fog but do not guarantee sufficient cooling.

references.title: National Weather Service — Radiation Fog
references.locator: Light winds, clear skies and overnight cooling; saturation still required.

authorNotes: Enough overnight cooling occurs to reach the 3°C dew point.

items.explanation: Differential GPS uses a reference receiver at a surveyed position to estimate errors affecting nearby GPS measurements. Corrections sent to the vessel can reduce common satellite, clock and atmospheric errors. The benefit depends on correction age, coverage and receiver compatibility; local multipath can remain.

references.title: GPS.gov — GPS Accuracy
references.locator: Differential corrections and sources of positioning error.

items.explanation: Atmospheric stability depends on how the surrounding, or ambient, temperature changes with height. Compare this environmental lapse rate with the cooling rate of a rising air parcel. A parcel that remains warmer than its surroundings can continue rising; a colder parcel tends to sink back.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Atmospheric stability and environmental lapse rate.

items.explanation: A constellation is a recognised grouping of stars traditionally associated with a figure such as an animal or person. The stars appear grouped when viewed from Earth, although they can lie at very different distances and need not form a physical cluster.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigational astronomy: constellations.

items.explanation: The bank favours entering at a weak or rotten section of the pack edge, as nearly perpendicular as practicable. A square approach reduces sideways contact and exposure of the hull. Entry still requires low controlled speed, suitable ice conditions and compliance with the vessel's operating limits.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Ice navigation: entering pack ice and ice-edge approach.

items.explanation: A buoy is a floating aid held by a mooring, so wind, current and its watch circle can displace it from the charted position. It may also drag or be moved. Identify it carefully and cross-check with fixed marks or other independent position information.

references.title: USCG — Light Lists and Coast Pilots, General Information
references.locator: General information: floating aids may be off station.

items.explanation: The radar heading marker must represent the ship's fore-and-aft direction. Check its bearing alignment against a reliable reference and correct the installation or bearing-alignment setting according to the equipment instructions. An uncorrected offset makes radar bearings systematically wrong, even when measured ranges remain useful.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Radar navigation: bearing alignment and heading marker.

items.explanation: Plot a new dead-reckoning position at each change of course or speed, marking the time of the change. That point starts the next leg of the DR track. Otherwise, applying the new movement to the wrong interval accumulates an avoidable plotting error.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Dead reckoning: plotting at course and speed changes.

items.explanation: The geographic range is approximately 1.17 × (√26 + √20) = 11.2 nautical miles, close to the bank's table-based 11.1-mile answer. With 14-mile visibility the light's luminous range exceeds this, so curvature and the two heights limit the expected first sighting.

references.title: USCG — Light Lists and Coast Pilots, General Information
references.locator: Geographic range and luminous range; distances-of-visibility table; calculation from supplied heights.

authorNotes: Normal terrestrial refraction and approximate visibility-table values.

items.explanation: At otherwise similar temperature and pressure, increasing seawater salinity increases the speed of sound. An echo sounder converts pulse travel time into depth using an assumed sound speed. If the actual speed differs from that assumption, the indicated depth requires correction.

references.title: NOAA — Surveying and Mapping
references.locator: Sound speed varies with temperature, salinity and pressure.

items.explanation: Snow develops from ice crystals growing in clouds; crystals can collide and join into larger flakes. This aggregation explains the selected answer. For snow to reach the surface without melting completely, the temperature profile beneath the cloud must also be sufficiently cold.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Snow and snowflake formation.

items.explanation: The current sets 150° from the intended 040° track. Its opposing component is 1.4 cos 150° = −1.21 knots, while its cross-track component is 0.70 knot. Cancelling that component leaves about 9.98 knots along track through the water, giving approximately 8.76, or 8.8 knots, over ground.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Sailing calculations: current vectors and course made good; calculation from supplied data.

authorNotes: The vessel compensates leeway and the cross-track current; engine speed is treated as speed through water.

items.explanation: VDR means Voyage Data Recorder. It records selected bridge, navigation and ship-system information so investigators can reconstruct events surrounding an incident. Depending on the installation, this includes time, position, movement, bridge audio and other data; it supports investigation rather than replacing navigation monitoring.

references.title: IMO — Voyage Data Recorders
references.locator: Purpose and performance standards: sequential recording of preselected ship-equipment and command/control data for casualty investigation.

items.explanation: The bank describes the mid-latitude tropopause as lower and warmer in winter. Its height commonly decreases in colder seasons, and a lower tropopause can have a higher temperature than a higher summer one. Actual height and temperature vary with latitude, weather systems and the local atmospheric profile.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather elements: tropopause and seasonal variation.

references.title: NWS — Prevailing Winds
references.locator: JET STREAM: deeper summer troposphere and higher summer tropopause; seasonal height variation.

authorNotes: General mid-latitude seasonal description, not a universal temperature rule.

items.explanation: A west cardinal mark is yellow with one broad black horizontal band around its middle: yellow–black–yellow. Its two black cone topmarks point toward each other. The mark indicates that the named, western side is the side on which to pass, subject to charted conditions.

references.title: IALA — R1001, The Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: Section 3.3.4: west cardinal mark colours and topmarks.

items.explanation: A constellation is a traditional star pattern resembling a person, animal or other figure. Apparent closeness on the sky does not mean the stars are neighbours in space. Modern astronomy also defines constellations as bounded regions of the celestial sphere.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigational astronomy: constellations.

items.explanation: Air and sea exchange heat across their surface: warmer air can transfer heat to cooler water, while warm currents can also warm the air above them. The bank selects warming by warm air masses, but the direction of heat transfer depends on the actual temperature difference.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Oceanography and weather: air–sea heat exchange.

authorNotes: The stem intends air masses; heat-transfer direction depends on air and sea temperatures.

items.explanation: The selected answer refers to the traditional 32-point compass rose. Its points divide the full circle into 11¼° intervals and can be related to the degree graduations. A chart's true and magnetic roses additionally distinguish geographic north from magnetic north; printed layouts vary.

references.title: NGA/NOAA — U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section B: directions and compass roses.

items.explanation: A fix establishes position from suitable observed position information, usually intersecting independent lines of position or a reliable electronic solution. It is generally more dependable than a position advanced only by course and speed. Its actual accuracy still depends on observation errors, geometry and equipment integrity.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Piloting: fixes, estimated positions and errors.

items.explanation: A triangular daymark is used for one side of the lateral marking system; square or rectangular dayboards identify the other side in systems such as U.S. buoyage. The triangle is therefore a valid listed shape, but lateral marks are not all triangular.

references.title: IALA — R1001, The Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: Lateral marks and shape conventions; compare triangular lateral daymarks.

items.explanation: On an analogue echo sounder, register intensity controls how strongly the recorder marks the paper. Set it high enough to show a clear seabed trace without excessive darkening or noise. It improves readability of the record but does not correct sound-speed or transducer-offset errors.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Depth measurement: analogue echo-sounder recorder controls.

items.explanation: The bank selects the Flinders bar, which compensates for effects of vertically induced magnetism. Its usual fore-and-aft arrangement produces no useful deviation signal for setting it on magnetic north or south. However, other correctors also require particular headings, so this wording does not uniquely establish the answer.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses: Flinders bar and compass corrector heading dependence.

authorNotes: The bank key is not uniquely established by the stated headings and list of correctors.

items.explanation: Middle clouds are commonly placed at approximately 6,500–20,000 feet in temperate latitudes, including altostratus and altocumulus. These are approximate cloud-base ranges rather than rigid worldwide limits. The heights change with latitude and season, and individual cloud layers can extend beyond the category's typical band.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather elements: cloud classification and altitude.

items.explanation: A squall line or its gust front can bring an abrupt rise in pressure as cooler, denser downdraft air spreads beneath the storm. A sudden wind shift and increase in wind may accompany it. The pressure jump is a useful sign of passage, rather than a guarantee of improving conditions.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Squall lines, gust fronts and pressure changes.

items.explanation: A west cardinal mark has a yellow–black–yellow body, with one broad black band in the middle. Its two cone topmarks point together, and its white light, if fitted, shows groups of nine quick or very quick flashes. Pass on the western side using the chart to assess clearance.

references.title: IALA — R1001, The Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: Section 3.3.4: west cardinal mark.

items.explanation: Assuming the hurricane centre travels directly toward the stated position, time equals distance divided by speed: 600 nautical miles ÷ 20 knots = 30 hours. This is a constant-track calculation; a moving vessel and changes in storm speed or direction alter the actual encounter time.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents — Glossary
references.locator: Knot as nautical mile per hour; supplied distance–speed calculation.

items.explanation: Relative humidity is the existing water-vapour amount compared with the saturation amount at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage. At 100% the air is saturated. Because saturation depends strongly on temperature, relative humidity can change even when no water vapour is added or removed.

references.title: NOAA NESDIS — What Is Humidity?
references.locator: Definition of relative humidity and temperature dependence.

items.explanation: An isoclinal line joins places with the same magnetic inclination, also called dip. Dip is the angle the Earth's magnetic field makes with the horizontal. This differs from an isogonic line, which joins places having the same magnetic variation or declination.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigation glossary: isoclinal line and magnetic dip.

items.explanation: A short transmitted pulse lets an echo sounder distinguish reflecting surfaces that are close together vertically. A longer pulse spreads the return over more time and can merge separate echoes. Pulse length therefore affects resolution, although longer pulses can provide more transmitted energy for deeper sounding.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Depth measurement: echo-sounder pulse duration and resolution.

items.explanation: A buoy's charted position is a reference, not a guarantee of its exact position at observation. Its mooring permits movement, and storms or damage can put it off station. Use its identification and other independent observations to check position before relying on it.

references.title: USCG — Light Lists and Coast Pilots, General Information
references.locator: General information: buoy position limitations.

items.explanation: A south cardinal mark shows a white light when fitted, in both IALA Regions A and B. Its identifying rhythm is six quick or very quick flashes followed by a long flash. The long flash distinguishes the six-flash group from other cardinal characteristics.

references.title: IALA — R1001, The Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: South cardinal mark: white light and six flashes plus long flash.

items.explanation: A chart catalogue lists available charts by number, title and geographic coverage, usually with index diagrams. Use it during passage appraisal to identify the charts and scales needed. Then check their current editions and correction status before treating them as ready for navigation.

references.title: UKHO — ADMIRALTY Digital Catalogue User Guide
references.locator: Catalogue search and chart/publication coverage information; identifying products by location and details.

items.explanation: Buoys can move within their moorings, drag off station or be repositioned by the responsible authority. Their actual locations may therefore differ from the charted positions. Prefer suitable fixed, well-defined objects for visual fixes and use buoy observations with independent checks.

references.title: USCG — Light Lists and Coast Pilots, General Information
references.locator: General information: floating aids and off-station positions.

items.explanation: Low pressure commonly encourages air to converge and rise. As rising moist air cools, cloud and precipitation can develop, making wet or stormy weather the intended answer. The actual conditions depend on moisture, pressure gradients and the system's structure; one low reading alone does not prove a storm.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Low-pressure systems and associated weather.

items.explanation: A sea breeze blows from sea toward land near the surface. During daytime, land usually warms faster than the adjacent water, encouraging air to rise over land and cooler marine air to flow inland. A return circulation develops aloft when the local sea-breeze pattern is established.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Sea breeze: onshore surface flow driven by daytime land heating.

items.explanation: Use true = magnetic + variation, taking east as positive and west as negative. Here 086° − 098° = −12°, so the variation is 12° west. This compares true and magnetic headings only; deviation would be needed if the supplied heading were a compass heading.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses: true and magnetic direction; calculation from supplied headings.

items.explanation: The stated approximation is correction = 1.1 × height in feet ÷ 30, in hectopascals. Add it to a barometer above sea level because pressure normally decreases with height. It is a rough sea-level reduction for modest heights, not an exact atmospheric correction.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather instruments: reducing barometric pressure to sea level; approximation given in item.

items.explanation: Speed error is not a standard barometer instrument correction in the sense used here. Barometer readings may need calibration, temperature and height corrections, depending on instrument type. Poor exposure to wind can still cause pressure errors, so the selected answer should not imply motion can never affect an installation.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather instruments: barometer corrections and exposure.

items.explanation: The prefix fracto denotes ragged or broken cloud fragments, such as fractostratus or fractocumulus. These often occur beneath precipitating clouds in turbulent, moist air, explaining the bank's association with rain and strong winds. The prefix itself describes cloud form and does not guarantee either rain or strong wind.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather elements: cloud fragments, fractostratus and fractocumulus.

items.explanation: A single line of position gives only one constraint: the vessel can lie anywhere along it. Combining that line with the best available dead-reckoning estimate gives an estimated position. It is not a full observational fix because the along-line position remains dependent on estimation.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Piloting: estimated position from a line of position and dead reckoning.

items.explanation: The mature stage of a thunderstorm contains both updraughts feeding the cloud and downdraughts descending with precipitation. This stage can produce heavy rain, gusts, lightning and severe turbulence. The coexistence of rising and sinking air distinguishes it from the mainly updraught-driven developing stage.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Thunderstorm mature stage: simultaneous updraughts and downdraughts.

items.explanation: The selected description is an isolated danger mark: two black spherical topmarks and a white group-flashing light, Fl(2). It can mark a wreck with navigable water around it. The bank's F(2) notation is imprecise, and wrecks may instead require other marks, including emergency wreck marking buoys.

references.title: IALA — R1001, The Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: Isolated danger marks: two black spheres and group-flashing white Fl(2); emergency wreck marks distinguished.

authorNotes: The intended aid is an isolated danger mark over a wreck, not the emergency wreck marking buoy.

items.explanation: A psychrometer compares dry-bulb air temperature with the cooler reading of a wetted, ventilated bulb. Evaporation causes the wet-bulb depression. Using the appropriate psychrometric table or calculation, these readings provide relative humidity and dew point; pressure and adequate ventilation affect the result.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather instruments: dry/wet-bulb psychrometry.

items.explanation: The bank refers to weekly Notices to Mariners, such as the established NGA and Admiralty weekly series. These contain corrections to charts and nautical publications. Urgent navigational warnings and continuously updated maritime safety services also exist, so weekly publication is not the timing of every safety notification.

references.title: UKHO — Weekly Notices to Mariners
references.locator: Weekly Notices to Mariners publication series.

items.explanation: Binnacle magnets compensate for deviation caused by the vessel's magnetic field acting on the compass. They reduce selected permanent-magnetism effects rather than the Earth's magnetic variation. Correct adjustment is checked over headings, with remaining errors recorded in a deviation table for navigational use.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses: permanent magnets, deviation and variation.

items.explanation: Twenty-five minutes equals 25/60 hour. Current drift is therefore 0.9 ÷ (25/60) = 2.16 knots. The bank's 2.1 knots is the closest listed option, not the ordinary one-decimal rounding. The southwest displacement gives the current's set; drift names its speed.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents — Glossary
references.locator: Drift is current speed; supplied displacement and time calculation.

items.explanation: Add the 2° east gyro error to 330° gyro to obtain 332° true. With 13° west variation, the corresponding magnetic heading is 345°. That equals the steering-compass heading of 345°, so magnetic minus compass heading is zero: there is no deviation on this heading.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses: gyro error, variation and deviation; calculation from supplied headings.

items.explanation: In IALA Region A, a starboard lateral buoy may be conical, pillar or spar shaped. When a topmark is carried it is a single upward-pointing cone, and the mark is green. Identify its side using the charted conventional direction of buoyage, not simply the vessel's current heading.

references.title: IALA — R1001, The Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: Region A lateral marks: starboard colours, shapes and topmarks.

items.explanation: Differential GPS corrects errors shared between the reference station and the vessel. It does not improve the arrangement of satellites in the sky, which determines geometric dilution of precision. Poor geometry can therefore still magnify remaining measurement errors even when differential corrections are available.

references.title: GPS.gov — GPS Accuracy
references.locator: Satellite geometry and sources of error; differential corrections do not change geometry.

items.explanation: Nimbostratus is a widespread, thick precipitation cloud commonly associated with prolonged rain or snow. Near a ship, rain and associated low cloud or mist can reduce visibility. Its appearance supports expecting deteriorating visibility and persistent precipitation rather than the brief convective showers typical of cumulonimbus.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Nimbostratus and persistent precipitation.

items.explanation: A gyro repeater receives heading information from the master gyrocompass and uses an electrical or electronic follow-up system to reproduce it. Servo action brings the repeater indication into agreement with the transmitted heading. Check repeaters against the master because alignment or transmission faults can introduce differences.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses: gyrocompass master and repeaters.

items.explanation: Cutting, welding, hammering and other energetic processes during construction can leave steel magnetised in the Earth's field. Some magnetism remains after the inducing influence changes, producing permanent ship magnetism. Its compass effect depends on heading and must be compensated and checked after significant structural work.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses: acquisition of permanent magnetism by ship steel.

items.explanation: The legacy GPS L2 carrier frequency is 1227.60 MHz; L1 is 1575.42 MHz. Using measurements on more than one frequency helps estimate ionospheric delay because the delay depends on frequency. Modern GPS also includes additional civil signals, so the two-frequency wording describes the traditional system.

references.title: GPS.gov — Space Segment
references.locator: Legacy L1 and L2 signals; L2 carrier at 1227.60 MHz.

items.explanation: A fix is the vessel's position determined for a stated time from observed position information. Several independent lines of position may be intersected, or an electronic positioning system may supply the solution. Always attach the observation time, since the vessel continues moving after the fix is obtained.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Piloting: fix and time of observation.

items.explanation: Compass deviation results from the vessel's own magnetic field disturbing the compass's alignment with the Earth's magnetic field. Steel structure, permanent magnetism and electrical equipment can contribute. Because their combined effect changes with heading, use the deviation appropriate to the ship's present compass heading.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses: shipboard magnetic fields and deviation.

items.explanation: The bank selects traffic lane. A traffic lane is an area within defined limits where one-way traffic is established; natural features or separation zones can form its boundaries. The stem describes boundaries without specifying one-way traffic, so it gives an incomplete definition rather than a unique identifying feature.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigation glossary and routeing: traffic lane definition.

authorNotes: The intended definition includes one-way traffic, which is missing from the stem.

items.explanation: The bank uses a rough marine estimate: surface wind speed is about two-thirds of geostrophic wind speed. Friction near the surface reduces speed and turns the wind across isobars toward lower pressure. The actual reduction depends on stability, surface conditions and height, so this is not a fixed conversion.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather elements: geostrophic versus surface wind and friction.

authorNotes: Approximate open-sea surface-wind estimate, not a precise local prediction.

items.explanation: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure, commonly reported in hectopascals or millibars. Pressure trends help identify approaching or departing weather systems. A reading becomes more useful when compared with previous corrected observations and the pressure expected for the locality and time.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Barometer.

items.explanation: The wet-bulb depression is 30 − 28 = 2°C. At around standard sea-level pressure, a ventilated-psychrometer calculation gives roughly 86% relative humidity; tables and assumptions can shift the result slightly. The bank uses 85%, but the supplied readings alone do not uniquely distinguish these closely spaced options.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather instruments: psychrometric tables; wet-bulb depression and pressure dependence.

authorNotes: A properly ventilated psychrometer near sea-level pressure is assumed; the bank value depends on table/convention.

items.explanation: The bank identifies DGPS within its correction-service coverage as the intended high-accuracy commercial method. Differential corrections improve ordinary standalone GPS by reducing common measurement errors. This is a historical comparison rather than a universal ranking: modern augmentation and carrier-phase techniques can achieve substantially better accuracy.

references.title: GPS.gov — GPS Accuracy
references.locator: Augmentation and high-accuracy positioning; historical DGPS comparison.

authorNotes: Historical comparison with ordinary standalone GPS; not a claim of the best current positioning technology.

items.explanation: Jet streams are narrow bands of strong winds high in the atmosphere that help steer weather systems. Their bends and changes in position affect storm tracks and the movement of warm and cold air. The bank's description of pushing weather systems refers to this steering influence.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather elements: upper-air circulation and jet streams.

items.explanation: Tidal Current Tables give predicted tidal-current times, directions and speeds for their listed stations, with instructions for subordinate locations. They are the appropriate reference for the tidal component in a harbour. Wind, river discharge and local effects may produce actual currents different from the predictions.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents — Glossary
references.locator: Tidal Current Tables: predicted currents and reference/subordinate stations.

items.explanation: The bank selects metre-and-decimetre soundings between 21 and 31 metres, illustrating extra detail useful to deep-draught navigation. Decimal depth presentation depends on the chart authority, purpose and survey quality. Do not treat this particular interval as a universal rule; check the chart's sounding units and notes.

references.title: NGA/NOAA — U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section I: depths, sounding units and decimal presentation; chart-specific practices apply.

authorNotes: The numeric interval is retained as the bank convention; the reference does not establish a universal 21–31 m rule.

items.explanation: In the Northern Hemisphere, face the oncoming wind and the low-pressure centre lies generally to the right, usually somewhat behind that direction because surface winds spiral inward. This is Buys Ballot's law. It gives an approximate bearing, not a precise cyclone fix, especially near land or disturbed winds.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Tropical cyclone navigation: Buys Ballot's law and surface wind.

items.explanation: A semidiurnal tide has two high waters and two low waters in approximately one lunar day. The bank's answer of two counts the two tidal cycles or high waters. A mean lunar day is about 24 hours 50 minutes, rather than the 24 hours 53 minutes stated here.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents — Glossary
references.locator: Semidiurnal: two high and two low waters per tidal day; lunar-day duration.

authorNotes: Two refers to two tidal cycles/high waters; the stated lunar-day duration is approximate and inaccurate.

items.explanation: If atmospheric moisture remains similar, daytime warming lowers relative humidity because saturation vapour pressure rises. Night-time cooling raises it, potentially reaching saturation and producing dew or fog. This common daily pattern can be interrupted by changing air masses, precipitation or moisture supply.

references.title: NOAA NESDIS — What Is Humidity?
references.locator: Same vapour content produces changing relative humidity as temperature changes.

items.explanation: The bank flags the 90° phase statement as incorrect, but legacy GPS L1 C/A and P(Y) carrier components are in quadrature, so that statement is supported by the GPS interface specification. C/A is an open civil code; the option saying it is encrypted for military use is the clearer incorrect statement.

references.title: GPS Interface Specification IS-GPS-200K
references.locator: Section 3.2.3, L1/L2 signal structure, and Table 3-III: L1 carrier components in phase quadrature.

authorNotes: The bank key conflicts with the official GPS signal specification; key and options remain unchanged.

items.explanation: The cold wall is the sharp oceanic boundary associated with warm Gulf Stream water and colder water of the Labrador Current system. It describes a sea-temperature contrast, not an atmospheric cold front. Such boundaries can influence fog, local weather and the distribution of marine life.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Oceanography: Gulf Stream and the cold wall.

items.explanation: SPS means Standard Positioning Service, the GPS service made available for civil use. In the legacy system it uses the open L1 coarse/acquisition signal. PPS is the restricted precise service for authorised users; modern civil GPS also provides additional signals beyond legacy L1 C/A.

references.title: GPS.gov — Space Segment
references.locator: Civil C/A code and restricted P(Y) code.

items.explanation: In the Southern Hemisphere, when facing the wind blowing toward you, the low-pressure centre lies generally to your left. Surface friction causes winds to cross isobars inward, so the direction is approximate. Keep the facing convention clear: turning your back to the wind reverses the stated side.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather elements: Buys Ballot's law in the Southern Hemisphere.

items.explanation: A dry-bulb thermometer measures ordinary air temperature without evaporative cooling from a wet covering. It should be suitably exposed and shielded from direct radiation. In a psychrometer, its reading is compared with the ventilated wet bulb to determine humidity-related quantities.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather instruments: dry-bulb temperature and exposure.

items.explanation: A barometer is the instrument used to measure atmospheric pressure aboard ship. Aneroid instruments sense pressure through a flexible sealed capsule, while mercury instruments use a liquid column. Corrected pressure and its trend help the navigator interpret changing weather conditions.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Barometer.

items.explanation: A starboard-hand lateral buoy in IALA Region B may be conical, pillar or spar shaped. The buoy is red, with a single cone point upward if a topmark is fitted. Region B reverses lateral colours relative to Region A, while retaining the starboard conical shape convention.

references.title: IALA — R1001, The Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: Region B lateral marks: starboard colours, shapes and topmarks.

items.explanation: Here bell refers to an audible aid producing a ringing tone when a hammer strikes a bell. An electrically operated hammer is the arrangement selected by the bank. Other bells may be manually or wave operated, so electrical actuation is not essential to the general meaning of a bell signal.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigation glossary: bell and audible aids to navigation.

items.explanation: Air in a hydraulic steering circuit compresses under pressure, unlike the working fluid to a useful approximation. It can cause spongy, delayed or irregular steering response. Check fluid level and leakage and have the circuit vented according to the maker's procedure; other hydraulic faults are also possible.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Ship handling and steering: hydraulic response; general incompressible-fluid principle.

items.explanation: A falling barometer with a low cloud ceiling can indicate an approaching low or warm-frontal system bringing moister, warmer air. That is the interpretation behind the bank's answer. These observations support deteriorating weather but cannot by themselves guarantee that both humidity and temperature will increase.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather systems: warm fronts, falling pressure and lowering cloud.

authorNotes: Approach of warmer, moister air is an unstated weather-system assumption.

items.explanation: Advection fog can form when warm, moist air moves over a surface cold enough to cool that air to its dew point. Condensation then creates suspended droplets and reduces visibility. Unlike radiation fog, this process relies on horizontal air movement and can occur with appreciable wind.

references.title: National Weather Service — Advection Fog
references.locator: Warm moist air moving over a cooler surface.

items.explanation: Earth travels around the Sun at an average speed of about 29.8 kilometres per second. Dividing by 1.852 kilometres per nautical mile gives approximately 16.1 nautical miles per second. Its orbital speed varies through the year because the orbit is slightly elliptical.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigational astronomy: Earth orbital motion; conversion to nautical miles.

items.explanation: A jet stream is a long, narrow band of strong winds near the tropopause, generally flowing west to east in mid-latitudes. Its path meanders and helps steer weather systems. Speeds can exceed 250 miles per hour, but that is a possible strong-jet speed rather than a defining minimum.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather elements: jet streams near the tropopause.

items.explanation: The bank describes an inner guard zone as warning of newly detected targets already close to the vessel, including small targets missed at longer range. Guard-zone layouts and alarm logic vary by radar. Confirm the actual settings and manual; an alarm does not ensure every dangerous target will be detected.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Radar navigation: acquisition/guard zones; model-specific alarms.

authorNotes: Alarm behaviour must be checked for the actual ARPA model and configuration.

items.explanation: If the vessel is making good the leading line toward the lights, its track is 001° true, the charted range direction. The bow may need to point elsewhere to counter current or leeway. Thus the bank's answer describes the intended true track, not necessarily the actual heading being steered.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Piloting: leading lines and distinction between heading and track.

authorNotes: Proceeding toward the lights; 001° is the track, not necessarily the heading.

items.explanation: Convert Fahrenheit to Celsius by subtracting 32, then multiplying by 5/9. For 152°F, (152 − 32) × 5/9 = 66.666…°C, which rounds to 66.7°C. Subtracting 32 must come before applying the scale factor.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigation tables: Fahrenheit–Celsius conversion; arithmetic from supplied temperature.

items.explanation: A pressure reading about 5 millibars or more below the local normal is a traditional warning of a possible nearby tropical cyclone. Normal daily pressure variation must be considered. It is a warning clue, not proof or the universally surest indicator; assess official warnings, pressure trends, wind and swell together.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Tropical cyclones: pressure abnormalities and warning signs.

authorNotes: The bank threshold is a traditional warning clue, not diagnostic proof.

items.explanation: The bank uses the geometric centre of a small triangle formed by three position lines as an estimated fix. This assumes comparable, mainly random observation errors. A cocked hat does not guarantee the vessel lies inside it; assess error sources and proximity to danger before relying on its centre.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Piloting: intersecting position lines, cocked hats and uncertainty.

authorNotes: Comparable random errors are assumed; systematic errors can place the vessel outside the triangle.

items.explanation: The bank's answer makes sense if direct means a straight rhumb line drawn on a Mercator chart: that need not be the shortest spherical route, which is a great circle. Weather, hazards and operational constraints also affect passage choice. The other listed planning considerations are valid too.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Sailings and voyage planning: great circles, rhumb lines and route selection.

authorNotes: Direct is interpreted as a charted rhumb line; all other listed considerations are also relevant.

items.explanation: Fine stippled dots along a shore commonly represent sand, identifying a sandy beach in the intended chart-symbol convention. Read the complete symbol and surrounding shoreline, then confirm it in the chart's legend or Chart No. 1; isolated dots elsewhere can have different meanings.

references.title: NGA/NOAA — U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section C: natural features, sand and shoreline symbols.

items.explanation: Variation, also called magnetic declination, is the angle between true north and magnetic north at a location. It changes with position and time. Deviation is different: it is the additional compass error caused by the vessel's own magnetic influences.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses: magnetic variation versus deviation.

items.explanation: The safest general approach is to avoid the tropical cyclone and its hazardous wind and sea area. Assess forecasts, uncertainty, vessel capabilities and sea room early, then change the passage as needed. Do not plan merely to miss the centre; dangerous conditions extend well beyond it.

references.title: IMO — Resolution A.893(21), Guidelines for Voyage Planning
references.locator: Appraisal and planning: weather, dangers, vessel capabilities and contingency planning.

items.explanation: Beaufort force 8 is a gale, corresponding to winds of 34–40 knots, with about 37 knots as the midpoint. At sea it is associated with moderately high waves, breaking crests and spindrift. The scale describes wind force; observed sea state also depends on fetch and duration.

references.title: National Weather Service — Beaufort Scale
references.locator: Beaufort force 8: gale, 34–40 knots.

items.explanation: An echo sounder calculates depth from the round-trip travel time of a sound pulse: depth = sound speed × time ÷ 2. Using the correct sound speed is therefore essential. Transducer offset, vessel motion, seabed slope and false returns can introduce additional errors.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Depth measurement: pulse travel time and sound-speed assumptions.

items.explanation: Take avoiding action early, while adequate sea room and route choices remain available. Tropical cyclones can change track or intensity, and their dangerous seas extend beyond the centre. Use current forecasts and uncertainty information to keep a prudent margin rather than delaying until close approach.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Tropical cyclone navigation: avoidance and early manoeuvring.

items.explanation: The bank uses about 10 metres as a conventional DGPS horizontal-accuracy figure. Differential corrections can reduce errors shared with a nearby reference station, but achieved accuracy depends on the service, geometry, correction age and receiver. It is not a guaranteed error limit for every observation.

references.title: GPS.gov — GPS Accuracy
references.locator: Accuracy depends on receiver, geometry, atmosphere and augmentation.

authorNotes: 10 metres is a broad historical service figure, not a universal accuracy guarantee.

items.explanation: Knowing whether a new edition is due helps manage Sailing Directions, but it does not keep the existing book current by itself. Check the edition and apply the publisher's current supplements and Notices to Mariners. The bank's selected answer highlights revision awareness rather than a complete updating method.

references.title: UKHO — About Notices to Mariners
references.locator: Corrections and amendments to charts and publications; keeping editions current.

authorNotes: Revision awareness supplements, rather than replaces, applying current corrections.

items.explanation: Four satellite measurements normally solve the receiver's three position coordinates plus its clock error. Each pseudorange can be pictured as a sphere around a satellite, although receiver-clock uncertainty affects the apparent radii. Additional satellites improve redundancy and can strengthen the solution, depending on geometry and data quality.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Satellite navigation: pseudorange solution and receiver clock uncertainty.

items.explanation: Relative humidity compares the actual water-vapour content with saturation at the same temperature, usually as a percentage. It is not simply the mass of water vapour present. For unchanged moisture content, cooling raises relative humidity and warming lowers it.

references.title: NOAA NESDIS — What Is Humidity?
references.locator: Relative humidity versus absolute humidity.

items.explanation: Port-hand lateral marks are red in IALA Region A. Their characteristic shape is can-shaped, pillar or spar, with a single cylindrical topmark when fitted. Determine port and starboard using the conventional direction of buoyage shown or described for the waterway.

references.title: IALA — R1001, The Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: Region A lateral marks: port-hand colour and shape.

items.explanation: Use tide tables covering the locality and referenced to the same vertical datum as the charted depths. That compatibility lets you combine predicted tidal height with charted depth to estimate water depth. Also check the date, time zone and any secondary-port corrections.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents — Glossary
references.locator: Chart datum, tide tables and tidal-height reference.

items.explanation: At six-mile meteorological visibility, the luminous-range diagram gives approximately 10 nautical miles for a light of 14-mile nominal range. Geographic range from a 12.8-metre light and 6-metre eye is about 12.8 miles. The smaller luminous range therefore limits the expected sighting distance.

references.title: USCG — Light Lists and Coast Pilots, General Information
references.locator: Luminous range diagram and geographic range; apply the smaller limiting range.

authorNotes: Approximate luminous-range diagram reading and ordinary refraction.

items.explanation: Centering error occurs when a sextant's index-arm pivot is not exactly at the centre of the graduated arc. Its size can vary with the angle measured, unlike a simple constant index error. Calibration or an instrument correction table may be needed to account for it.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Instruments: sextant centering error.

items.explanation: A mackerel sky consists of small cloud elements, commonly cirrocumulus or altocumulus, arranged in patches or ripples. Traditional weather lore treats it as a possible precursor of unsettled weather. It is not a reliable forecast alone; combine it with cloud development, pressure trends and official forecasts.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather elements: altocumulus/cirrocumulus and limits of cloud-based forecasts.

items.explanation: Suspended particles and turbulent water can scatter or reflect sound before the pulse reaches the seabed. An echo sounder may display these returns as a false bottom or additional layer. Check the trace, settings and independent depth information before interpreting every strong return as the seabed.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Depth measurement: scattering and false echoes.

items.explanation: A correction tracing helps transfer a Notice to Mariners amendment to its proper position on the chart. Align the tracing's reference points with the chart, then verify the correction against the notice. It is a positioning aid; chart edition, scale and the written instruction must still match.

references.title: UKHO — About Notices to Mariners
references.locator: Notices to Mariners tracings and chart maintenance record.

items.explanation: A sling psychrometer measures humidity using dry- and wet-bulb thermometers swung through the air for ventilation. Evaporation cools the wetted bulb. The temperature difference, interpreted with the appropriate table or formula, gives relative humidity and can also provide dew point.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Weather instruments: sling psychrometer.

items.explanation: A tropical depression has maximum sustained surface winds below 34 knots under the classification used here. Expressed in whole knots, its upper limit is 33 knots. At 34 knots it reaches tropical-storm strength; use the relevant warning agency's averaging convention when comparing observations.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Tropical depression: sustained wind upper limit of 33 knots.

items.explanation: Multipath occurs when a GPS signal reaches the antenna by reflected paths as well as directly. Those reflections depend on the vessel's local surroundings, so a remote differential reference station generally cannot remove them. Antenna siting and receiver processing help reduce this local error.

references.title: GPS.gov — GPS Accuracy
references.locator: Local multipath versus errors shared with a differential reference.

items.explanation: Two position lines crossing near 90° provide the strongest geometry for a two-bearing fix. Small bearing errors then cause less uncertainty at the intersection than when the lines meet at a shallow angle. Choose identifiable fixed objects and take the bearings as nearly simultaneously as practicable.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Piloting: two-bearing fix geometry.

items.explanation: A drying rock rises 0.9 metre above chart datum. At a tidal height of 2.8 metres, the water over it is 2.8 − 0.9 = 1.9 metres. Subtract the 1.5-metre draught to obtain 0.4 metre static under-keel clearance, before squat, waves and other allowances.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Tides and chart datum: drying heights and under-keel-clearance arithmetic.

authorNotes: Tidal height and drying height share a datum; static draught only, before dynamic allowances.

items.explanation: The eight principal winds are north, northeast, east, southeast, south, southwest, west and northwest. They form the familiar eight-point compass pattern. More detailed traditional roses subdivide these into 16 or 32 points, while modern chart roses also carry degree graduations.

references.title: NGA/NOAA — U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section B: compass directions; eight principal compass directions and subdivisions.

items.explanation: A transverse Mercator projection places its line of best representation along a meridian instead of the equator. It can depict the poles and a narrow area on either side of that meridian with limited distortion. This explains its suitability for the narrow pole-to-pole coverage described by the bank.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I
references.locator: Chart projections: Transverse Mercator Projections; narrow meridional coverage and star-chart use.

items.explanation: A coastal passage plan should combine the intended route with weather, navigational hazards, position-checking methods and watchkeeping responsibilities. Detailed preparation helps the bridge team anticipate course alterations, traffic and changing conditions. Brief the team and monitor execution so the plan remains useful throughout the passage.

references.title: IMO — Resolution A.893(21), Guidelines for Voyage Planning
references.locator: Annex sections 2–5: appraisal, planning, execution and monitoring.

items.explanation: Tidal Current Tables, and associated current diagrams where provided, give the tidal stream's predicted direction and speed. Rotary-current information describes how the direction changes through the tidal cycle. Tide Tables primarily predict water levels, which are a different quantity from current velocity.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents — Glossary
references.locator: Rotary current and Tidal Current Tables.

items.explanation: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure. On board, readings and their trend help assess the development or approach of weather systems. Apply the instrument's required corrections and compare observations consistently; pressure alone does not describe all the wind, cloud and sea conditions to expect.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Barometer.

items.explanation: A low-pressure system often involves rising air, cloud development and precipitation, so stormy and wet is the intended answer. The severity depends on moisture and pressure gradients. A weak low can produce modest weather, while rapidly falling pressure and strengthening winds warrant closer attention.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Low-pressure systems and rising air.

items.explanation: Magnetic dip, or inclination, is the angle between the Earth's magnetic-field direction and the horizontal plane. It describes the field's upward or downward tilt. Magnetic declination instead measures the horizontal angle between magnetic north and true north.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses: magnetic dip or inclination.

items.explanation: Deviation from a fixed horizontal permanent magnetic force generally decreases as the Earth's horizontal directive force strengthens toward the magnetic equator. The stronger restoring field makes the same shipboard disturbance produce a smaller angular error. Actual deviation also depends on heading, local field strength and other magnetic components.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses: permanent magnetic forces relative to horizontal Earth field.

items.explanation: Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated when cooled at constant pressure without changing its water-vapour content. The selected option omits the final saturation condition, which completes the definition. Cooling to this point can initiate condensation when suitable surfaces or particles are present.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Dew point: cooling to saturation at constant pressure and vapour content.

items.explanation: First confirm that the chart edition is current, then use the cumulative list and correction record to identify outstanding notices. The bank additionally says to work backwards from the latest correction; do not adopt that as a general procedure. Follow the publisher's sequence and supersession instructions so later changes are not undone.

references.title: NGA — Summary of Corrections, Volume 5
references.locator: Introduction: chart corrections listed in ascending Notice to Mariners order; follow individual correction instructions.

authorNotes: The bank wording is preserved; reverse-order application is not endorsed as a general correction method.

items.explanation: A pressure departure of 5 millibars or more below local normal is a traditional tropical-cyclone warning sign used by the bank. Account for the normal daily pressure oscillation before interpreting it. No single threshold proves proximity; combine trends, winds, swell and current cyclone warnings.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Tropical cyclone navigation: pressure departures and warning signs.

authorNotes: The threshold is a traditional warning clue and must be compared with local normal pressure.

items.explanation: Broad, prolonged rainfall from warm air rising gradually over cooler air is characteristic of a warm front, so it is the statement that does not describe a cold front. At a cold front, advancing dense cold air undercuts warmer air and forces it upward more abruptly.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Cold front versus warm-front precipitation.

items.explanation: A lightning strike can expose the hull to a strong transient magnetic field and alter its retained magnetism, potentially changing polarity. Recheck compass error after such an event. Cargo changes and movement between magnetic latitudes can also change deviation, though through different magnetic effects.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses: changes in ship magnetism after lightning or other magnetic disturbances.

items.explanation: The useful relationship is between the tide table's height datum and the chart's depth datum. Use compatible tables for the charted locality so predicted heights can be added to charted depths correctly. The selected option is awkwardly phrased; locality alone does not establish datum compatibility.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents — Glossary
references.locator: Chart datum: reference for charted depths and predicted tidal heights.

authorNotes: Interpret the intended answer as requiring compatible locality and vertical datum.

items.explanation: The Gulf Stream is a strong warm current carrying water through the Florida Straits and northward along the eastern United States before turning into the North Atlantic. It forms part of a wider circulation connected with the Gulf of Mexico, matching the bank's broad description.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Oceanography: Gulf Stream system.

items.explanation: Echo sounders assume a sound speed when converting travel time to depth. Temperature, salinity and pressure change the actual speed, so an inappropriate assumed value gives an incorrect depth. Wavelength also changes at fixed frequency, but the depth error arises directly from the travel-time conversion.

references.title: NOAA — Surveying and Mapping
references.locator: Underwater sound propagation and water-property dependence.

items.explanation: At new moon, the Moon lies near the Sun's direction in the sky. It therefore rises approximately with the Sun, around sunrise, and sets around sunset. Exact times depend on location, lunar latitude and the precise time relative to new moon.

references.title: USNO — Phases of the Moon and Percent Illuminated
references.locator: New moon geometry: Moon near the Sun in apparent direction.

items.explanation: A diurnal tide has one high water and one low water in a lunar day, approximately 24 hours 50 minutes. This differs from a semidiurnal tide, which has two of each. Count complete high-and-low cycles rather than assuming the pattern repeats within exactly 24 solar hours.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents — Glossary
references.locator: Diurnal: one high water and one low water in a tidal day.

items.explanation: A tropical storm has maximum sustained surface winds of 34–63 knots under the classification used here. Below 34 knots it is a tropical depression; at 64 knots it reaches hurricane strength in basins using that term. The classification concerns sustained wind, not individual gusts.

references.title: National Weather Service — Weather Glossary
references.locator: Tropical storm: sustained winds 34–63 knots.

items.explanation: An electronic depth finder times a sound pulse travelling to the bottom and back, then calculates depth as sound speed × elapsed time ÷ 2. The bank's constant-speed wording describes the simplifying assumption. Actual sound speed varies with water conditions and may require correction.

references.title: NOAA — Surveying and Mapping
references.locator: Acoustic depth measurement and sound-speed assumptions.

authorNotes: Constant sound speed is a calculation assumption; actual water properties vary.

items.explanation: Heading is the direction in which the vessel's bow points at a given moment. Current and leeway can make the vessel move over ground in another direction. State the reference as true, magnetic or compass when recording or communicating a heading.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigation terminology: heading, course and track.

items.explanation: A search datum position is the estimated most probable location of the search object at the specified time. It is developed from available information and expected drift, with uncertainty considered when planning the search. It is not necessarily the object's original distress position.

references.title: USCG — Search and Rescue Addendum, COMDTINST 16130.2H
references.locator: Search planning and datum determination; search-object position advanced for drift.

items.explanation: Leave the sail or float plan with a responsible person ashore who can notify rescue authorities if the vessel becomes overdue. Include vessel identification, intended route, persons aboard and expected return or check-in time. Update that person when plans change and confirm safe arrival.

references.title: USCG — Float Plan
references.locator: Leave the completed float plan with a reliable person who can raise the alarm.

items.explanation: One line of position constrains the vessel to that line but does not independently determine where along it the vessel lies. Combining it with dead reckoning produces an estimated position. A fix needs sufficient suitable observed information to establish the position independently of that remaining estimate.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Piloting: estimated positions and single position lines.

items.explanation: A deep-draught vessel in confined shallow water can experience increased effective draught through squat, with changes in trim and increased resistance. The bank's phrase drag more water is best understood as draw more water. Reduced under-keel clearance and sluggish handling require careful speed control.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Shallow-water ship handling: squat and restricted-water effects.

authorNotes: Interpret drag more water as increased effective draught through squat.

items.explanation: Away from constraining channels, tidal currents commonly rotate progressively through different compass directions during the tidal cycle. This is a rotary current. In a narrow channel, the boundaries more often force the current into an approximately reversing flood-and-ebb pattern instead.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents — Glossary
references.locator: Rotary current: flow direction changes through compass points during the tidal period.

items.explanation: A celestial altitude observation places the observer on a circle of equal altitude centred on the body's geographical position. Over the small area used for plotting, a short section of that circle is treated as a straight line of position. A second suitable observation helps establish a fix.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Celestial navigation: circle of equal altitude and line-of-position approximation.

items.explanation: A mackerel sky is traditionally taken as a precursor of bad weather. Its rippled high cloud can accompany a changing weather pattern, but the cloud pattern alone does not establish that rain or a storm will follow. Treat this as weather lore requiring support from other observations.

references.title: NWS, High Clouds
references.locator: Cirrocumulus: unstable layer aloft does not necessarily indicate approaching significant weather.

authorNotes: The question asks about the traditional belief, rather than a certain forecast.

items.explanation: Precession is the intended answer, although the stem is incomplete. An applied turning moment changes the angular momentum of a spinning gyroscope, causing its spin axis to reorient. The axis tends toward the applied torque axis; the familiar right-angle response refers to the applied force, not the torque vector.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 818, Principles of the Gyroscope: applied force and perpendicular precessional motion.

authorNotes: The incomplete stem is interpreted as asking for the gyroscopic response to an applied torque.

Peer review: Confuses applied force with torque: the spin-axis direction changes along the perpendicular torque component, not at right angles to the torque vector. NGA Bowditch 2019 Vol. 1 section 2004 says the spin axis tends to align with the applied torque axis; section 818 gives the right-angle response relative to force.

items.explanation: A running fix combines lines of position observed at different times. Advance the earlier line by the vessel’s estimated movement to the time of the later observation, then intersect them. This permits fixing from one object, but errors in the assumed course, speed or current affect the result.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, running fixes and advancing lines of position to a common time.

items.explanation: Precession is the change in orientation of a spinning gyroscope under an applied torque. The spin axis tends toward the torque axis, while the axis about which it precesses is perpendicular to both. Gyrocompasses use controlled precession with gravity and Earth’s rotation to seek the meridian.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Sections 818–819, Principles of the Gyroscope and Gyrocompass Operation.

authorNotes: Peer review: Says the spin axis changes direction perpendicular to the applied torque, confusing torque with force. NGA Bowditch 2019 Vol. 1 section 2004 describes the spin axis tending toward the applied torque axis; the precession rotation axis is perpendicular to spin and torque axes.

items.explanation: Isogonic lines join places having the same magnetic variation, also called magnetic declination. Variation is the angle between true north and magnetic north at a place. These lines therefore describe the geographic pattern of magnetic direction, rather than compass deviation caused by the vessel.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, magnetic variation and isogonic lines.

items.explanation: A chart’s isogonic lines connect positions with equal magnetic variation. A value associated with a line tells the angular difference between true and magnetic north for its stated epoch. Magnetic dip instead concerns the field’s vertical inclination, so it is not the quantity represented.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, magnetic variation and isogonic lines; variation changes with place and time.

items.explanation: An index error on the arc means the sextant reads a positive angle when the true angle is zero. That excess must be removed from an observation, so the index correction is negative. The correction has the opposite sign to the instrument’s index error.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 1412, Adjustable Sextant Error: index error and index correction.

items.explanation: AIS uses the VHF maritime band to exchange digital identification and navigation messages. Its principal channels are AIS 1 at 161.975 MHz and AIS 2 at 162.025 MHz. These are radio communication frequencies, rather than the microwave bands used by marine radar.

references.title: USCG, International VHF Marine Radio Channels and Frequencies
references.locator: Frequency table and notes: AIS 1, 161.975 MHz; AIS 2, 162.025 MHz.

items.explanation: Advection fog forms when relatively warm, moist air moves over cooler water and is cooled toward its dew point. Condensation then produces suspended droplets near the surface. Air moving over warmer water can produce evaporation or steam fog, which is a different formation process.

references.title: NWS, Advection Fog
references.locator: Advection fog formation: warm moist air passes over a colder surface.

items.explanation: Within 10 meters is the bank’s DGPS accuracy answer. Differential GPS uses corrections derived at a reference station of known position to reduce errors shared with nearby receivers. Actual horizontal accuracy depends on the correction service, receiver, geometry and conditions; 10 meters is not a universal limit for every DGPS installation.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 22, differential GPS and augmentation of satellite navigation.

authorNotes: The accuracy figure is treated as the bank’s broad service-level approximation, not a guaranteed specification.

items.explanation: Traffic lane is the intended routeing term. It is an area with defined limits in which one-way traffic is established; natural obstacles, including those forming separation zones, may constitute boundaries. A separation zone separates streams, while a recommended track supplies a suggested route.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Ships’ Routeing: definition of traffic lane.

items.explanation: A yellow buoy may mark an anchorage area as a special-purpose mark. Yellow identifies a special area or feature whose meaning must be checked on the chart or in nautical publications. It does not by itself identify the channel centre, and the stem allows more than one possible special use.

references.title: NGA/NOAA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section Q, Special marks: yellow colour; purpose shown on charts and in publications.

authorNotes: Anchorage is a possible use; other special areas may also be marked yellow.

items.explanation: The intended vertically striped buoy is a safe-water mark, with red and white vertical stripes. If lighted, it shows a white light. Safe-water marks can also be unlighted, so the bank’s lighted option describes an allowed characteristic rather than a requirement that every such buoy carry a light.

references.title: NGA/NOAA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section Q and Appendix 1, Safe-water marks: red/white vertical stripes and white light if fitted.

authorNotes: The unspecified vertical stripes are interpreted as the red-and-white safe-water pattern; unlighted is also possible.

items.explanation: A contact that remains at the same bearing and range has approximately zero motion relative to your vessel. The intended conclusion is that both vessels have the same course and speed over the ground. Your 10-knot through-water speed alone does not establish either vessel’s ground velocity.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 23, radar relative motion and target interpretation.

authorNotes: Same relative position means unchanged range as well as bearing, on a correctly interpreted radar display.
