items.explanation: A buoy may have moved from its charted position because of its mooring’s movement, damage or displacement. Its position is therefore less dependable than a fixed, positively identified shore feature. Use buoys as supporting aids and compare them with other evidence when fixing the vessel.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Sections 702 and 709, Buoy Moorings and Buoy Maintenance: movement and positioning limitations.

items.explanation: Always allow for a buoy being outside its charted position. A buoy swings around its mooring, and weather, current or damage can displace it farther. Identification by colour or light does not establish its exact coordinates, so an independent position check remains necessary.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Sections 702 and 709, Buoy Moorings and Buoy Maintenance.

items.explanation: A hydraulic current is driven by a difference in water level between connected bodies of water. When their tides rise and fall at different times or by different amounts, the resulting head can force a swift flow through the narrow connecting passage.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 3514, Tidal and Nontidal Currents: hydraulic current and differences in tidal level.

items.explanation: On a gnomonic chart, parallels other than the equator are curved. Great circles project as straight lines, so the equator and meridians are straight where represented. This makes gnomonic charts useful for drawing great-circle routes, although their scale changes rapidly away from the point of tangency.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 4, Gnomonic Projection: great circles and parallels.

items.explanation: A vessel trolling with lines that do not restrict manoeuvrability is excluded from the Rule 3 definition of a vessel engaged in fishing. The definition depends on the gear’s effect on manoeuvring, rather than simply whether the vessel is catching fish.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rule 3(d): fishing apparatus restricting manoeuvrability; exclusion of trolling lines or other unrestricted apparatus.

items.explanation: The displacement from the DR position is 0.5 nautical mile over two hours. Dividing distance by time gives a drift of 0.25 knot, setting east. This attributes the entire difference to current; uncorrected steering, speed or plotting errors could also contribute in practice.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, determining current set and drift from DR and observed positions.

authorNotes: All displacement from DR is attributed to a uniform current.

items.explanation: Human-factor-related risk is the intended answer. Decisions, communication, fatigue, competence and organisational practices influence how ships and equipment are operated. IMO recognises the human element as a major contributor to maritime casualties; the stem supplies no particular casualty study that would establish a numerical ranking.

references.title: IMO, Human Element
references.locator: Opening discussion: human element contributes to most shipping casualties and affects maritime safety.

items.explanation: A short, prolonged, short whistle sequence is the optional warning signal of a vessel at anchor in restricted visibility. It supplements the prescribed bell signal to warn an approaching vessel of the anchored vessel’s position and possible collision risk. It is distinct from one prolonged followed by two short blasts.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rule 35(g): anchor bell signal and optional short–prolonged–short whistle warning.

items.explanation: Parallel indexing monitors whether the vessel remains at its planned distance from a radar-conspicuous fixed feature. A reference line parallel to the intended track lets the watchkeeper detect movement toward or away from that track promptly. It supports continuous track monitoring in good visibility and restricted visibility.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2317, Parallel Indexing.

items.explanation: Climate is described by long-term patterns of temperature, precipitation, winds and seasonal variation. Considering these together distinguishes a region’s usual conditions from the weather on a particular day. No single variable in the other choices adequately describes the range and timing of conditions experienced.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: climate contrasted with day-to-day weather.

items.explanation: In IALA Region A, a starboard-hand lateral mark is green and normally conical or carries a cone topmark. When entering from seaward in the conventional direction of buoyage, keep it to starboard. Region B reverses the red and green lateral colours.

references.title: NGA/NOAA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Appendix 1, Region A lateral marks and conventional direction of buoyage.

items.explanation: A stereographic projection places the viewpoint on the sphere directly opposite the tangent point and projects onto the tangent plane. A gnomonic projection instead uses the sphere’s centre as its viewpoint. The opposite-point viewpoint is the feature that identifies the stereographic chart here.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 417, Stereographic Projection.

items.explanation: General charts are designed for coastwise navigation outside outlying reefs and shoals. They show a broader coastal area than coastal or harbour charts, with less local detail. Bowditch gives their usual NOS scale range as about 1:150,000 to 1:600,000.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 425, Chart Classification by Scale: General charts.

items.explanation: Five or more short, rapid blasts express doubt or danger concerning another vessel’s intentions or actions. The bank’s answer points to resolving that uncertainty by making your intentions clear. Communication must accompany a proper collision-risk assessment and any necessary safe manoeuvre; a message alone does not resolve danger.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rule 34(d): doubt signal; Rules 7–8: collision risk and avoiding action.

authorNotes: The option is interpreted as clarification of intentions, without treating radio agreement as a substitute for the Rules.

items.explanation: A scale of 1:700,000 suits a sailing chart because it covers a large area with relatively little coastal detail. Bowditch generally places sailing charts at scales smaller than 1:600,000. The much larger scales in the other choices are intended for closer coastal or harbour work.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 425, Chart Classification by Scale: Sailing charts.

items.explanation: Under the traditional NOS classification, 1:80,000 is a coastal-chart scale. Coastal charts typically range from about 1:50,000 to 1:150,000 and support inshore coastwise navigation and entry to broad bays. Chart classifications can overlap, so this answer uses the classification convention intended by the bank.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 425, Chart Classification by Scale: Coastal charts.

items.explanation: Capital-letter landmark legends indicate a conspicuous feature under the chart convention intended here. Such a feature is readily identifiable from seaward and can be useful for visual bearings. Confirm the symbol and chart convention rather than assuming that every capitalised label denotes a navigational danger.

references.title: NGA/NOAA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section E, Landmarks: conspicuous landmarks and lettering conventions.

items.explanation: GPS satellites carry multiple atomic clocks to provide highly stable timing. The receiver measures signal travel times to estimate satellite ranges, so timing accuracy directly affects position accuracy. Satellite clock corrections are also broadcast; carrying accurate clocks does not eliminate the need to monitor and correct their errors.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 22, GPS system description and satellite clock corrections.

items.explanation: The keyed event is a target initially selected within the guard zone. ARPA guard-zone functions can alert the watchkeeper to targets in a monitored area; exact acquisition and alarm behaviour depends on the equipment and settings. CPA/TCPA warnings are separate alarm conditions, so this wording does not uniquely describe all ARPA alarms.

references.title: NGA, Radar Navigation and Maneuvering Board Manual
references.locator: Chapter 5, Automatic Radar Plotting Aids: guard zones, acquisition and operational warnings.

authorNotes: The bank is interpreted as asking about a guard-zone target alarm, not every possible ARPA warning.

items.explanation: Thunder comes from the rapid heating and expansion of air around a lightning channel. That abrupt expansion creates a pressure wave heard as sound. You usually see the flash first because light reaches you much faster than sound travels through the atmosphere.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, thunderstorms, lightning and thunder.

items.explanation: Venus is generally the brightest celestial object visible from Earth after the Sun and Moon. Its proximity and highly reflective cloud cover make it exceptionally bright. Its actual visibility and brightness vary with its position relative to Earth and the Sun.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, Venus and navigational planets.

items.explanation: Answering your one-short-blast signal with two short blasts indicates incompatible intentions in this head-on situation. Sound at least five short, rapid blasts to express doubt or danger, then assess and take appropriate avoiding action. Continuing on the assumption of an agreed passing arrangement would be unsafe.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rules 14 and 34(d): head-on situation and doubt/danger signal.

items.explanation: Topographical names identify named geographic places or features shown on charts and described in Sailing Directions. They help the navigator connect the written description with the correct charted location. They are place names, rather than a category of depths, current data or navigational instructions.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Sailing Directions: geographic names and chart correspondence.

items.explanation: Pilot charts summarise broad ocean conditions such as prevailing winds, ocean currents and storm tracks. They are not the source for local tidal-current predictions. Consult tidal-current tables, atlases or appropriate local chart information for the current’s expected direction and speed at a particular time.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Pilot Charts; Chapter 35, Tidal Current Tables.

items.explanation: The intended Philippine Region B convention uses odd numbers for port-hand lateral marks. Entering from seaward in the conventional direction of buoyage, those marks are kept to port and are green. Numbering supports identification; the chart still establishes the applicable buoyage direction.

references.title: NGA/NOAA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Appendix 1, Region B lateral marking; Section Q, lateral buoy numbering.

authorNotes: The answer assumes the Philippine Region B numbering convention intended by the bank.

items.explanation: A marine weather forecast translates meteorological analysis into expected conditions useful to mariners. Plain-language conclusions help the watchkeeper assess wind, sea state, visibility and hazards when planning or adjusting a passage. The purpose here is forecasting operational weather, rather than presenting raw observations alone.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Sections 3826–3827, Forecasting Weather and Weather Dissemination.

items.explanation: Celestial navigation is the bank’s answer because observations of celestial bodies provide an independent ocean-position check without relying on satellite transmissions. Its availability depends on a visible horizon, suitable bodies, accurate time and competent observation. The wording does not establish that it is universally more reliable or accurate than GPS.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapters 13–19, celestial navigation observations and sight reduction.

authorNotes: “Most reliable” is treated as emphasis on independence from electronic navigation, not an absolute performance ranking.

items.explanation: A double star consists of two stars appearing close together in the sky. They may form a gravitationally bound binary, or simply lie near the same line of sight at different distances. The bank’s broader description includes both, whereas “a binary system” excludes an optical pair.

references.title: USNO, The Washington Double Star Catalog — Description
references.locator: Introduction and Growth of the WDS: double/multiple-star systems include physical, optical and undetermined associations.

items.explanation: A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre cannot manoeuvre as required by the Rules because of the nature of her work and consequently cannot keep out of another vessel’s way. Dredging is one example; the definition concerns the operational restriction rather than a vessel’s name alone.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rule 3(g): restricted in ability to manoeuvre and examples.

items.explanation: Plot a DR position whenever speed changes, so the earlier track segment ends at the correct time and the next segment uses the new speed. DR should also be maintained at course changes, fixes and regular intervals. An hourly schedule alone would miss these important changes.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 9, Dead Reckoning: rules for plotting DR positions.

items.explanation: Determine index error by turning the micrometer drum until the direct and reflected views of the horizon or a suitable object coincide, then read the sextant. The resulting nonzero reading is the error. Adjusting the horizon mirror is a separate operation used to remove that error.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 1412, Adjustable Sextant Error: determining index error.

items.explanation: Cross a traffic lane on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the general direction of traffic flow. This makes your crossing intention clearer and minimises time in the lane. Rule 10 specifies heading, so current may make the ground track differ from a perfect right angle.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rule 10(c): crossing traffic lanes on a heading nearly at right angles to traffic flow.

items.explanation: The GPS L1 carrier is centred on 1575.42 MHz. L2 uses 1227.60 MHz, which is another offered choice. The carrier frequency identifies the radio band carrying the navigation signal; the ranging codes and navigation message are modulated onto that carrier.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2201, GPS satellite frequencies and signal coding.

items.explanation: Four is the number of baseline GPS satellite slots in each of six orbital planes, giving the traditional 24-slot constellation. Actual operational satellites can exceed that baseline, so four should not be interpreted as an unchanging count in every plane at every date.

references.title: GPS.gov, Space Segment
references.locator: Constellation arrangement: six orbital planes, four baseline slots per plane, additional satellites possible.

items.explanation: GNSS means Global Navigation Satellite System and is the umbrella term for satellite positioning systems. GPS, GLONASS and Galileo are individual constellations within that broader category. A receiver using several constellations is therefore described as a multi-constellation GNSS receiver.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 22, satellite navigation systems: GPS, GLONASS and other GNSS constellations.

items.explanation: A conventional GPS receiver needs four independent satellite measurements to solve four unknowns: latitude, longitude, altitude and receiver clock bias. Three coordinates alone do not describe the full problem because the receiver’s clock is not perfectly synchronised with satellite time. Additional satellites improve redundancy and geometry.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2202, System Capabilities: four unknowns and four satellite measurements.

items.explanation: GLONASS matches the description of a constellation arranged in three orbital planes at roughly 19,000 kilometres altitude. GPS instead uses six baseline planes at about 20,200 kilometres. The orbit arrangement and height, rather than the general promise of position and time, distinguish the systems in this stem.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2219, GLONASS: three orbital planes and approximately 19,100 km altitude.

items.explanation: Differential GPS improves a user’s position by applying corrections determined at a reference station whose coordinates are known. Many errors affect both station and user similarly, allowing their effects to be reduced. Improvement depends on the service, distance from reference information, receiver and signal conditions.

references.title: GPS.gov, Augmentation Systems
references.locator: Augmentation systems: differential corrections improve GPS positioning performance.

items.explanation: Cirrostratus commonly produces a halo around the Sun or Moon because its ice crystals refract light. It often appears as a thin, extensive veil through which the body remains visible. A halo is therefore a useful clue to cirrostratus, rather than a defining feature of every high cloud.

references.title: NWS, High Clouds
references.locator: Cirrostratus: extensive thin high cloud and halo phenomena.

items.explanation: The high cloud described is cirrocumulus: small white cloudlets arranged in ripples, rows or a scaly pattern. Their fish-scale appearance gives rise to “mackerel sky.” Altocumulus can also form patterns, but its cloud elements are generally larger and occur at middle levels.

references.title: NWS, High Clouds
references.locator: Cirrocumulus description and distinction from middle-level cloud.

items.explanation: The bank emphasises that GPS service or reception must not be assumed continuously available without warning. Interference, equipment faults and service anomalies can interrupt a usable solution. Maintain independent navigation checks and monitor integrity information rather than interpreting a displayed position as proof of reliable reception.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 22, GPS limitations, interference and navigation safeguards.

authorNotes: The statement is interpreted as possible loss or interruption of usable service, not a prediction of intentional global shutdown.

items.explanation: The statement emphasises the human factor: automation still depends on people to enter information, interpret indications, monitor progress and respond appropriately. Technology can reduce some errors while leaving opportunities for poor judgement or misuse. Effective watchkeeping and teamwork therefore remain central to collision prevention.

references.title: IMO, Human Element
references.locator: Human element: crew, management, competence and operational activities affect maritime safety.

items.explanation: Index error occurs when the horizon glass and index mirror are not parallel with the index arm at zero. The instrument then indicates an angle even when the direct and reflected horizons coincide. Measure that zero offset and apply an equal correction of opposite sign.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 1412, Adjustable Sextant Error: index error.

items.explanation: Azimuth angle is the horizon-coordinate counterpart of meridian angle: each measures angular direction around its system’s pole. Azimuth uses the observer’s zenith and a reference direction on the horizon, while meridian angle uses the celestial pole and the observer’s celestial meridian. Altitude instead measures height above the horizon.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, celestial-equator and horizon coordinate systems; navigational triangle.

items.explanation: The darker limit of civil twilight is the bank’s preferred compromise: bright stars and planets become visible while the sea horizon can still be distinguished. Civil twilight ends or begins when the Sun is 6° below the horizon. Actual observing conditions depend on cloud, haze and the body’s brightness.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 1710, Twilight: centre of Sun about 3°–9° below horizon is effective for stars and planets; darker limit of civil twilight at 6°.

items.explanation: Centering error results when the index arm’s pivot is not at the exact centre of the sextant arc’s curvature. It changes the relationship between arm movement and the angle indicated. This is a construction error, distinct from adjustable mirror errors such as side or index error.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 1411, Non-adjustable Sextant Errors: centering error.

items.explanation: Condensation changes water vapour into liquid and releases latent heat to the surroundings. That is the physical concept in the stem. The keyed tracing-and-positioning option is unrelated to condensation, so it cannot supply a scientifically meaningful completion of this question.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, water-vapour phase changes and latent heat.

authorNotes: The keyed answer appears displaced or corrupted; no connection between tracing corrections and latent heat is supported.

items.explanation: A purse seiner hauling her net can be underway even though fishing gear restricts her manoeuvrability. Rule 3 defines underway by exclusion: not at anchor, made fast to shore or aground. Underway therefore does not necessarily mean moving through the water.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rule 3(i), underway; Rule 3(d), vessel engaged in fishing.

authorNotes: The purse seiner is assumed not anchored, made fast to shore or aground.

items.explanation: GPS L2 operates at 1227.60 MHz. The higher frequency 1575.42 MHz belongs to L1. Receiving signals on more than one frequency can help estimate frequency-dependent ionospheric delay, improving the navigation solution when the receiver and service support those measurements.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2201, GPS carrier frequencies; Chapter 22, ionospheric effects.

items.explanation: A lunar eclipse requires the full Moon to be at or sufficiently near a node, where its tilted orbital plane crosses the ecliptic. This permits the Moon to enter Earth’s shadow. Full Moon is also necessary, so the choices identify overlapping requirements rather than a uniquely sufficient condition.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, lunar orbit, nodes and lunar eclipses.

authorNotes: “At one of the nodes” is read as sufficiently near a node; full Moon is another necessary condition.

items.explanation: The bank describes a glow around the Sun or Moon seen through cloud as a corona. A corona is produced by diffraction of light by small water droplets, not ice-crystal refraction. The diffuse glow is its visible appearance; the cloud name alone does not identify the optical mechanism.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, optical phenomena: corona, diffraction and aureole.

authorNotes: The keyed option describes appearance; the separate diffraction option states the physical cause.

items.explanation: Relative motion contributes a special-relativistic clock-rate correction, which is the effect named in the keyed answer. GPS also accounts for general-relativistic effects caused by the satellites’ different gravitational potential. The option therefore identifies only one of the two effects requested, rather than a complete pair.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 22 and Appendix C, GPS timing and relativistic effects.

authorNotes: The keyed relative-velocity option is incomplete; both motion and gravitational potential affect satellite clock rates.

items.explanation: The prime vertical is the vertical circle passing through the east and west points of the horizon, as well as the zenith and nadir. It is perpendicular to the observer’s celestial meridian. The meridian instead passes through the north and south horizon points.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, horizon system: prime vertical and celestial meridian.

items.explanation: The shoreline on a nautical chart generally represents the mean high-water line. It is therefore distinct from the low-water datum commonly used for charted depths. Check the chart’s notes and national conventions because the shoreline reference and sounding datum describe different features and need not coincide.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 436, Heights: shoreline generally represents mean high water; sounding and height reference levels differ.

items.explanation: Rule 3 defines underway as neither at anchor, made fast to shore nor aground. The keyed statement, “riding at her anchor,” is therefore inconsistent with that definition. Making way through the water normally describes an underway vessel, although an underway vessel may also be stopped.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rule 3(i): definition of underway.

authorNotes: The preserved bank key contradicts the stated Rule 3 definition; the explanation does not endorse it.

items.explanation: A roll period is the time for one complete oscillation, returning to the same inclination and direction of motion. From upright to maximum inclination on one side is approximately a quarter-period in regular rolling. The keyed option describes that shorter interval, rather than the complete roll period.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 37, vessel motions in waves and rolling period.

authorNotes: The key is inconsistent with the standard meaning of roll period; quarter-period assumes approximately periodic motion.

items.explanation: The depressed pole is the celestial pole below the observer’s horizon, opposite the elevated pole above it. In the Northern Hemisphere the north celestial pole is elevated and the south pole depressed; in the Southern Hemisphere their roles reverse. The terms describe visibility relative to the observer’s horizon.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, celestial poles and the observer’s celestial sphere.

items.explanation: Apparent altitude is obtained after correcting sextant altitude for instrument errors and the reference level, including dip when using the sea horizon. Refraction and other astronomical corrections are then applied to obtain observed altitude. The keyed wording groups the earlier instrumental and horizon-reference adjustments together.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 1906, correct sextant altitude for index error and dip to obtain apparent altitude; subsequent altitude corrections.

items.explanation: The Nautical Almanac’s daily astronomical data are conventionally arranged in three-day page spreads. This is the layout being tested, rather than the total coverage of the publication, which is a year. Use the correct date and hour within that spread when extracting a body’s coordinates.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 17, The Almanacs: Nautical Almanac daily pages arranged for three days.

items.explanation: Official electronic navigational charts are issued by, or on the authority of, a government-authorised hydrographic office. Commercial distributors may supply them, but official status comes from the issuing authority. ECDIS compliance also requires suitable coverage, updates and the prescribed equipment and backup arrangements.

references.title: IMO, Electronic Nautical Charts and Electronic Chart Display and Information Systems
references.locator: ECDIS standards and official chart carriage; ENC data issued by or on the authority of government-authorised hydrographic offices.

items.explanation: The flag State is responsible for verifying that the ECDIS installation meets applicable statutory requirements. It may authorise a recognised organisation or nominated surveyor to carry out the survey on its behalf. A classification society can therefore perform the work without replacing the flag State’s responsibility.

references.title: IMO, Surveys, Verifications and Certification
references.locator: Opening discussion: surveys by flag-State officers or authorised recognised organisations and nominated surveyors.

authorNotes: The keyed flag-State answer concerns statutory responsibility, not necessarily the individual attending surveyor.

items.explanation: “Lighting cycle duration” describes the interval intended by the bank. The standard navigational term is the light’s period: the time for one complete repeating sequence of light and darkness. A phase is only one part of that sequence, such as an individual flash or eclipse.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 7, light characteristics: period and phases.

authorNotes: The bank selects a descriptive phrase although the standard term “Period” is also offered.

items.explanation: Take bearings to establish the vessel’s position promptly after anchoring. This provides a reference for plotting the anchor position and checking whether the vessel subsequently drags. At night, positively identify the observed lights and continue checking the position throughout the anchor watch.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Sections 1016–1017, choosing and approaching an anchorage; establishing and monitoring anchored position.

items.explanation: Plot the vessel’s position after the anchor is let go so the bridge has a definite reference for the anchorage. Subsequent observations can then reveal unexpected movement outside the expected swing. The pilot’s presence does not remove the watchkeeper’s responsibility to verify and monitor the position.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, anchoring and monitoring position at anchor.

items.explanation: The bank treats a vessel dragging her anchor as underway because she is no longer effectively held in her anchored position. This is different from lying securely at anchor. Recognise the movement promptly, monitor collision risk and take appropriate action rather than relying on the anchor’s presence alone.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rule 3(i), underway; anchoring status when dragging.

authorNotes: The dragging vessel is assumed to be moving because the anchor is no longer holding, rather than merely swinging within normal scope.

items.explanation: The bank’s intended measure is to let go a second anchor and veer sufficient cable to improve holding. A longer scope reduces the upward pull on the anchors. Suitability depends on depth, available room, bottom holding, cable leads and weather; deploying two anchors is not automatically the best response in every anchorage.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, anchoring precautions and scope in adverse conditions.

authorNotes: The question assumes adequate sea room and a suitable arrangement for using two anchors.

items.explanation: The claim that shade glasses cause no sextant error is incorrect. If a shade’s faces are not parallel, refraction can introduce prismatic or shade error into the measured angle. This error can be checked by comparing measurements made with and without the same shade in the optical path.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 1411, Non-adjustable Sextant Errors: prismatic error and shade error.

items.explanation: A great circle other than the equator crosses the equator at two opposite points, 180° of longitude apart. Both circles pass through Earth’s centre, so their planes intersect along a diameter. The equator itself is a special case because it coincides with the reference circle.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 1202, Great Circles: equator intersections.

authorNotes: The great circle is not the equator itself.

items.explanation: An east–west passage in high latitudes can save substantial distance by following a great circle rather than the parallel of latitude. The great circle bends poleward and is shorter between the endpoints. Westbound passages have the same geometric advantage; easterly direction alone does not create the saving.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Sections 1202–1204, great circles and comparison with rhumb lines.

authorNotes: The keyed easterly high-latitude case is a suitable example, not a unique global maximum for unspecified endpoints.

items.explanation: The second GPS carrier, L2, has a frequency of 1227.60 MHz. This corresponds to the first option’s number. Its written unit, mHz, would mean millihertz rather than megahertz, so the bank evidently intends MHz; L1 is 1575.42 MHz.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2201, GPS satellite carrier frequencies.

authorNotes: The option’s “mHz” is interpreted as a unit-capitalisation error for MHz.

items.explanation: A rhumb line crosses every meridian at the same angle, so its true course remains constant. It appears straight on a Mercator chart and is convenient to steer. A great-circle route generally requires changing true course as the vessel progresses, although it usually gives the shorter distance.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 1204, Rhumb Lines; Section 1202, Great Circles.

items.explanation: The intended concept is a three-dimensional satellite fix. Four independent measurements allow the receiver to determine latitude, longitude, elevation and its clock error. These are satellite range constraints, not literally four straight chart lines; two intersecting plotted lines normally supply only a horizontal fix.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2202, System Capabilities: four unknowns in three-dimensional GPS positioning.

authorNotes: “Fix with elevation” is interpreted as a conventional GPS solution with unknown receiver clock bias.

items.explanation: An easterly-setting current pushes a southbound vessel to port, toward the east. To maintain a southerly ground track, steer slightly to starboard, toward the west, to oppose that set. The required correction angle depends on current drift and the vessel’s speed through the water.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, compensating for current set and drift in a course-to-steer solution.

authorNotes: “Easterly current” means setting toward the east, rather than flowing from the east.

items.explanation: The voyage includes the accrued distance from the port of departure to the port of arrival. Intermediate offshore calls do not end or restart that voyage. Thus the keyed phrase “not including stops” concerns where a voyage ends; it does not remove miles sailed to and between offshore points from the total.

references.title: USCG, Offshore Supply Vessels of at Least 6,000 GT ITC, 2014 rulemaking
references.locator: Page 55, discussion of 46 CFR 15.810(b)(5)–(6): accrued port-to-port distance, offshore calls do not restart voyage.

authorNotes: The stem is interpreted using the U.S. offshore-supply-vessel manning convention in 46 CFR 15.810; offshore calls do not reset the accrued distance.

items.explanation: Recreation zones, mooring areas and cables are normally indicated by special marks, rather than cardinal marks. A cardinal mark tells the navigator which compass side has the safer water. Its black-and-yellow pattern, cone topmarks and white light rhythm encode that directional meaning.

references.title: NGA/NOAA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Appendix 1, cardinal marks and special marks.

items.explanation: “Hard Starboard” orders the rudder fully over to starboard and held there until another order is given. It is a rudder order, not a fixed 15° or 30° instruction and not a promise of an immediate heading change. The helmsman repeats and reports execution of the order.

references.title: IMO, Standard Marine Communication Phrases, Resolution A.918(22)
references.locator: Annex 1, A2/1, Standard wheel orders: hard-a-port/starboard means rudder held fully over.

items.explanation: With course 090°T, the relative bearings are 37° and 59° to port. Constant-course geometry gives about 71.16 minutes from 1940 to abeam, or approximately 2051H. The bank selects 1926H, which is not supported by the stated times and bearings; even the closest listed time, 1938H, is earlier than the second observation.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, successive bearings and time-to-abeam geometry.

authorNotes: Constant course and speed, fixed lighthouse and no current; the keyed time appears inconsistent with the problem data.

items.explanation: Head reach is the forward distance the ship continues along her original direction after full-astern stopping action begins until she is stopped in the water. Her inertia prevents an immediate stop. Actual stopping distance can be affected by speed, displacement, propulsion response and environmental conditions.

references.title: USCG, NVIC 6-95, incorporated IMO MSC/Circ.644
references.locator: MSC/Circ.644, Figure 4, Definitions Used in Stopping Test: head reach, track reach, astern order and ship dead in water.

authorNotes: The bank uses head reach for forward advance during the stopping manoeuvre; track reach can differ if the ship turns.

items.explanation: Buoys alone are unsuitable as the sole basis for a dependable position fix because floating aids can swing or be displaced from their charted positions. Visual bearings, radar ranges and electronic positions can be cross-checked against charted fixed features. Positively identifying a buoy does not prove its exact location.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Sections 702 and 709, buoy position limitations; Chapter 10, independent position fixing.

items.explanation: The ecliptic is the Sun’s apparent yearly path against the stars, corresponding to the plane of Earth’s orbit projected onto the celestial sphere. It is inclined to the celestial equator because Earth’s rotation axis is tilted relative to its orbital plane.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, celestial sphere: ecliptic and celestial equator.

items.explanation: A normal three-dimensional GPS solution requires four independent satellite range measurements. They determine three position coordinates plus the receiver’s clock bias. The bank calls these “4 theoretical position lines,” but they are range surfaces in space rather than four ordinary lines drawn on a navigation chart.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2202, System Capabilities: four satellite measurements and four unknowns.

items.explanation: An autopilot automatically controls steering to maintain a selected heading or, with suitable inputs, follow a track. It compares the commanded value with measured heading and orders corrective rudder. Holding a fixed geographic position requires a dynamic-positioning system; an ordinary autopilot cannot provide that function by steering alone.

references.title: IMO, Resolution A.822(19), Performance Standards for Automatic Steering Aids
references.locator: Annex, paragraph 2.1: automatic steering aid uses heading information to keep a preset course; cited for the automatic heading-control principle.

authorNotes: The keyed answer addresses automatic course keeping; the position-holding part of the stem is broader than ordinary autopilot capability.

items.explanation: GPS supplies position, velocity and time from satellite signals. On board, this supports plotting, ground-speed information and navigation-system timing. GPS velocity is relative to Earth, so it is speed over the ground; measuring speed through the water requires a different reference, such as a suitable log.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2202, System Capabilities: position, velocity and time.

items.explanation: Adding the ship’s draft is appropriate if the starting measurement is water clearance beneath the keel: total water depth equals that clearance plus draft. If starting from a charted sounding, the required addition is tidal height instead. The stem omits the reference from which “actual depth” is being calculated.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2604, Echo Sounders: transducer/keel reference; Chapter 35, charted depth and tide.

authorNotes: The keyed draft addition assumes a keel-referenced clearance reading, with relevant sensor offsets already applied.

items.explanation: Parallax depends on the observing baseline and the body’s distance, and changing Earth–planet distance can make planetary parallax vary substantially. The bank selects Polaris, but its very large distance makes stellar parallax tiny. The supplied wording gives no valid basis for identifying Polaris as the greatest annual variation among these choices.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, parallax, stellar distance and planetary motions.

authorNotes: The preserved Polaris key is not supported by the usual astronomical meaning of parallax.

items.explanation: Magnetism within the vessel changes the compass reading through deviation. Magnetic variation instead comes from the difference between true north and the direction of Earth’s magnetic field at the vessel’s position. The keyed option identifies the shipboard magnetic influence, so the stem appears to use “variation” imprecisely.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, variation versus deviation and shipboard magnetic fields.

authorNotes: The intended concept is deviation caused by the vessel, not geographic magnetic variation.

items.explanation: A running fix intersects lines of position obtained at different times after allowing for the vessel’s movement between observations. One fixed object may supply successive bearings. The earlier line must be advanced to the later time; simply intersecting the original lines would place the fix at incompatible observation times.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, running fixes and advancing earlier lines of position.

items.explanation: 24 kHz is the low-frequency echo-sounder value selected by the bank. Lower-frequency sound generally suffers less absorption and is useful for deeper soundings. There is no single universal low-frequency setting: commercial sounders use different frequencies and selectable modes according to transducer design and operating depth.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2604, Echo Sounders: frequency selection and deep-water versus shallow-water sounders.

authorNotes: The keyed 24 kHz is an equipment/example frequency, not a mandatory setting for all echo sounders.

items.explanation: GPS uses code division multiple access: satellites transmit distinguishable pseudorandom ranging codes while sharing carrier frequencies. A receiver correlates each received signal with the corresponding code to separate the satellites and measure signal travel time. It does not need a separate carrier frequency for each GPS satellite.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2201, GPS unique C/A and P codes and code division multiple access.

items.explanation: A scale of 1:5,000,000 means one unit on the chart represents five million of the same units on Earth. Therefore one inch represents 5,000,000 inches, as keyed. Equally, one centimetre represents 50 kilometres; the ratio works only when the units on both sides are handled consistently.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 424, Chart Scale: representative fraction and consistent units.

items.explanation: Current set and drift are needed to combine the vessel’s through-water motion with the water’s movement over the ground. Adding those velocity vectors gives course and speed made good. Set is the current’s direction toward which it flows, while drift is its speed.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, current triangles and track/speed made good.

authorNotes: The ship’s course and speed through the water are already known; current information alone is insufficient.

items.explanation: Index error is caused by the index mirror and horizon glass not being parallel when the index arm is set at zero. The sextant then has a zero-reading offset. This differs from perpendicularity and side errors, which concern how each mirror stands relative to the sextant frame.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 1412, Adjustable Sextant Error: index, perpendicularity and side errors.

items.explanation: Radar ranges to clear fixed targets combined with visual observations provide useful independent position checks in confined waters. X-band radar can resolve nearby detail, while visual identification helps confirm the correct target. The best method still depends on visibility, target geometry, chart accuracy and equipment performance.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, piloting fixes; Chapter 23, radar navigation and range-based position fixing.

authorNotes: Suitable fixed radar targets and visible identifiable features are available; the answer is not a blanket rejection of GNSS.

items.explanation: Ensure that the chart and GPS coordinates refer to the same horizontal datum. A position expressed in one datum can plot incorrectly on a chart using another unless the proper transformation is applied. The first three choices substantially repeat this requirement, so the keyed wording is not uniquely different in meaning.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 2, geodetic datums; Chapter 22, satellite positions and datum compatibility.

authorNotes: The chart datum in this question means horizontal geodetic datum, not the vertical sounding datum; options overlap.

items.explanation: Fine dots along the coastal beach symbol indicate a sandy beach under the chart convention intended here. This is a shoreline portrayal, rather than a mineral identification. For seabed samples offshore, chart abbreviations such as S for sand provide the bottom description.

references.title: NGA/NOAA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section C, Natural Features: sandy shore; Section J, Nature of the Seabed: sand abbreviation.

items.explanation: A daymark identifies a beacon primarily through its colour and shape, often supplemented by numbers or letters. These features can be recognised in daylight and matched to the charted aid. A light’s flash rhythm is a night-time identifying characteristic, rather than the daymark itself.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 7, beacons and daymarks: visual shape and colour characteristics.

items.explanation: Reading “21, 0” as 210°, true heading 215° minus magnetic heading 210° gives 5°. East variation is added to magnetic heading to obtain true heading, so the result is 5°E. Compass deviation is not involved because the comparison is between true and magnetic headings.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 830, Heading Relationships: true heading equals magnetic heading plus east variation.

authorNotes: The malformed magnetic heading “21, 0” is interpreted as 210°.

items.explanation: Sailing Directions provide voyage-planning information about ocean-basin conditions and routes, making them the intended publication for a San Francisco-to-Japan passage. Planning Guides supply broad regional context, while Enroutes describe coasts and approaches. The Nautical Almanac instead supplies astronomical data for celestial navigation.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Sailing Directions Planning Guides and Enroutes; ocean passage planning.

items.explanation: A normal three-dimensional GPS fix needs four satellites to solve latitude, longitude, altitude and receiver clock bias. The bank selects three, which would require additional information such as an independently known clock offset. Three is therefore not the typical minimum for the conventional receiver described by the stem.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2202, System Capabilities: four satellites for position and time.

authorNotes: The preserved key of three conflicts with the typical unaided GPS solution; a known receiver clock is not stated.

items.explanation: A white group-flashing light Fl(2) with two black spherical topmarks identifies an isolated-danger mark. Such a mark can identify a wreck with navigable water around it. Not every wreck uses this mark: cardinal, lateral or emergency wreck-marking arrangements may be used according to the danger and local system.

references.title: NGA/NOAA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Appendix 1, isolated-danger mark: two black spheres and white Fl(2).

authorNotes: The wreck is assumed suitable for isolated-danger marking; the stem is broader than this single buoy type.

items.explanation: A small-scale chart covers a large area, making it suitable for planning and following a long ocean passage. It omits much of the close coastal detail that would clutter that broad view. Use progressively larger-scale charts as the vessel approaches hazards, coastal waters and the arrival port.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 425, Chart Classification by Scale: sailing charts and ocean passages.

items.explanation: A free gyroscope has freedom about its spin axis and two mutually perpendicular gimbal axes, commonly described as tilt and azimuth. Thus spin axis is part of the standard description, despite the bank excluding it. “Latitude axis” is not a standard member of that three-axis description.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 818, Principles of the Gyroscope: horizontal, vertical and spin axes.

authorNotes: The preserved spin-axis key conflicts with the standard three-axis description.

items.explanation: Tangent latitude error arises in a mercury-ballistic gyrocompass when damping torque is introduced by offsetting the ballistic force. The resulting settling error varies with latitude and changes sign between hemispheres. It is distinct from transient ballistic errors following a change of course or speed.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Sections 819–820, mercury-ballistic damping and tangent latitude error.

items.explanation: A phase correction can apply to planetary observations because a partly illuminated planetary disc does not present its light symmetrically about the geometric centre. The correction accounts for that displaced apparent centre. Stars are effectively point sources in marine sextant observations and do not require this disc-phase correction.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Section 609, Phase Correction (F): apparent versus actual planetary centres; Venus and Mars corrections; other navigational-planet phase corrections insignificant.

items.explanation: A mercury ballistic is the connected reservoir system used in some gyrocompasses to apply gravity-dependent torque to the gyro. Mercury shifts when the sensitive element tilts, helping produce north-seeking precession. The rotor is the spinning element itself, rather than the reservoir-and-tube assembly.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 819, Gyrocompass Operation: mercury reservoirs and gravity control.

items.explanation: Swell direction is named for where the waves come from. New swell arriving from the east therefore indicates that its generating storm was east of the MODU when those waves formed. Wave travel time means this identifies the earlier generating area, rather than proving the storm’s current position.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 37, swell generation, propagation and wave direction.

items.explanation: Cooling moist air to its dew point can cause water to condense on cargo and compartment surfaces, a condition commonly called sweat. The bank selects precipitation, but precipitation normally describes water falling from the atmosphere. Surface condensation is the relevant process, so the keyed term does not accurately match the stem.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 40, moisture observations and sweat on ships and cargo.

authorNotes: The preserved precipitation key appears inconsistent with the described surface condensation.

items.explanation: Parallel indexing shows whether the vessel is maintaining the planned lateral distance from a fixed radar target. Changes in the target’s position relative to the index line reveal cross-track tendency immediately. The method works in good or poor visibility provided the radar target remains identifiable and properly selected.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2317, Parallel Indexing.

items.explanation: Use the corrected altitude, observation time and almanac data in a sight reduction, then plot the resulting position line. Reduction compares observed and calculated altitudes and obtains the body’s azimuth. A single star altitude normally provides one line, so another suitable observation is needed for a full fix.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 19, Sight Reduction: corrected altitude, calculated altitude, azimuth and intercept plotting.

items.explanation: The keyed order is IV, II, III, I: index-mirror perpendicularity, horizon-glass perpendicularity, index alignment, then telescope collimation. Correcting the basic mirror geometry first prevents a later adjustment from upsetting an earlier check. The zero-setting step means making the mirrors parallel to each other, not parallel to the frame.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 1412, Adjustable Sextant Error: prescribed adjustment order.

authorNotes: Statement III is interpreted as mirror-to-mirror parallelism at zero; its wording about parallelism to the frame is imprecise.

items.explanation: The bank recalls an old provision allowing a fishing vessel under about 20 metres (65 feet) to substitute a basket for the fishing day shape. Current Rule 26 prescribes two cones with their apexes together and does not retain that basket substitution. Treat the keyed answer as historical, not current COLREG practice.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rule 26(b)–(c), current fishing day shapes.

authorNotes: The basket choice reflects superseded wording; it is not a current requirement under Rule 26.

items.explanation: A vessel under 7 metres at anchor need not show the prescribed anchor light or shape when she is outside a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage or area where other vessels normally navigate. The small-vessel exemption depends on that location; length alone does not remove the lighting requirement everywhere.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rule 30(e): anchored vessel under 7 metres and location-dependent exemption.

items.explanation: AIS transponders exchange messages in the VHF maritime band, chiefly on 161.975 MHz and 162.025 MHz. They transmit vessel identity and navigation information as digital radio messages. X-band and S-band describe radar frequencies and are not the AIS radio channels.

references.title: USCG, International VHF Marine Radio Channels and Frequencies
references.locator: AIS 1 and AIS 2 frequencies in the international VHF marine channel table.

items.explanation: A gyropilot is an automatic steering device that uses heading information from the gyrocompass to maintain the ordered heading. The controller detects a heading difference and commands corrective rudder. A gyro repeater only displays transmitted heading; it does not by itself control the steering gear.

references.title: IMO, Resolution A.822(19), Performance Standards for Automatic Steering Aids
references.locator: Annex, paragraph 2.1: automatic steering aid uses heading information to keep a preset course; cited for the automatic heading-control principle.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 821, Using the Gyrocompass: heading information, master compass and repeaters.

authorNotes: Gyropilot is the specific gyro-referenced form of the more general automatic pilot also offered.

items.explanation: Pseudorange rate is the true satellite-to-user slant-range rate plus an offset from the receiver clock’s frequency error. It relates to relative velocity, rather than distance alone. The stem omits “rate” after slant range; a true range plus a clock-time bias would describe pseudorange instead.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 2202, System Capabilities: pseudorange versus pseudorange rate.

authorNotes: The keyed rate answer requires reading “true slant range” as “true slant-range rate.”

items.explanation: Aphelion is the point in Earth’s orbit where its distance from the Sun is greatest. The prefix apo- indicates the farther orbital point, while -helion identifies the Sun as the central body. Apogee instead describes the farthest point of an Earth-centred orbit.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, Earth’s orbit: perihelion and aphelion.

items.explanation: Perihelion is the point in Earth’s orbit closest to the Sun. It is the opposite of aphelion, the farthest point. The similar term perigee applies to minimum distance from Earth, so the central body distinguishes the two kinds of orbital terminology.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, Earth’s orbit: perihelion and aphelion.

items.explanation: Water flowing around a river bend commonly moves faster along the outside bank, scouring a deeper channel while sediment collects on the inside. That explains the keyed outside-bend answer. “Always” is too strong for navigation: surveyed depths, marks, local knowledge and current conditions determine the safe track.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 35, nontidal river currents and channel effects.

authorNotes: The answer describes the usual natural scouring pattern, not a guarantee of safe depth on every outside bend.

items.explanation: A radar range combined with a visual bearing can provide a strong fix because radar measures distance well and an optical bearing can give accurate direction to a positively identified feature. This is the bank’s preferred combination. Actual certainty also depends on target selection, instrument errors and intersecting-line geometry.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, combined visual/radar fixes; Section 2313, Fix by Radar Ranges.

authorNotes: A clear identifiable target and properly corrected visual bearing are available; no method is universally most accurate.

items.explanation: The keyed option appears to describe a broad radar echo from moderate or heavy rain. Precipitation can return radar energy and reveal rain areas, but detection range depends on radar characteristics and weather. The incomplete stem supplies no basis for guaranteeing continuous detection to at least 50 nautical miles.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 23, radar precipitation echoes, attenuation and interpretation.

authorNotes: The stem is malformed; the explanation addresses the rain-echo concept without endorsing the unsupported 50-mile claim.

items.explanation: A gyrocompass repeater receives the master compass’s heading signal and uses an electrical servo or follow-up mechanism to reproduce that indication. Its reading must be synchronised and checked against the master. Different transmission designs exist, so the closely related mechanism labels in the choices can overlap.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 821, Using the Gyrocompass: master and repeaters; heading transmission.

authorNotes: The keyed servo wording is treated as the general closed-loop replication concept, not a uniquely exclusive mechanism name.

items.explanation: Two independent steering-gear control systems provide redundancy: failure in one must not disable the other. Independence concerns mechanical and electrical failure paths as well as separate controls. The requirement applies to the steering arrangements covered by the relevant SOLAS provisions, rather than indiscriminately to every vessel.

references.title: IMO MSC.1/Circ.1398 — MPA Singapore publication
references.locator: Annex, paragraph 2.1: mechanical, hydraulic and electrical independence of two steering control systems.

items.explanation: A short, prolonged, short whistle signal is an optional warning from a vessel at anchor in restricted visibility. It draws attention to her position and possible collision risk, supplementing the prescribed anchor bell signal. Towing and not-under-command signals use one prolonged followed by two short blasts instead.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules International and U.S. Inland
references.locator: Rule 35(c) and (g): restricted-visibility signals and optional anchored-vessel warning.

items.explanation: Increasing cable scope can improve anchor holding by making the pull on the anchor more nearly horizontal and providing additional catenary. That is the intended response in strong wind. Check available swinging room, hazards and whether the anchor is actually holding; more cable alone may not arrest every dragging situation.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, anchoring, cable scope and monitoring for dragging.

authorNotes: There is sufficient depth allowance, cable and sea room to veer safely.

items.explanation: A buoy is a floating aid anchored or otherwise moored at an assigned position. Its shape, colour and any light or sound identify its navigational meaning. The keyed option includes those identifying characteristics, but a buoy can move around its mooring and should not be assumed to occupy an exact charted point.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Section 701, Definitions and Types; Section 702, Buoy Moorings.

items.explanation: Polar distance is the celestial counterpart of terrestrial co-latitude. Both measure angular distance from a selected pole instead of from the equator. For a body in the same hemisphere as that pole, polar distance equals 90° minus declination, just as co-latitude equals 90° minus latitude.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, celestial equator coordinates: declination and polar distance.

items.explanation: A great circle can curve well poleward of a rhumb line between widely separated points in the same high-latitude hemisphere. That difference can produce a useful distance saving. The effect depends on longitude separation as well as latitude; nearby points can still have nearly equal distances.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 12, The Sailings: great-circle and rhumb-line tracks.

items.explanation: Isobars show equal pressure, and their spacing indicates the pressure gradient that drives wind. Closely packed isobars generally mean stronger winds; their arrangement also helps estimate direction. Together, these features help predict wind velocity rather than directly measuring humidity or temperature.

references.title: NOAA JetStream, Origin of Wind
references.locator: Pressure gradient, isobar spacing and wind circulation.

items.explanation: Steering and conning knowledge includes understanding how the vessel responds to orders and how its steering arrangements are selected. Knowing the changeover to a secondary method allows control to be maintained if the primary system fails. The exact procedure must follow the ship’s installed equipment.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Piloting and steering systems: steering control and conning.

items.explanation: Kochab is Beta Ursae Minoris, a bright star in Ursa Minor commonly recognized with Pherkad as a guardian of the pole. It helps identify the region containing Polaris. Do not confuse these stars with Dubhe and Merak, the better-known pointer pair in Ursa Major.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, Navigational Astronomy: star identification and Ursa Minor.

items.explanation: Grivation measures the angular difference between grid north and magnetic north. A chart grid need not follow the local true meridian, so ordinary magnetic variation alone does not describe this relationship. The word combines the grid reference with magnetic variation.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary: grivation and grid magnetic angle.

items.explanation: Middle clouds are classified by the altitude of their bases, commonly about 6,500–20,000 feet in the simplified classification used here. Altocumulus and altostratus belong to this group. These are approximate limits: actual cloud-height bands vary with latitude and the classification convention used.

references.title: NWS, Weather Education
references.locator: Cloud classification: mid-level cloud bases.

items.explanation: The Kuroshio is a strong, warm western-boundary current of the North Pacific, broadly comparable to the Gulf Stream in the North Atlantic. Both carry warm water poleward along the western side of an ocean basin before extending eastward into the ocean.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents, Glossary
references.locator: Glossary entries: Kuroshio and Gulf Stream.

items.explanation: Water flowing around and beneath a moving hull accelerates, especially where shallow or restricted water limits the available flow area. The associated pressure reduction can make the vessel sink deeper and change trim. This loss of under-keel clearance is squat and generally increases with speed.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, section 1018, Effects of Banks, Channels, and Shallow Water: squat, bank cushion, bank suction; effects increase with speed.

items.explanation: Magnetic flux represents the total magnetic field passing through a specified surface, traditionally pictured as lines of force crossing it. The wording here intends that total. If the question meant the number per unit area, the more precise term would be magnetic flux density.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary: magnetic flux and magnetic flux density.

items.explanation: Perigee is the nearest point to Earth in the Moon’s elliptical orbit. The Moon’s distance changes throughout its orbit, so its apparent size and tide-raising effect also vary. The corresponding farthest point is apogee; the terms describe distance, not lunar phase.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents, Glossary
references.locator: Glossary: perigee.

items.explanation: Apogee is the point where the Moon is farthest from Earth in its elliptical orbit. At this greater distance its apparent diameter is smaller than near perigee. Apogee can occur at different phases; it does not mean that the Moon is necessarily full or new.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents, Glossary
references.locator: Glossary: apogee.

items.explanation: The bank locates the revision information in the lower left portion of the chart. This marginal information identifies the edition or correction history so the navigator can check currency. Its precise placement depends on the chart producer and format, so inspect the actual chart’s margins.

references.title: NOAA/NGA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section A, chart layout: publication and correction information.

items.explanation: Rule 8(c) permits an alteration of course alone when sufficient sea room exists, provided it is made early, is substantial, and avoids another close-quarters situation. The point is an effective, readily apparent manoeuvre; a small or late alteration may leave the collision risk unresolved.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules
references.locator: Rule 8(c), Action to Avoid Collision.

items.explanation: The environmental, or ambient, lapse rate describes how actual air temperature changes with height. Compare it with the cooling rate of a rising air parcel to judge whether the parcel remains buoyant or returns to its original level. This comparison determines atmospheric stability.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: atmospheric stability and lapse rates.

items.explanation: Earth reaches aphelion, its greatest distance from the Sun, in early July in the present era. That places it in Northern Hemisphere summer. The seasons mainly result from Earth’s axial tilt, so summer warmth does not imply that Earth is nearest the Sun.

references.title: USNO, Earth’s Seasons, Equinoxes, Solstices, Perihelion and Aphelion
references.locator: Annual aphelion and solstice dates.

items.explanation: The bank selects ephemeris error: an error in the satellite’s predicted position causes an error in the receiver’s computed position. Its importance depends on the application and corrections available. It is not universally the largest GPS error; atmosphere, multipath and satellite geometry can also dominate.

references.title: GPS.gov, GPS Accuracy
references.locator: Causes of GPS error: satellite orbit, atmospheric and receiver effects.

items.explanation: Gyro error equals true bearing minus gyro bearing, with east positive. Here 221.5° − 223° = −1.5°, so the error is 1.5° west. The magnetic variation is irrelevant because the given range direction is true and the observed bearing is gyro.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: comparison of true and gyro bearings.

items.explanation: A safe-water mark can show a white Morse A light: a short flash followed by a long flash. This distinguishes it from the red and green lights of lateral marks. Other authorized white rhythms also exist, so Morse A is one permitted characteristic, not the only one.

references.title: NOAA/NGA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Appendix 1, IALA Maritime Buoyage System: safe-water marks.

items.explanation: Variation is the angle between true north and magnetic north at a location. Earth’s magnetic field changes across the globe, so a new geographical position can require a different allowance. Variation also changes over time; use the chart’s date and annual-change information where applicable.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: magnetic variation.

items.explanation: ARPA combines a target’s relative movement with own-ship course and speed to calculate its true vector. An incorrect speed input therefore distorts the displayed true target motion. A log and ground-speed difference may also reflect current, so confirm whether the display uses sea or ground stabilization.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 23, Radar Navigation: true-motion vectors and own-ship speed input.

items.explanation: Lightning carries a powerful electrical current that can change a vessel’s magnetization and consequently its compass deviation. A substantial magnetic disturbance is a reason to check compass error again. Do not assume that the previous deviation table remains valid after such an event.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: changes in a ship’s permanent magnetism.

items.explanation: The California Current carries relatively cool water southward along the western coast of North America. Warm, moist air moving over this colder sea surface can cool to its dew point and form advection fog. The current encourages those conditions but does not make fog inevitable.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents, Glossary
references.locator: Glossary: California Current.

items.explanation: The bank keys “green conical buoy,” but that is a buoy description and does not name a segment of a celestial position line. A celestial observation gives a line of position, commonly plotted using an intercept and azimuth. No supported connection makes the keyed buoy term fit this stem.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapters 13 and 19, Navigational Astronomy and Sight Reduction: celestial lines of position and intercept plotting.

authorNotes: The supplied key is retained despite a stem/answer mismatch; no buoy term is asserted to name a celestial position-line segment.

items.explanation: At new and full Moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth are approximately aligned. Lunar and solar tide-raising effects reinforce each other, producing the larger tidal range called spring tides. “Spring” describes that increased range and has no connection with the season of spring.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents, Glossary
references.locator: Glossary: spring tides.

items.explanation: A rhumb line maintains a constant angle with every meridian it crosses. This gives a constant true course and produces a straight line on a Mercator chart. Except on a meridian or the equator, it is generally longer than the corresponding great-circle route.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 12, The Sailings: rhumb line.

items.explanation: A torque applied to a spinning gyro changes the direction of its angular-momentum axis, producing precession. The resulting motion is at right angles to the applied torque in the standard gyro demonstration. The clue is the applied torque; apparent motion from Earth’s rotation is a different effect.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: gyroscopic precession.

items.explanation: A running fix combines observations made at different times by transferring the earlier line of position through the estimated movement of the vessel. Its intersection with the later line gives a position at the later time. One shore object can provide both bearings as its bearing changes.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: running fix.
