items.explanation: The bank calls this “Stream error.” The described behaviour is a transient gyro error after manoeuvring: the compass requires time to settle after changes in motion. The unusual keyed term is retained here, but should not be treated as a standard name for all such gyrocompass errors.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: gyrocompass transient and manoeuvring errors.

authorNotes: Stream error is the bank wording, not a verified standard gyrocompass term.

items.explanation: A fix establishes the vessel’s position for a stated observation time using sufficient position information, such as intersecting lines of position or a valid electronic position. The time matters because the vessel continues moving. A position advanced only by course and speed is dead reckoning.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: fixes and lines of position.

items.explanation: At a true zero angle, the index mirror and horizon glass should be parallel. If they are not, the direct and reflected images fail to coincide when the index reads zero, producing index error. Their relative alignment can be adjusted, or the measured error applied as a correction.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 14, Instruments for Celestial Navigation; sextant index error.

items.explanation: Height of tide is measured vertically from the stated tidal datum to the water surface at that time. It is therefore different from depth measured from the seabed. In chart calculations, confirm that the predicted tidal height and the charted depth use compatible datums before combining them.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents, Glossary
references.locator: Glossary: height of tide.

items.explanation: The bank uses 24 kHz as its low-frequency echo-sounder value. Lower acoustic frequencies generally suffer less absorption and are useful for deeper sounding. However, 24 kHz is an equipment-specific example rather than a universal low-frequency standard; the installed sounder’s manual determines its actual frequency.

references.title: NASA CASEI, Singlebeam Echo Sounder (SBES)
references.locator: Instrument description and Measurement Frequency: typical 24–33 kHz deeper-water frequencies and 200–400 kHz shallow-water frequencies.

items.explanation: Precise geodesy requires very accurate satellite orbit information, or ephemerides, because uncertainty in the satellite position propagates into the measured baseline or receiver position. That explains the keyed ephemeris answer. High-precision work also models clocks, atmospheric delays, antenna effects and other errors; no single limitation applies universally.

references.title: GPS.gov, GPS Accuracy
references.locator: High-accuracy GPS positioning and satellite orbit errors.

items.explanation: The relieving helmsman must know the ordered course and the compass reference used to steer it. For the magnetic-steering arrangement assumed here, that includes the course on the magnetic steering compass. Clear transfer prevents accidentally steering a true or gyro value as though it were a compass course.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: steering and compass reference.

items.explanation: A dry-bulb thermometer measures ordinary air temperature without the evaporative cooling used on a wet bulb. In a psychrometer, comparing dry- and wet-bulb readings helps determine humidity. The dry-bulb reading itself is atmospheric temperature, provided the instrument is properly exposed and shielded from direct heating.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: air-temperature measurement and psychrometers.

items.explanation: Wavelength equals propagation speed divided by frequency. Using about 300 million metres per second and the GPS L1 frequency of 1575.42 MHz gives approximately 0.190 metres, or 19 centimetres. This is the carrier wavelength, not the much longer length associated with the navigation-message data rate.

references.title: USNO, Global Positioning System Overview
references.locator: GPS satellite transmission frequencies: L1 = 1575.42 MHz.

items.explanation: On ordinary tidal charts, the shoreline is generally represented by the high-water line, commonly mean high water. It therefore differs from the low-water datum often used for soundings. Read the chart’s stated conventions because shoreline and sounding datums are separate references and can vary by producer.

references.title: NOAA/NGA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Introduction: shoreline and vertical reference levels.

items.explanation: The question asks which consideration is not primarily about local weather. A fast or short route alone does not assess coastal squalls, visibility, winds or tropical hazards. Efficiency belongs in passage planning, but choosing speed without evaluating these conditions does not address the weather issue in the stem.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Weather Routing and Piloting: coastal weather and route appraisal.

items.explanation: The bank selects Polaris, but its enormous distance makes its parallax extremely small. Nearby planets such as Venus have much greater geocentric parallax, which changes as their distance from Earth changes. The keyed choice cannot support a general claim that Polaris has the greatest yearly parallax variation among these choices.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, Navigational Astronomy: parallax and the distances of celestial bodies.

authorNotes: The bank choice is retained; it is not treated as a supported parallax ranking.

items.explanation: After letting go the anchor, establish and record the vessel’s position using suitable charted objects. Bearings taken promptly provide a reference for checking the anchor’s location and later detecting dragging. In clear night conditions, identifiable navigation lights may supply those bearings, preferably with supporting ranges or additional lines.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: anchoring and establishing an anchor position.

items.explanation: The Agulhas Current flows generally southwestward along South Africa’s east coast. A vessel proceeding northeastward toward Durban may therefore encounter it as a strong opposing current. The answer assumes the route enters that current; its actual strength and limits must be assessed from current information.

references.title: NOAA Tides & Currents, Glossary
references.locator: Glossary: Agulhas Current.

items.explanation: A gnomonic projection maps great circles as straight lines because projection is from Earth’s centre onto a tangent plane. This makes it convenient for initially laying out a great-circle route. Intermediate points are then normally transferred to a chart suited to practical navigation.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 4, Nautical Charts: gnomonic projection and great-circle plotting.

items.explanation: A vessel engaged in fishing must not impede the passage of any vessel following a traffic lane. This protects the flow of traffic through the scheme while leaving the other collision-avoidance duties in force. The rule concerns a vessel engaged in fishing, not merely every vessel built as a fishing boat.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules
references.locator: Rule 10(i), Traffic Separation Schemes.

items.explanation: The bank selects aphelion as an approximate seasonal association. Maximum northerly solar declination occurs at the June solstice, while Earth reaches aphelion in early July. These events are near each other in the calendar but are not identical; declination and orbital distance describe different quantities.

references.title: USNO, Earth’s Seasons, Equinoxes, Solstices, Perihelion and Aphelion
references.locator: Dates distinguish June solstice from July aphelion.

authorNotes: The keyed aphelion answer is interpreted only as an approximate seasonal association.

items.explanation: A seasonal buoy’s operating dates are recorded in the Light List, normally in its descriptive remarks or relevant notes. This gives information that a chart alone may not show in full. Check current notices as well, since weather or maintenance can change deployment and withdrawal dates.

references.title: USCG, Light List Annual Publication
references.locator: Light List introductions and remarks for seasonal aids.

items.explanation: An ex-meridian sight is observed near, rather than exactly at, meridian passage and reduced to obtain a latitude-related result. The bank uses within 28 minutes before local apparent noon. This is its stated timing convention; the usable interval depends on latitude, declination, accuracy and the reduction method.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapters 13 and 19, Navigational Astronomy and Sight Reduction: ex-meridian sights and reduction to the meridian.

items.explanation: Knowing the amount of helm already required helps the relieving helmsman maintain the course immediately. Wind, current and the ship’s handling may require a steady rudder offset even when the course is constant. Taking over with the rudder centred could otherwise start an unwanted sheer.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: steering a steady course and helm relief.

items.explanation: The weather adjustment changes the pilot’s response to yaw caused by waves and sea conditions. Proper adjustment avoids excessive corrective rudder for every short-lived swing while maintaining acceptable course keeping. Use the maker’s procedure because control names and the relationship between settings and response vary among systems.

references.title: IMO, Resolution MSC.64(67), Heading Control Systems
references.locator: Annex 3, paragraphs 3.1 (adaptation to steering characteristics and environmental conditions) and 3.4 (avoid unnecessary rudder activation due to normal yaw). Official URL discovered in published references; full PDF not retrievable through the web tool.

items.explanation: A sextant measures twice the angle between its index mirror and horizon mirror. With the mirrors at 45° to one another, the measured angle is therefore 2 × 45° = 90°. Its graduated arc is marked to display this doubled angle directly.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 14, Instruments for Celestial Navigation; double-reflection principle of the sextant.

items.explanation: Parallel index and horizon mirrors represent zero angular separation in a correctly adjusted sextant. The instrument should therefore read 0°, with the drum at zero minutes when the main index is at zero. A nonzero reading at image coincidence is evidence of index error.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 14, Instruments for Celestial Navigation; sextant zero and index error.

items.explanation: Rule 12 gives the responsibilities of sailing vessels approaching one another with risk of collision. It distinguishes vessels with wind on different sides and those with wind on the same side. Apply it alongside the general requirements for lookout, risk assessment and effective collision avoidance.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules
references.locator: Rule 12, Sailing Vessels.

items.explanation: A spoil ground is an area designated for depositing dredged material. Deposits may alter depths or make seabed conditions unsuitable for some activities, so the charted limits and associated notes matter. The term identifies the disposal area, rather than the channel from which material was dredged.

references.title: NOAA/NGA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section N, Areas and Limits: spoil ground.

items.explanation: At meridian transit, the celestial body, observer’s zenith and celestial pole lie in the observer’s meridian plane. Drawing that plane makes the relationships among altitude, zenith distance, latitude and declination clear. A horizontal plan view would not show these vertical angular relationships directly.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapters 13 and 19, Navigational Astronomy and Sight Reduction: meridian-altitude diagrams.

items.explanation: AIS automatically transmits dynamic information including course over ground, allowing suitably equipped recipients to follow the vessel’s movement. Course over ground describes the track over Earth and can differ from heading when current or leeway acts. It is one of several transmitted data fields, not the entire AIS message.

references.title: IMO, AIS Transponders
references.locator: AIS information automatically supplied to ships, shore stations and aircraft.

items.explanation: Australia uses IALA Region A. Region B includes the Americas and certain western Pacific countries, where the lateral-mark colours are reversed. Check the region before interpreting red or green marks; their meaning depends on both the buoyage region and the conventional direction of buoyage.

references.title: NOAA/NGA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Appendix 1, IALA buoyage regions.

items.explanation: An electronic depth finder times the echo of a transmitted sound pulse. Depth is approximately sound speed multiplied by round-trip time and divided by two. The keyed statement assumes a known, effectively constant speed; real sound speed varies with temperature, salinity and pressure and may require correction.

references.title: NOAA, Surveying and Mapping PEIS
references.locator: Sound propagation and sonar: travel time and sound speed.

items.explanation: A vessel is not under command when exceptional circumstances make it unable to manoeuvre as required by the rules and therefore unable to keep out of another vessel’s way. The condition is more specific than simply being stopped, drifting, or choosing not to use the engines.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules
references.locator: Rule 3(f), vessel not under command.

items.explanation: Rule 6 requires every vessel to proceed at a safe speed so effective collision-avoidance action remains possible and the vessel can stop within an appropriate distance. The required speed depends on conditions such as visibility, traffic, manoeuvrability and hazards, rather than a single universal speed limit.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules
references.locator: Rule 6, Safe Speed.

items.explanation: Rule 36 permits directing a searchlight beam toward the danger to attract another vessel’s attention, provided it does not embarrass that vessel. Avoid confusing the signal with a navigation aid or authorized signal. High-intensity intermittent or revolving lights are specifically discouraged by the rule.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules
references.locator: Rule 36, Signals to Attract Attention.

items.explanation: A gnomonic projection sends points from Earth’s centre onto a tangent plane. It is a particular planar projection whose useful navigation property is that great circles appear straight. A tangent plane alone does not uniquely define gnomonic projection; the central projection point is also essential.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 4, Nautical Charts: gnomonic projection.

items.explanation: Zenith distance is the complement of the observed altitude: 90°00′ − 75°11′ = 14°49′. The latitude and declination are unnecessary for that subtraction. The bank appends “South”; the numerical angular distance is 14°49′, while the direction depends on the chosen meridian-diagram convention.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapters 13 and 19, Navigational Astronomy and Sight Reduction: zenith distance from corrected altitude.

items.explanation: Plotting a true bearing from the identified lighthouse supplies one line on which the vessel lies. Additional independent bearings or ranges are needed to establish a fix. Prefer fixed, positively identified charted objects; floating buoys can be displaced and should be used with appropriate caution.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: visual bearings and intersecting lines of position.

items.explanation: The bank specifies every 30 minutes, but pilotage requires intervals short enough to reveal danger before the vessel reaches it. Speed, channel width, nearby hazards and position uncertainty determine that interval, which may be far shorter than half an hour. Treat the keyed interval as this item’s answer, not a universal operating rule.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: selecting position-fixing intervals.

authorNotes: Thirty minutes is the bank interval; actual pilotage fixing intervals must suit the immediate hazards and speed.

items.explanation: The bank keys increasing speed with right full rudder. Right rudder may oppose a bow sheer away from a starboard bank, but increasing speed generally strengthens bank effects. This answer therefore needs ship-specific context and is not a general safe response; restore control using the vessel’s procedures and available sea room.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, section 1018, Effects of Banks, Channels, and Shallow Water: squat, bank cushion, bank suction; effects increase with speed.

authorNotes: The bank manoeuvre is not promoted as generally safe; increasing speed strengthens the documented bank effects.

items.explanation: The bank places the vessel farther from the coast than the plotted running fix. Advancing the first bearing too short a distance can shift its intersection with the second bearing shoreward in the usual passing-object geometry. The amount and direction of error depend on the actual bearings and movement.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, section 1019, Assuming Current Values to Set Safety Margins for Running Fixes, including Figures 1019a–b. Relationship of assumed advance to plotted offshore distance.

items.explanation: Two lines crossing at about 90° give a well-conditioned fix: a small bearing error causes less positional uncertainty than when the lines intersect at a shallow angle. Nearly parallel bearings produce a long, uncertain intersection area and are poor geometry even when the objects are well identified.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: geometry of intersecting lines of position.

items.explanation: Australia follows IALA Region A, where port-hand lateral marks are red and starboard-hand marks green in the conventional direction of buoyage. This contrasts with Region B’s reversed colours. Shape and topmarks provide additional identification, but the charted direction of buoyage must still be checked.

references.title: NOAA/NGA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Appendix 1, IALA buoyage regions.

items.explanation: Take east as positive and use true = compass + deviation + variation. Substitution gives 232° = 235° + deviation + 4°, so deviation = −7°, or 7° west. Checking back, 235° − 7° + 4° returns the given true course of 232°.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: true, magnetic and compass conversion.

items.explanation: Variation 10° west and deviation 6° east combine algebraically to 4° west compass error. Since true = compass + error, compass = 130° − (−4°) = 134°. The opposing corrections partly cancel; adding their magnitudes would give the wrong course.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: combined compass error and course conversion.

items.explanation: The bank selects “Distance maintained but ahead of the charted fix.” On an unchanged coast-parallel track, the vessel maintains its actual offshore distance. Underestimating distance run normally places the running fix too close to the coast; whether the vessel is ahead of that plotted fix also depends on the second bearing.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, section 1019, Assuming Current Values to Set Safety Margins for Running Fixes, including Figures 1019a–b. The keyed along-track statement is not a complete general description of transferred-bearing error.

authorNotes: The bank wording is an along-track description; full running-fix error depends on bearing geometry.

Peer review: The explanation endorses an along-track position ahead of the plotted running fix without knowing whether the second bearing was taken before or after passing abeam. A later caveat does not correct this unsupported geometric assertion.

items.explanation: Using the minimum reasonable speed-over-ground estimate gives a conservative transfer distance when a head current is suspected. In the usual coastal running-fix geometry, assuming too much progress can make the plotted position appear safer offshore than it is. The estimate is for plotting and is not an order to reduce speed.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, section 1019, Assuming Current Values to Set Safety Margins for Running Fixes, including Figures 1019a–b. Relationship of assumed advance to plotted offshore distance.

items.explanation: An aeronautical light is identified by its own chart abbreviation rather than the magenta radar-aid circle intended by this question. Read the complete symbol and legend because magenta is used for several kinds of chart information; colour alone is not enough to identify an aid.

references.title: NOAA/NGA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Sections P and S: aeronautical lights and radar aids.

items.explanation: The heading marker should represent the ship’s fore-and-aft direction, consistent with the heading reference supplied to the radar. Compare it with a known target dead ahead and verify the compass input. A wrong heading input or misaligned scanner can shift displayed bearings even when target echoes look normal.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 23, Radar Navigation: heading-line alignment checks.

items.explanation: AIS repeats information supplied by sensors and entered by operators, so its accuracy is limited by those inputs. Incorrect position, heading or manually entered data can be transmitted convincingly. Compare AIS with radar, visual observations and other navigation information before relying on a target’s reported movement.

references.title: USCG, AIS Frequently Asked Questions
references.locator: AIS data accuracy and information supplied by connected sensors.

items.explanation: A magnetostrictive transducer uses the small dimensional change of suitable material in a magnetic field to produce acoustic vibration. It converts electrical energy into a sound pulse for echo sounding. This is one transducer principle; piezoelectric devices are another, so not every echo sounder is magnetostrictive.

references.title: NASA Technical Reports Server, Magnetostrictive Transducer
references.locator: Technical brief and diagram: magnetostrictive transducer conversion between magnetic excitation and mechanical motion; indexed official NASA document.

items.explanation: Standard atmospheric pressure is 1,013.25 millibars, numerically the same as 1,013.25 hectopascals. It is a reference value, not the pressure that must be observed at sea level on any particular day. Actual pressure rises and falls with weather systems and also decreases with height.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: standard atmospheric pressure and barometer units.

items.explanation: Earth is nearest the Sun at perihelion, which occurs in early January in the present era. The yearly distance change follows Earth’s elliptical orbit. Northern Hemisphere winter still occurs then because the tilt of Earth’s axis, rather than orbital distance, controls the seasonal sunlight pattern.

references.title: USNO, Earth’s Seasons, Equinoxes, Solstices, Perihelion and Aphelion
references.locator: Perihelion dates in the present era.

items.explanation: Region B port-hand marks may be can-shaped, pillar or spar buoys. A can-shaped body or cylindrical topmark identifies the port side in the conventional direction of buoyage. Their colour is green in Region B; the shape convention remains useful when colour is hard to distinguish.

references.title: NOAA/NGA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Appendix 1, IALA Region B port-hand lateral marks.

items.explanation: The bank keys the position ahead of the fix on the track line. A speed underestimate does not establish that result for a running fix: transferring the first bearing too little generally plots the fix shoreward of the vessel. The along-track error depends on whether the second observation is before or after abeam.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, section 1019, Assuming Current Values to Set Safety Margins for Running Fixes, including Figures 1019a–b. The keyed along-track statement is not a complete general description of transferred-bearing error.

authorNotes: The bank wording is an along-track description; full running-fix error depends on bearing geometry.

Peer review: Calling the keyed answer the along-track effect of a speed underestimate falsely suggests that effect always points ahead. For a coastal running fix it can point ahead or behind, depending on the second bearing; the plotted fix also has cross-track error.

items.explanation: The magnetic equator joins points where magnetic inclination, or dip, is zero. There the field is horizontal rather than tilted downward or upward. This line is also called the aclinic line and does not generally coincide exactly with the geographical equator.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary: magnetic equator and aclinic line.

items.explanation: Dip is the angle Earth’s magnetic field makes with the horizontal. A freely suspended magnetic needle would tilt along that field instead of remaining level. Dip concerns vertical inclination; magnetic variation describes the horizontal angle between true north and magnetic north.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary: magnetic dip and inclination.

items.explanation: A falling barometer indicates pressure decreasing at the vessel, consistent with an approaching low-pressure system. Counterclockwise circulation is characteristic of Northern Hemisphere lows. A local wind shift alone does not locate the centre, so combine the trend with forecasts and repeated observations when evaluating the system.

references.title: NOAA JetStream, Origin of Wind
references.locator: Low-pressure circulation and pressure gradients.

items.explanation: Mercator spacing increases toward high latitude. With 4 inches per longitude degree, a spherical calculation gives about 8.12 inches between 60° and 61°; ellipsoidal meridional-parts treatment gives about 8.11 inches, the bank’s result. The calculation concerns expanding latitude spacing, not the fixed spacing between meridians.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 4, Nautical Charts: Mercator meridional parts and latitude expansion.

items.explanation: The receiver measures satellite signal travel times and uses the transmitted orbital data to calculate its position and clock offset. Signals from enough suitably placed satellites allow the position solution to be displayed. The satellites broadcast information; they do not individually send the user a finished position fix.

references.title: USNO, Global Positioning System Overview
references.locator: GPS receiver positioning from satellite signals.

items.explanation: Nearby energized equipment or wiring can create magnetic fields that disturb a magnetic compass. This local effect is deviation, whereas variation arises from Earth’s field at the geographical location. Keep magnetic and electrical equipment at suitable distances and investigate any heading change associated with switching equipment on.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: local magnetic disturbances and deviation.

items.explanation: The bank keys 133°. Using the standard convention, compass = true − variation − deviation = 135° − (−5°) − 3° = 137°. Thus the supplied figures do not produce the keyed result. Keep 133° as the bank answer without treating it as a verified compass conversion.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: sign convention for variation and deviation.

authorNotes: The unchanged bank answer is 133°, while the stated signed corrections calculate 137°.

items.explanation: The vessel runs 17 × 12/60 = 3.4 nautical miles. With relative bearing angles 39° and 67° and a 28° bearing change, the sine rule gives second distance 3.4 × sin 39° / sin 28° ≈ 4.56 miles. This rounds to the bank’s 4.6 nautical miles.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: distance off from two bearings and distance run.

items.explanation: At the December solstice the Sun’s declination is near 23°27′ south in the traditional approximation. An observer at that latitude sees the Sun at the zenith at local apparent noon. Modern obliquity is slightly smaller; use the dated almanac for precise work rather than treating the traditional value as exact.

references.title: USNO, Earth’s Seasons, Equinoxes, Solstices, Perihelion and Aphelion
references.locator: December solstice and solar declination.

items.explanation: Sailing Directions must be maintained using the publisher’s applicable correction notices. The bank describes recording affected pages through the Notice to Mariners correction index. Keep an orderly record so changes can be traced and verified; the exact correction format and update method depend on the issuing hydrographic office.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 6, Nautical Publications: maintaining Sailing Directions and corrections.

items.explanation: Variation connects true north, used for ordinary charted courses, with magnetic north, used for magnetic headings. Apply its stated east or west sign when converting between them. A compass course requires the additional allowance for deviation; variation by itself does not account for the vessel’s magnetic influence.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: true and magnetic directions.

items.explanation: Westerly variation means magnetic north lies west of true north. Looking from magnetic north toward true north therefore requires an eastward turn, which explains the keyed relationship. Keep the reference explicit: the sign describes magnetic north measured from true north, not the other way around.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: east and west magnetic variation.

items.explanation: Passage planning brings hazards, depths, weather, traffic and vessel limits into a workable route before and during the voyage. This supports safe navigation while allowing efficient use of time and fuel. The plan must be monitored and amended when conditions change rather than followed mechanically.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Voyage Planning: appraisal, planning, execution and monitoring.

items.explanation: Radar ranges are generally more precise than radar bearings, so two ranges to clearly identified charted targets can provide a strong fix. Plot an arc from each target and use their intersection, choosing suitable crossing geometry. Target identification and ambiguity must still be checked.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 23, Radar Navigation: position fixing by ranges.

items.explanation: A magnetic compass direction differs from magnetic north through deviation, and magnetic north differs from true north through variation. Both corrections are therefore required to convert compass course to true course. With east positive, true = compass + deviation + variation; retain the signs throughout.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: magnetic compass error.

items.explanation: A magnetic compass needs sufficient horizontal magnetic force for a reliable directional response. That component is generally stronger in low magnetic latitudes and weak near the magnetic poles, explaining the bank’s near-equator answer. Geographic latitude alone is only an approximation because the magnetic and geographic equators differ.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: horizontal magnetic force and high-latitude limitations.

items.explanation: Hard iron can retain magnetization after the magnetizing influence is removed, producing the vessel’s permanent magnetic effects. Soft iron more readily develops induced magnetism in the surrounding field. These different behaviours explain why compass adjustment uses different correctors for permanent and induced deviation.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: hard iron and permanent magnetism.

items.explanation: The bank intends repeated bearings of an identified landmark, with the vessel’s movement between observations used to transfer the first line. Two bearings from different times do not intersect meaningfully until brought to a common time. The ship’s unknown position cannot be established merely by labelling its observation positions as known.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: running fixes using bearings of a known object.

items.explanation: The weather control adjusts how the gyro-pilot responds to short-term yaw in different sea states. A suitable setting balances course keeping against excessive rudder activity. Set it according to the equipment instructions and observed performance; the control does not remove the need to monitor steering.

references.title: IMO, Resolution MSC.64(67), Heading Control Systems
references.locator: Annex 3, paragraphs 3.1 (adaptation to steering characteristics and environmental conditions) and 3.4 (avoid unnecessary rudder activation due to normal yaw). Official URL discovered in published references; full PDF not retrievable through the web tool.

items.explanation: Prismatic error results from optical faces that are not correctly parallel, causing an unwanted deflection of light. It is an inherent instrument defect rather than a routine onboard mirror-alignment adjustment. The navigator uses calibration information or professional servicing instead of trying to remove it with the normal adjustment screws.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 14, section 1411, Non Adjustable Sextant Errors: prismatic error from nonparallel faces of shade glasses and mirrors.

items.explanation: Assuming the question means the Sun, removing Earth’s axial tilt would put the celestial equator in the plane of Earth’s orbit. The Sun would then remain at declination 0° throughout the year. This does not imply that every star’s declination would become zero.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, Navigational Astronomy: obliquity of the ecliptic and solar declination.

authorNotes: Declination refers to the Sun, not to every celestial body.

items.explanation: The bank says the obtained position is closer to the coast. In the usual coastal geometry, underestimating distance run transfers the first bearing too little and can place its intersection shoreward of the true position. This describes an error in the plotted running fix, not an actual change in offshore distance.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, section 1019, Assuming Current Values to Set Safety Margins for Running Fixes, including Figures 1019a–b. Relationship of assumed advance to plotted offshore distance.

items.explanation: Denebola is Beta Leonis, a bright star in Leo and a recognized navigational star. Its name is associated with the lion’s tail, helping distinguish it from Deneb in Cygnus. Accurate identification matters because using the wrong star’s almanac data produces a wrong sight reduction.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, Navigational Astronomy: navigational stars and constellations.

items.explanation: Azimuth gives the direction from the observer toward the celestial body’s geographical position. Zenith distance, equal to 90° minus corrected altitude, gives the angular great-circle separation from it. Each minute of that angular distance corresponds to approximately one nautical mile on Earth.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapters 13 and 19, Navigational Astronomy and Sight Reduction: geographical position, azimuth and zenith distance.

items.explanation: With the sextant index at zero, adjust the horizon glass so the direct and reflected horizon images coincide. This makes the mirrors parallel in the relevant plane and removes index error. Check the other mirror adjustments as well, since changing one setting can affect another.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 14, Instruments for Celestial Navigation; adjustment of sextant index error.

items.explanation: Lines observed at different times must be advanced or retired by the vessel’s estimated movement before they can be combined. Their intersection at a common time is a running fix. Its accuracy therefore depends on both the observations and the assumed course, speed, current and leeway between them.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: advancing lines of position for a running fix.

items.explanation: MMSI identifies the transmitting maritime radio station and is configured as a relatively fixed identity field. It does not change with the vessel’s moment-to-moment movement, so it is static information. Position, speed and course are dynamic information because they are continually updated underway.

references.title: USCG, AIS Frequently Asked Questions
references.locator: AIS identification fields and static/voyage-related reports.

items.explanation: Earth’s magnetic field exerts a torque on the compass magnets, turning them toward the local magnetic meridian. This provides the compass’s directional reference. Nearby shipboard magnetic fields also act on the magnets, which is why deviation must be checked and compensated.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: magnetic directive force.

items.explanation: Like magnetic poles repel and unlike poles attract. These interactions underlie the torque that aligns a compass magnet with an external magnetic field. For navigation, Earth’s field supplies that reference, while local shipboard fields can disturb the final alignment and create deviation.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: magnetic attraction, repulsion and compass magnets.

items.explanation: The composite group (2+1) indicates two flashes followed by one flash, with the complete pattern repeating every 15 seconds. The keyed string also includes 20 m elevation and 10 M nominal range, which the stem does not establish. “Fl” is the standard flashing abbreviation; the bank renders it “F1.”

references.title: NOAA/NGA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section P, Lights: composite group flashing and light descriptions.

authorNotes: Only the flash grouping and period are supplied; elevation and nominal range are extra keyed details.

items.explanation: First match the observed rhythm and colour to the charted light so the object is positively identified. Its corrected bearing supplies a line of position to compare with the existing fix. One bearing alone normally cannot confirm both coordinates; combine it with another independent bearing or range.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 10, Piloting: identifying lights and plotting visual bearings.

items.explanation: Magnetic variation is the angle between true and magnetic north caused by the geometry of Earth’s magnetic field at a location. It differs from deviation, which arises from the vessel’s own magnetic influences. Both may be needed to convert a compass bearing into a true bearing.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: magnetic variation versus deviation.

items.explanation: Earth’s magnetic field gives a magnetic compass its approximate north-south alignment. The indicated direction is magnetic north, which usually differs from geographic north by the local variation. Shipboard magnetism can cause an additional deviation, so the compass does not automatically indicate true north.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: Earth’s field and magnetic north.

items.explanation: Soft-iron spheres counter the induced magnetic effects of horizontal soft iron in the ship. These effects produce quadrantal deviation, which changes with heading and has four principal lobes over a full turn. Their function differs from the permanent magnets used to correct permanent magnetic effects.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: soft-iron spheres and quadrantal deviation.

items.explanation: Compare the known true bearing with the gyro observation: 090° − 087° = +3°. A positive correction is east, so the gyro error is 3° east. Adding that correction to the observed gyro bearing returns the true bearing of the headland.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: gyro error from a known true bearing.

items.explanation: New cyclone information requires reassessment of the route even after approval. Evaluate forecast uncertainty, storm movement, vessel capability and escape room, then adjust the plan to maintain a safe separation. A commercial arrival target does not justify entering dangerous cyclone conditions merely to preserve the schedule.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 41, Weather Routing: tropical cyclone avoidance and revising a voyage plan.

items.explanation: The bank calls the process triangulation. In practical celestial navigation, each corrected sight supplies a line of position, and suitable lines from different bodies intersect to establish a fix. The geometry and observation times matter; two poorly crossing sights may give a weak result even when both bodies are identified correctly.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapters 13 and 19, Navigational Astronomy and Sight Reduction: intersecting celestial lines of position.

items.explanation: Venus orbits closer to the Sun than Earth, so it can pass between Earth and the Sun at inferior conjunction. Mercury can do the same. Outer planets cannot occupy that geometry because their orbits lie beyond Earth’s; they do not have inferior conjunctions as seen from Earth.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 13, Navigational Astronomy: inferior planets and conjunctions.

items.explanation: A Region A port-hand mark may carry one red cylindrical topmark, also called a can. It marks the port side when following the conventional direction of buoyage. The topmark shape supports identification when the buoy’s body is a pillar or spar rather than a can.

references.title: NOAA/NGA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Appendix 1, IALA Region A port-hand lateral marks.

items.explanation: The bank assumes a Doppler log that automatically falls back to water track when a reliable bottom return is unavailable. Water track measures movement relative to a water layer rather than the seabed. This change affects how the speed should be interpreted; automatic switching depends on the installed model.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 25, Doppler Sonar Navigation: bottom-referenced and water-referenced Doppler measurements. Automatic fallback is an equipment assumption, not a universal requirement established by this reference.

authorNotes: Automatic fallback to water track is assumed for the particular Doppler log represented by this item.

items.explanation: Beaufort force 8 is a gale, corresponding to 34–40 knots. At sea it is associated with moderately high waves and breaking crests producing spindrift. The scale links wind speed to typical observable conditions; actual wave heights also depend on fetch and the wind’s duration.

references.title: NWS, Beaufort Scale
references.locator: Beaufort force 8 row: gale, 34–40 knots.

items.explanation: Side error occurs when the horizon glass is not perpendicular to the sextant frame. Adjust its relevant screw to bring the direct and reflected images into proper alignment in that plane. This is distinct from index error, which concerns the mirrors’ parallelism when the instrument is set to zero.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 14, Instruments for Celestial Navigation; sextant side-error adjustment.

items.explanation: Place the EBL through the target and monitor whether its bearing changes as the range decreases. A steady bearing with decreasing range indicates collision risk, subject to the rule’s cautions. Ensure the reference is stable: yaw or a course alteration can make a relative bearing misleading.

references.title: USCG, Amalgamated Navigation Rules
references.locator: Rule 7(d)(i), compass bearing and collision risk.

items.explanation: An isoclinic line connects places with equal magnetic inclination, or dip. It therefore concerns the angle of the field above or below the horizontal. An isogonic line instead connects equal magnetic variation; similar names refer to different components of Earth’s magnetic field.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator, Volume II
references.locator: Glossary: isoclinic line.

items.explanation: Compass adjustment uses correctors to reduce the vessel’s magnetic influence. Swinging the ship on several headings then reveals the residual deviation to record in a table or curve. Calibration does not remove geographical variation; that separate correction must still be applied when converting to true directions.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: adjustment, swinging and residual deviation.

items.explanation: A difference between a compass bearing and a known true bearing is compass error, the combined effect of variation and deviation. The observation alone does not separate those components. Confirm the comparison carefully before assigning a correction sign, since an indication east of true requires a westward correction.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 8, Compasses: total compass error.

items.explanation: A very slow pressure fall within a stationary high is consistent with a gradual weakening of that pressure system. It is a trend to monitor rather than proof of immediate bad weather. Compare successive observations and current weather charts to distinguish weakening from movement of the pressure field.

references.title: NOAA JetStream, Origin of Wind
references.locator: Pressure changes and the strength of high- and low-pressure systems.

items.explanation: Dead reckoning advances a known position using the vessel’s course, speed and elapsed time. It does not include a separate allowance for estimated current or wind effects. Comparing this predicted position with a later fix helps reveal the combined effects of current, leeway and other errors.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 9, Dead Reckoning: advancing a known position by course and speed.

items.explanation: An estimated position adds assessed current and wind or leeway effects to the course-and-speed advance. It is more informed than an uncorrected dead-reckoning position but still depends on estimates. It should not be labelled a fix unless independent observations actually establish the position.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 9, Dead Reckoning: estimated positions and environmental allowances.

items.explanation: The familiar 29.92 inches of mercury is the rounded inch-unit expression of one standard atmosphere, conventionally 1,013.25 millibars. Since 29.92 itself is rounded, direct multiplication gives a slightly different last decimal. The bank uses the standard reference equivalence rather than a precision conversion.

references.title: NGA — The American Practical Navigator, Volume I (2019)
references.locator: Chapter 38, Weather Elements: atmospheric-pressure units and standard atmosphere.

items.explanation: A useful approximate speed of sound in seawater is 1,500 metres per second, equal to 1.5 kilometres per second. Echo sounders use sound travel time to estimate depth. Temperature, salinity and pressure change the actual speed, so precise acoustic work needs an appropriate sound-speed correction.

references.title: NOAA, Surveying and Mapping PEIS
references.locator: Sound propagation: average speed in seawater and environmental variation.

items.explanation: The Flinders bar is a vertical soft-iron corrector for deviation associated with magnetism induced by Earth's vertical field. Its correction changes with magnetic latitude. It does not halve every compass error; quadrantal spheres serve a different correction function.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Magnetic compass adjustment; Flinders bar

items.explanation: Apply east error positively: true heading = 330° + 2° = 332°. With 10°W variation, magnetic heading is 342°. Deviation = magnetic minus compass = 342° − 345° = −3°, so the deviation is 3°W.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compass corrections; east-positive convention

items.explanation: On a spherical Earth, the shorter arc of the great circle through two positions gives their shortest surface distance. A rhumb line instead maintains constant direction, and is generally longer unless it coincides with a meridian or the equator.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Sailings; great circles

items.explanation: A small-scale chart shows a large geographical area because each chart unit represents a large distance on Earth. For example, 1:1,000,000 covers more ground per centimetre than 1:50,000, but provides less detail for close navigation.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Nautical charts; scale

items.explanation: The bank calls the nautical-mile figure printed beside a light its charted range. Read the chart notes and light list to interpret that figure, commonly nominal range on modern charts; actual visibility also depends on weather, light intensity and the observer's horizon.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Aids to navigation; ranges of lights

items.explanation: Mercator is a cylindrical conformal projection. Its meridians and parallels form a rectangular grid, but that appearance does not make “rectangular projection” the appropriate classification here. Increasing latitude spacing allows rhumb lines to plot as straight lines.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Chart projections; Mercator projection

items.explanation: Co denotes coral in the seabed descriptions. The other abbreviations identify different materials: R is rock and Sh is shells, while clay is normally Cy. Bottom descriptions help assess anchoring suitability as well as interpret the charted seabed.

references.title: NOAA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section J; nature of seabed

items.explanation: Sailing Directions provide the regional oceanographic information needed when planning a trans-Pacific passage, including current information in the appropriate Planning Guide. A Coast Pilot concentrates on coastal waters, while a World Port Index primarily supplies port particulars rather than ocean routing guidance.

references.title: NGA, Sailing Directions Planning Guides
references.locator: Planning Guides; ocean-basin information

items.explanation: The keyed 100 m is the older civilian GPS horizontal-accuracy figure associated with Selective Availability. It describes a historical 95% performance expectation, not a present-day universal limit. Actual accuracy depends on the service, receiver, satellite geometry and interference.

references.title: USCG Navigation Center, GPS Frequently Asked Questions
references.locator: Historical GPS Standard Positioning Service accuracy

items.explanation: The bank's DGPS figure is 10 m. A differential reference station compares known coordinates with satellite-derived coordinates and broadcasts corrections for shared errors. This improves positioning, but usable accuracy still depends on correction age, reception, geometry and the particular service.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Satellite navigation; differential GPS

items.explanation: Precession is the change in direction of a spinning gyro's axis when an external torque acts on it. Gyroscopic inertia describes resistance to changing that direction; it is the underlying property, rather than the name of the resulting motion.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Gyrocompasses; precession

items.explanation: A compass supplies a directional reference from which headings, courses and bearings can be expressed. A pelorus measures relative bearings, an azimuth circle assists bearing observations, and a sextant measures angles; these accessories do not independently supply the same heading reference.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Compasses and bearing instruments

items.explanation: The rose gives magnetic variation for a stated year and its annual change, allowing the navigator to update variation to the date of use. Deviation belongs to the individual vessel's magnetic environment and is obtained from its compass records, not the chart.

references.title: NOAA, U.S. Chart No. 1
references.locator: Section B; compass rose and magnetic variation

items.explanation: Standard atmospheric pressure is 760 mm of mercury, equivalent to approximately 29.92 inches of mercury or 1013.25 hPa. The unit in the question matters: 29.92 is correct in inches, but not in millimetres.

references.title: NOAA, Air Pressure
references.locator: Standard sea-level pressure and units

items.explanation: Switch to hand steering first to regain direct control and arrest the uncommanded turn. Monitor the vessel's response and heading immediately. Calling the Master and investigating the gyro-pilot follow, while emergency steering is used if normal steering control cannot be restored.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Steering control; automatic-pilot failure

items.explanation: Using the conventional latitudes in this question, the Arctic Circle is 66°33′N and the Tropic of Cancer is 23°27′N. Their separation is 66°33′ − 23°27′ = 43°06′, not the keyed 44°06′N; the Arctic Circle is farther north.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Earth coordinates; tropics and polar circles

items.explanation: An international nautical mile is exactly 1852 metres, approximately 6076.12 feet. Thus 6076 feet is the suitable rounded choice. The 5280-foot figure belongs to the statute mile, while 1850 metres is only a rough approximation.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigational units; nautical mile

items.explanation: The reference to the Sun's centre reaching 12° below the horizon identifies nautical twilight. Strictly, evening nautical twilight is the interval from 6° to 12° below the horizon; the stem uses the broader sunset-to-nautical-twilight-end convention found in some navigation questions.

references.title: USNO, Rise, Set, and Twilight Definitions
references.locator: Nautical twilight; dark limit at 12 degrees

items.explanation: Zone descriptions +4 and +5 have central meridians 60°W and 75°W. Their standard boundary lies halfway between them, at 67°30′W. Nautical zone descriptions are positive west, the opposite sign to many civil UTC-offset notations.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Time; nautical zone descriptions

items.explanation: The bank excludes aligning peloruses with the fore-and-aft line, but the wording is problematic: a relative-bearing pelorus needs that alignment. Compass north should follow the reference meridian, while the lubber line follows the ship. Synchronization and physical-condition checks remain necessary.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Bearing instruments; pelorus alignment and compass lubber line

items.explanation: Diffraction lets wave energy bend around an edge or spread into the region behind an obstruction. Refraction instead changes a wave's direction as propagation speed changes between media or atmospheric layers; attenuation describes loss of strength.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Radio and radar wave propagation; diffraction

items.explanation: Sailing Directions are chiefly descriptive text about coasts, approaches and regional conditions. Almanacs and sight-reduction publications chiefly supply numerical tables, while Light Lists arrange aid particulars in tabular form. That distinction makes Sailing Directions the exception among these choices.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigational publications; texts and tables

items.explanation: An East Cardinal mark has black above and below a yellow middle band: black–yellow–black from top to bottom. The keyed wording places the yellow between the black sections; reversing those colours describes a West Cardinal instead.

references.title: IALA Recommendation R1001, Maritime Buoyage System
references.locator: Cardinal marks; East Cardinal colours

items.explanation: The bank selects the navigation officer, who commonly prepares and maintains the voyage plan as an assigned duty. The Master nevertheless retains overall responsibility and must approve the plan before the voyage. Read the keyed answer as preparation responsibility, rather than final command accountability.

references.title: IMO Resolution A.893(21), Guidelines for Voyage Planning
references.locator: Section 3.4; Master's approval of the voyage plan

items.explanation: The intended choice is 1°, despite the stray word “draft.” Polaris lies close to the north celestial pole, making its altitude useful for finding latitude after correction. “Always” is an approximation for the navigational era, since precession changes the pole's position over centuries.

references.title: USNO, Navigational Star Chart
references.locator: Polaris and the north celestial pole

items.explanation: The bank's conservative touchdown guideline is 0.10 knot for a ULCC. A massive vessel retains substantial momentum even at very low speed, so contact must be closely controlled. The actual permissible approach speed depends on displacement, fenders, berth limits and conditions.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Shiphandling; berthing momentum

items.explanation: The intended course is 001°T, matching the charted inbound range direction. Being on the range is actually established by the two marks lining up. Wind or current may require a different heading to maintain a 001° ground track.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Piloting; ranges and leading lines

items.explanation: A nautical zone description of −1 corresponds to the zone centred on 15°E. Each hour represents 15° of longitude; the 7½° choices are zone boundaries, not its standard meridian. Negative nautical zone descriptions apply east of Greenwich.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Time; zone descriptions and standard meridians

items.explanation: One astronomical unit represents the scale of the mean Earth–Sun distance, about 149.6 million kilometres. The modern au is a fixed defined length. A parsec and a light-year describe far larger stellar distances, so neither suits this solar-system distance.

references.title: USNO, Astronomical Almanac Glossary
references.locator: Astronomical unit

items.explanation: On a conventional micrometer sextant, one full drum revolution advances the reading by 60 minutes of arc, or 1°. The drum provides the minute subdivision within each degree, while the main arc and index arm indicate the degree reading.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Sextants; micrometer drum

items.explanation: The 1° choice expresses Polaris's approximate closeness to the north celestial pole in modern navigation. It is not exactly at the pole, so precise latitude work uses the appropriate Polaris corrections rather than treating every measured altitude as latitude without adjustment.

references.title: USNO, Navigational Star Chart
references.locator: Polaris and the north celestial pole

items.explanation: The keyed maximum is 0.10 knot at contact. This small speed reflects the enormous mass of a ULCC and the energy its berth must absorb. Treat it as the question's general guideline; the vessel's manoeuvring plan and berth criteria determine operational limits.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Shiphandling; berthing momentum

items.explanation: 001°T is the charted range direction and the intended answer. A vessel is on range when the leading marks align vertically, rather than merely because its compass shows that course. Current or leeway can require a compensating heading while the marks stay aligned.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Piloting; ranges and leading lines

items.explanation: The standard meridian is 15°E: 1 hour of zone difference corresponds to 15° longitude. Under nautical notation, an eastern zone has a negative zone description. The 7½°E meridian marks a boundary of the zone, not its centre.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Time; zone descriptions and standard meridians

items.explanation: The expected unit is 1 astronomical unit, approximately 149.6 million km. It is based on the scale of Earth's orbit around the Sun, whereas light-years and parsecs are much larger distances used for stars and other objects beyond the solar system.

references.title: USNO, Astronomical Almanac Glossary
references.locator: Astronomical unit

items.explanation: A complete revolution covers 60′, equal to 1°. Individual graduations on the drum permit minute readings, with finer interpolation where provided. Confusing a single drum division with a complete revolution would lead to the 1-minute distractor.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Sextants; micrometer drum

items.explanation: The keyed 12 miles per second is approximately 19 km/s, the traditional description of solar motion toward the solar apex near Vega relative to nearby stars. It is not the Sun's much faster orbital speed around the Galactic centre.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Celestial bodies; solar motion

items.explanation: 100 metres is the historical 95% civilian GPS accuracy figure used by this bank. It comes from the Selective Availability era and should not be treated as the expected performance of every modern receiver. Current service specifications and local reception conditions govern actual accuracy.

references.title: USCG Navigation Center, GPS Frequently Asked Questions
references.locator: Historical GPS Standard Positioning Service accuracy

items.explanation: One hectopascal equals 100 pascals, exactly the same pressure as 1 millibar. Consequently a chart reading of 1013 hPa has the same numerical value in millibars; the “hecto” prefix does not mean 100 millibars.

references.title: NOAA, Air Pressure
references.locator: Pressure units; hectopascals and millibars

items.explanation: The intended value is 1013.25 millibars, equivalently 1013.25 hPa. The option's words “of mercury” are misplaced: millibars are pressure units, whereas inches or millimetres of mercury express pressure as the height of a mercury column.

references.title: NOAA, Air Pressure

items.explanation: The bank selects a 10-knot wind. For equal exposed areas and comparable drag coefficients, force varies approximately with fluid density times speed squared. items.explanation: A sidereal day is about 23 h 56 min 4 s, approximately 3 min 56 s shorter than a mean solar day. Earth advances along its orbit each day, requiring a little additional rotation for the Sun to return to the meridian.

items.explanation: At perihelion Earth is closest to the Sun, so the Sun's apparent diameter is largest, approximately 32.6′. Its semidiameter is half of that, about 16.3′. The question asks for the full visible diameter, not the limb-to-centre correction.

items.explanation: Polar distance is angular distance measured from a specified celestial pole along an hour circle. A body at the opposite pole is 180° away, the maximum. The 90° limit applies to declination measured north or south from the celestial equator.

items.explanation: Apparent wind is the air's velocity relative to the moving vessel. If true wind blows from astern at exactly the vessel's speed, air and vessel move together and their relative velocity is zero. Doubling the wind speed would leave a following apparent wind.

items.explanation: The keyed scope is 1½–2 times water depth, intended to let the offshore anchor assist control during the manoeuvre. This is a docking technique, distinct from the longer scope used for secure anchoring. Bottom, depth, equipment and the planned manoeuvre determine safe use.

items.explanation: The bank selects an increase exceeding 2 m in mean draft. High-speed flow in shallow or restricted water can produce substantial sinkage and trim, but there is no universal 2 m threshold. Estimate the vessel's squat for its speed and channel before assessing under-keel clearance.

items.explanation: The incomplete keyed choice means prescribed lights must also be displayed during daylight in restricted visibility. Rule 20 requires lights from sunset to sunrise in all weathers, and extends their display to daytime restricted visibility; absence of nearby vessels does not remove that duty.

items.explanation: The bank calls for recording water density. Fresh and brackish water provide less buoyancy per unit volume than seawater, so a vessel draws more at the same displacement. Density is needed when evaluating draft, freshwater allowance and loading compliance before departure.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Ship stability and loading; water density and draft

items.explanation: Speed over ground is the vessel's instantaneous speed relative to Earth. It combines motion through the water with current and other drift effects. Speed through the water can therefore differ from it even while engine settings and heading remain steady.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Navigation terminology; speed over ground

items.explanation: Squat is the speed-related bodily sinkage and trim change of a vessel, especially in shallow or confined water. The relevant increase is the draft at the lowest part of the hull, because that point governs remaining under-keel clearance.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Shiphandling; squat and under-keel clearance

items.explanation: Slack water minimizes tidal-current flow, making it easier to control a boat's movement into a slip. High or low water does not necessarily coincide with slack current. Wind, local eddies and berth geometry must still be considered when choosing the manoeuvre time.

items.explanation: A free gyroscope has a spinning rotor mounted so its axis can turn about two additional mutually perpendicular axes. This allows the spin axis to retain its orientation in space within practical limits; a north-seeking compass adds control and damping to that free gyro.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator

items.explanation: GHA Aries is measured westward from the Greenwich celestial meridian to the hour circle through the First Point of Aries. SHA uses Aries as its reference for other bodies, while right ascension is measured eastward; the Greenwich reference identifies GHA here.

items.explanation: Binnacle magnets compensate for magnetic effects of the vessel, reducing deviation. Variation is the angle between true and magnetic north produced by Earth's magnetic field, so shipboard corrector magnets do not remove the charted geographical variation.

items.explanation: The bank identifies the mature stage, when the cyclone has developed its full circulation and further pressure changes need not produce a corresponding increase in maximum wind. references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Tropical cyclones; stages of development

items.explanation: Damping suppresses the oscillation of a gravity-controlled gyro about the meridian so it settles as a usable compass. Gravity control supplies the north-seeking behaviour; damping makes that behaviour stable. Precession is the gyro's response to torque rather than the settling process itself.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator
references.locator: Gyrocompasses; damping

items.explanation: Different periods can distinguish nearby groups of cardinal marks while retaining each mark's prescribed directional rhythm. items.explanation: Eastbound passages from Japan toward Seattle can benefit from the Kuroshio Extension and eastward North Pacific Current. references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator

items.explanation: Slack water reduces the river's tidal flow, easing control when docking without tug assistance. items.explanation: Four independent satellite pseudoranges are normally needed to solve three position coordinates plus receiver-clock error. That yields a three-dimensional GPS fix including altitude. The question calls them position lines, but satellite measurements are range constraints rather than conventional charted bearing lines.

references.title: NGA, The American Practical Navigator

items.explanation: The relieving helmsman needs the ordered course on the magnetic steering compass so steering continues without ambiguity. The course and any standing steering instructions should be clearly passed and acknowledged. Variation and gyro error inform navigation calculations, but do not substitute for knowing the course to steer.
